title: Compilation, main, and the toolchain
body: Rust source is checked and compiled before it runs. A binary starts at fn main(); statements execute in order, and println! formats text followed by a newline. A compiler diagnostic describes a rejected program, while a runtime error happens after compilation.

Cargo manages a package: cargo new starts one, cargo check checks types without producing the final executable, cargo run builds and runs, and cargo test runs tests. A package can contain library and binary crates. This lesson is a single file so it can go straight into the Lab.

This guide targets Rust 1.99.0 with edition 2024. A compiler version and an edition are different: editions select compatibility rules inside Cargo.toml; upgrading rustc does not automatically change a crate’s edition. Run rustc --version and inspect edition before comparing examples.
challenge: Print two lines: your learning language, then the result of 8 * 8.
question: What does cargo check primarily do?
correct: Check compilation without building the final executable
wrong: Run the program’s main function
Change the package’s edition automatically
reasoning: Type checking precedes execution. check is a quick feedback loop; run is needed to observe stdout.

title: Bindings, mutability, and shadowing
body: A let binding is immutable unless written let mut. Mutability applies to that binding’s access to a value; it is not permission to ignore borrowing rules. Assigning to an immutable binding is rejected.
Shadowing creates a new binding with the same spelling. Its type can differ from the old one, which is useful when parsing text into a number. Assignment to a mut binding keeps the same type.

const declares a compile-time value with an explicit type; static declares storage with program lifetime. Prefer a constant for a reusable numerical parameter, and a local let for a value computed from input.
challenge: Shadow the text "20" with a parsed i32, then double a mutable total.
question: Which can change a name’s type?
correct: A new shadowing let binding
wrong: Assignment to the same mut binding
Adding mut to an existing value at runtime
reasoning: The parse produces a new i32 binding. += and *= update that binding without changing its type.

title: Numeric types and deliberate overflow
body: Rust distinguishes signed integers, unsigned integers, floating-point values, bool and char. usize is sized for the target’s pointer width and commonly indexes collections; it is not a portable substitute for a fixed-width serialized number.

Integer arithmetic can overflow. Ordinary arithmetic depends on overflow checking settings; do not make correctness depend on debug versus release behavior. checked_add returns Option, wrapping_add performs modular arithmetic, and saturating_add clamps at the boundary.

An as cast can truncate or reinterpret an integer conversion. TryFrom/TryInto report out-of-range conversions. State the valid range at an input boundary and use a checked conversion where loss would corrupt meaning.
challenge: Compare the same operations on 255u8 + 1 and explain the three outcomes.
question: Which operation reports overflow as a value?
correct: checked_add
wrong: wrapping_add
An unchecked as cast
reasoning: checked_add returns None when the result is outside u8. Wrapping reduces modulo 256; saturation keeps 255.

title: Tuples, arrays, and indexing
body: A tuple groups a fixed number of potentially different types; a tuple pattern extracts its fields. An array [T; N] stores N elements of one type, and its length is part of its type.
Indexing an array or slice panics if the index is outside its length. get returns Option instead, which makes an untrusted index an ordinary branch in the program.
A Vec can grow, but an array’s length is fixed. Choose an array for a fixed-size vector or protocol field; choose a tuple for a small heterogeneous result whose positions have clear meaning.
challenge: Read the second item using get, then query an absent fourth item.
question: How can you handle an unknown index without an indexing panic?
correct: Use get and handle Option
wrong: Assume all usize indexes are valid
Change the array’s length through indexing
reasoning: The zero-based index 1 exists; 3 does not. get represents both possibilities in its return type.

title: Expressions, branches, and loops
body: An expression produces a value. if can produce a value when its branches agree on a type, and a block evaluates to its final expression without a semicolon. A trailing semicolon usually changes that result to unit ().
loop can return a value through break value. while repeats while a Boolean is true; for works through IntoIterator. A range a..b excludes b, while a..=b includes it.

Use labels to break or continue a particular enclosing loop. Prefer for over manual indexing when the program needs elements rather than index arithmetic; it also makes the iteration boundary visible.
challenge: Sum 1 through 5 inclusively using for.
question: Which range includes 5?
reasoning: The inclusive boundary adds the fifth value. The exclusive range stops before its upper bound.

title: Functions and explicit interfaces
body: Function parameters have explicit types, and -> names the return type. Returning the last expression is idiomatic; return is useful for an early exit. A block’s semicolon is therefore part of the function’s meaning.

Pass the smallest information a function needs. A pure calculation with inputs and an output is easier to test than a function that mutates hidden global state. Side effects still matter, but put them at a clear boundary.

Functions are items and can be called before their textual definition. A function pointer such as fn(i32) -> i32 describes a callable with a fixed signature; closures have additional captured state and distinct types.
challenge: Write a function that returns the larger of two i32 values and call it on 9 and 4.
question: What does an expression-ending semicolon usually return from a block?
correct: Unit ()
wrong: The preceding expression’s unchanged value
An automatically inferred Result
reasoning: n * n is the return expression of square; n * n; would produce unit in that body.

title: Moves, Copy, and Clone
body: A value has an owner responsible for its lifetime. Moving an owned String transfers responsibility to the destination binding; the old binding can no longer be used. This prevents two independent owners from freeing the same buffer.

Copy types are implicitly duplicated on assignment, such as ordinary integer values. Clone requests an explicit duplication whose cost depends on the type: cloning a String copies its allocation, while cloning an Rc increments a count.

A function argument can take ownership, borrow, or borrow mutably. Read the signature to predict which caller values remain available afterward. A return value can transfer ownership back; you do not need a global owner.
challenge: Move a String into a function that returns its uppercase owned replacement.
question: After moving a String, what can you do with the old binding?
correct: Use it only after assigning a new valid value
wrong: Continue using its former buffer
Assume it was implicitly deep-copied
reasoning: The owner moved; backup is separately cloned. Reinitialization can give a moved binding a new value.

title: Shared and exclusive borrowing
body: A reference borrows a value without becoming its owner. &T permits shared access; &mut T permits exclusive access. While an exclusive borrow is in use, overlapping access to that location is restricted.

Non-lexical lifetimes allow many borrows to end after their last use, before the end of the block. The rule concerns actual loan usage, not merely the spelling of a scope. The compiler still rejects aliases used concurrently with an exclusive borrow.

For a read-only API, a borrowed slice or str is often more flexible than &Vec or &String. A mutable slice gives permission to update existing elements without exposing resizing or the whole container.
challenge: Write an in-place function that doubles every element in a mutable slice.
question: Why can the mutation follow the shared reference in the example?
correct: The shared borrow’s last use has ended
wrong: String disables alias checks
Mutable references are always Copy
reasoning: view is last used in the first println!. Each mutable slice element then has exclusive access for its update.

title: UTF-8, String, str, and characters
body: String owns a growable UTF-8 buffer; str is a dynamically sized text view commonly used behind &str. A char is a Unicode scalar value, not an arbitrary byte and not necessarily a user-perceived character.

len on String or str counts bytes. chars iterates scalar values; bytes iterates encoded bytes. Grapheme clusters can contain multiple scalars, so a cursor-oriented editor needs a Unicode segmentation policy beyond chars.

String slices require UTF-8 boundaries and a valid range. get on a range returns None when the range is invalid. Never use an arbitrary byte offset from untrusted input as though it were a character index.
challenge: Count bytes and scalar values in "aé", then safely get the é substring.
question: What does str::len count?
correct: UTF-8 bytes
wrong: Grapheme clusters
Unicode scalar values
reasoning: é occupies two UTF-8 bytes. The range 1..3 in aé includes both of them and starts at a valid boundary.

title: Slices, split borrows, and windows
body: A slice is a view of contiguous elements with a runtime length. &[T] and &mut [T] borrow storage owned elsewhere; slicing does not copy the underlying values. Reallocation of an owner cannot happen while a slice into it is still used.

split_at_mut proves that two output slices are disjoint. It lets safe code mutate separate ranges without constructing overlapping mutable references. For fixed neighborhoods, windows returns overlapping shared views; chunks divides a slice into groups.

A view’s lifetime is tied to the source. A function cannot return a slice into a local vector that will be destroyed. Return the owned vector, borrow an input, or let the caller provide storage instead.
challenge: Produce sums for every adjacent pair in [1, 2, 3, 4] using windows.
question: Why is split_at_mut useful?
correct: It safely produces two disjoint mutable slices
wrong: It copies all elements into new allocations
It extends storage to program lifetime
reasoning: The split boundary separates the two ranges; mutation cannot overlap through those views.

title: Structs, methods, and encapsulation
body: A struct names a product of fields. Associated functions belong to the type; methods take self, &self or &mut self to state ownership/access. Choose the receiver from the operation’s needs.

Private fields let a module maintain invariants. A public constructor can reject invalid data before a value is created; callers then use methods that preserve that condition. Public fields shift that responsibility to every caller.

Tuple structs provide a distinct type with positional fields, useful for newtypes such as UserId rather than interchangeable integers. Deriving Debug helps inspection; a derived trait is generated code with the trait’s own constraints.
challenge: Add a reset method and show increment followed by reset.
question: Which receiver fits an operation that updates an existing value?
correct: &mut self
wrong: &self without interior mutability
No receiver for every operation
reasoning: increment and reset change the existing counter; value only reads it.

title: Enums and exhaustive matching
body: An enum describes alternatives, and each variant may carry different data. A message is either one variant or another; unlike a struct of optional fields, the type can exclude combinations that make no sense.

match analyzes a value and must cover all cases. Adding a variant makes missing cases visible at compilation, unless a catch-all deliberately absorbs them. if let is concise for one interesting case; let else gives an early exit for a failed pattern.

Pattern matching can bind, borrow, destructure and guard values. A guard adds a runtime condition; it does not generally prove type-level exhaustiveness. Keep a catch-all when guarded alternatives leave possibilities.
challenge: Model an event with Add(i32) and Reset; fold [Add(3), Add(4), Reset, Add(2)].
question: Why use an enum for mutually exclusive message shapes?
correct: It encodes which combinations are valid
wrong: Every variant occupies separate live storage
It avoids type checking
reasoning: Each event carries only the data its operation needs. Reset cannot accidentally require an Add payload.

title: Option and absence without sentinel values
body: Option<T> has Some(T) and None. It makes absence visible in the type instead of reserving an ordinary value such as -1 or an empty string. A caller must decide what absence means.

map transforms a present value; and_then chains a function that can itself return None. unwrap_or provides an eager fallback; unwrap_or_else computes a fallback only when needed. unwrap panics on None and needs a justified invariant.

Borrowing methods as_ref and as_mut let you inspect or modify the inside without moving it out of its owner. take replaces an Option with None and returns the old value, which is useful for transferring a resource exactly once.
challenge: Use take to consume a pending message once, then show it is absent.
question: What does Option::take leave behind?
correct: None
wrong: A clone of the payload
A dangling reference
reasoning: take transfers the old Some value and empties the slot; a later consumer sees None.

title: Result, ?, and error propagation
body: Result<T, E> represents success or a typed failure. Match when recovery is local; use ? when the caller should decide. ? returns early on Err and converts compatible error types through From.
map transforms success, map_err transforms failure, and and_then chains another fallible step. Give errors enough context to identify the boundary that failed without discarding the original cause.

Use Result for expected failures such as invalid input or missing files. panic expresses a failed invariant or unrecoverable policy, not an ordinary parser branch. A library should avoid surprising callers by panicking for routine input errors.
challenge: Parse two values with ? and return their sum. Demonstrate valid and invalid input.
question: What does ? do to an Err in a Result-returning function?
correct: Return it early, converting the error when needed
wrong: Panic unconditionally
Replace it with a default success
reasoning: The second parse is reached only if the first succeeds. The caller observes failure as a value.

title: Vec growth, retention, and iteration
body: Vec<T> owns contiguous storage with a length and capacity. Length counts initialized elements; capacity describes allocated space. Pushing may reallocate, which explains why a live reference into a vector restricts mutation of its owner.
iter borrows elements, iter_mut borrows them exclusively, and into_iter consumes a vector. Choose the iteration mode deliberately; it determines what happens to the collection afterward.

retain removes elements failing a predicate, and drain transfers a range out while borrowing the vector. Reserve for a justified expected size; do not treat a guessed capacity as initialized storage or access beyond length.
challenge: Borrow every retained element mutably and multiply it by ten.
question: Which iteration mode consumes an owned Vec?
correct: into_iter
wrong: iter
iter_mut
reasoning: Borrowing iteration leaves the vector owned by the caller; consuming iteration transfers its elements.

title: HashMap entries and ordered alternatives
body: HashMap stores key/value associations with hash-based lookup. Keys need Eq and Hash with consistent behavior. Never assume iteration order; use BTreeMap or explicitly sort when deterministic order matters.
entry combines a lookup with conditional insertion. or_insert supplies a default and returns mutable access to the value, so a frequency counter avoids separate contains/get/insert branches.

Lookup can often borrow a compatible key representation, such as &str for a String key. Values and keys still have owners. Holding a mutable entry access restricts other overlapping access to that map.
challenge: Count the same words with a BTreeMap and print the ordered map.
question: Which standard map maintains sorted key order?
correct: BTreeMap
wrong: HashMap
Every map has identical iteration order
reasoning: The ordered tree returns learn before rust; the hash map does not promise that order.

title: Traits, defaults, and generic bounds
body: A trait specifies behavior that implementing types provide. A default method can compose required methods, allowing shared behavior without sharing a representation. A generic bound states the capabilities needed by a function.

impl Trait in an argument is a concise generic parameter; a named T is useful when several parameters must have the same type. Return-position impl Trait hides one concrete type chosen by the implementation; it does not mean any unrelated type can be returned per branch.

Trait implementations must satisfy coherence rules. You can implement your own trait for a foreign type or a foreign trait for an appropriate local type. A newtype gives a local wrapper when you need custom behavior around an external representation.
challenge: Write a generic function accepting any Named value by shared reference.
question: What does a generic trait bound specify?
correct: Capabilities the implementation may rely on
wrong: The value’s exact runtime memory address
An automatic heap allocation
reasoning: T: Named guarantees name is callable. It does not force dynamic dispatch or heap storage.

title: Lifetime relationships and elision
body: A lifetime annotation describes relationships between borrowed values; it does not lengthen storage duration. When a return reference might come from either input, the signature must express the shared usable lifetime.
Elision rules cover many common signatures, especially a single input reference or a method receiver. Explicit annotations are useful when those rules cannot identify the source of an output borrow.

A struct holding a reference needs a lifetime parameter tied to the referent. An owned String field avoids that relationship at the cost of owning storage. Choose based on whether the value is a temporary view or independent data.
challenge: Define a borrowed Label struct and return its text from a method.
question: Do lifetime annotations keep an expired local alive?
correct: No; they constrain valid borrow relationships
wrong: Yes, by extending the stack frame
Yes, by implicitly cloning it
reasoning: longer can return either input, so the output cannot be used beyond the lifetime accepted for both.

title: Associated types, GATs, and iterator contracts
body: An associated type is selected by a trait implementation, rather than independently selected at each use. Iterator::Item is the element type chosen by that iterator. Bounds such as Iterator<Item = i32> constrain it.

A generic associated type can vary with parameters such as a borrow lifetime. This permits lending interfaces whose returned item borrows from the current receiver. Constraints such as where Self: 'a make the required lifetime relation explicit.

A trait generic parameter and an associated type solve different problems. A type can sometimes implement a generic trait for several argument types; each non-generic trait implementation chooses its associated type once.
challenge: Sum the custom countdown from 4 using Iterator::sum.
question: Who chooses Iterator::Item?
correct: The Iterator implementation
wrong: Each call to next chooses an unrelated type
The operating system at runtime
reasoning: Countdown fixes Item to u32. collect and sum build on the same next contract.

title: Trait objects and dynamic dispatch
body: A dyn Trait value erases the concrete implementing type behind a pointer. Dynamic dispatch calls through trait metadata, letting a collection hold different concrete implementations of one contract.

Generic dispatch can specialize machine code for each concrete type. Dynamic dispatch trades that specialization for runtime heterogeneity and an indirect call. Box<dyn Trait> owns an erased value; &dyn Trait borrows one.

Only dyn-compatible traits can form trait objects. Generic methods and some uses of Self need special treatment, often a Self: Sized bound excluding those methods from the object interface. Check the trait contract before choosing an erased API.
challenge: Add a second implementation that always returns 20 and place both types in the collection.
question: Why use a trait object collection?
correct: To hold different concrete implementations of one interface
wrong: To bypass the borrow checker
To make every trait automatically dyn-compatible
reasoning: The vector’s element type is one pointer type even though Number and Fixed have different representations.

title: Const generics and fixed-size APIs
body: Const generics parameterize a type or function by compile-time values. [T; N] uses a length value in its type, so a function can preserve array length without accepting every input as a runtime slice.

Stable const-generic expressions have restrictions. A parameter N can appear as an array length, but arbitrary type-level arithmetic involving generic parameters is not generally available on stable Rust. Do not silently introduce nightly feature gates into a stable lesson.

Use a slice when runtime-sized inputs are natural and a const generic when size is a useful compile-time invariant. A fixed dimension is not automatically faster; measure the actual algorithm and generated code.
challenge: Write a const-generic function that returns an array’s length.
question: What information does [T; N] carry in its type?
correct: The element type and compile-time length
wrong: Only a runtime pointer
An arbitrary growable capacity
reasoning: Each invocation infers N from its array. This preserves length information at the API boundary.

title: Closures and capture contracts
body: A closure combines behavior with captured environment. Capture mode follows how the body uses a value; move requests ownership of captures. move does not by itself imply the closure is callable only once.

FnOnce permits consuming captured state, FnMut permits mutating it, and Fn permits repeated calls through shared access. A closure can implement several of these traits; APIs should request the weakest contract their algorithm needs.
A closure returning a reference still has lifetime constraints. Capturing owned state is useful for a spawned task, but state must also meet that task’s thread/lifetime requirements.
challenge: Create a move closure that consumes a captured String exactly once and returns its byte length.
question: Which contract permits consuming a captured value?
correct: FnOnce
wrong: Only Fn
Only a plain function pointer
reasoning: add mutates its environment and is FnMut; consume moves its String out and is callable once.

title: Lazy iterators and fallible collection
body: Iterator adapters are lazy: map, filter and take describe work that a consumer drives. collect, fold, sum and for consume the sequence. Creating an adapter without consuming it does not perform all its transformations.
Collecting Iterator<Item = Result<T, E>> into Result<Vec<T>, E> stops at the first error. This composes parsing while preserving failure instead of silently throwing away bad records with filter_map.

Iterator chains can avoid intermediate collections, but order and side effects remain significant. Use clear loops when early control flow is clearer than a chain, and benchmark rather than assuming either style is faster.
challenge: Parse ["1", "2", "x"] into Result<Vec<i32>, _> and report failure.
question: When does map normally execute its transformation?
correct: As the iterator is consumed
wrong: Eagerly for every item when constructed
Only when the compiler optimizes
reasoning: collect drives the chain. Result collection propagates the first parse failure.

title: Box, recursive data, and dereferencing
body: Box<T> owns a heap allocation and releases it when dropped. Moving a Box moves the owning pointer rather than ordinarily relocating its allocated payload. Heap storage is useful for large or recursive values, but it does not remove type or lifetime checks.
A directly recursive enum has no finite size when a variant embeds the same enum without indirection. Box provides a fixed-size indirection so each node contains a pointer to the next node.

Deref lets pointer-like types expose borrowed access to a target. Implementing Deref is an API choice: use it for transparent pointer behavior, not as a substitute for every conversion or inheritance relationship.
challenge: Compute the node count without consuming the boxed list.
question: Why does Box make a recursive enum representable?
correct: It introduces fixed-size indirection
wrong: It makes the entire recursive value Copy
It disables destructor execution
reasoning: A node stores a Box pointer rather than embedding an unbounded chain directly.

title: Rc, Weak, and ownership cycles
body: Rc<T> shares ownership inside one thread. Cloning an Rc increments its strong count rather than deep-cloning T. The payload is dropped when no strong owners remain.
Weak<T> is a non-owning link that can be upgraded to Option<Rc<T>>. It may fail after the last strong owner disappears. Use weak parent/back links to avoid strong cycles in graphs.

Rust’s memory safety does not guarantee freedom from leaks: Rc cycles can keep resources alive forever. Draw the owning edges and explain which external owner releases the final strong reference; use Arc for corresponding cross-thread ownership.
challenge: Clone the strong owner, drop the original, then drop the clone and observe the weak link.
question: Can safe Rust leak through a strong Rc cycle?
correct: Yes; memory safety does not prevent ownership cycles
wrong: No; all graphs are automatically collected
Only if every link is Weak
reasoning: Weak does not keep the payload alive. The remaining clone does, until it too is dropped.

title: Cell and RefCell: controlled interior mutation
body: Interior mutability allows mutation through a shared reference using a type that enforces an appropriate policy. Cell moves/copies values without handing out ordinary references to its interior. RefCell tracks borrowing at runtime.

RefCell::borrow allows shared loans, and borrow_mut requests an exclusive one. Violations panic; try_borrow and try_borrow_mut report failure instead. Runtime checking replaces a particular static check, not the overall aliasing contract.

Rc<RefCell<T>> is a common single-threaded shared mutable model. It still needs a cycle policy. For threads, choose synchronized primitives such as Mutex; neither Rc nor RefCell is a general cross-thread replacement.
challenge: Use Cell to increase a shared counter twice.
question: What happens to try_borrow_mut while a shared RefCell loan remains?
correct: It returns an error
wrong: It silently aliases a mutable reference
It waits for another OS thread
reasoning: Dropping read ends the shared loan, allowing the following exclusive update.

title: Drop, RAII, and resource boundaries
body: Drop runs cleanup when an owned value is destroyed. This is the basis of resource acquisition is initialization: an owner can manage a file, lock guard, buffer, or subscription. Cleanup should be tied to an explicit lifetime.

std::mem::drop consumes a value and ends ownership early. You do not call its Drop::drop method directly. Local owners are generally destroyed in reverse declaration order, while moving a value transfers the eventual cleanup responsibility.

Destructors are not guaranteed in all circumstances: process abort, intentional forget, leaks and cycles can prevent cleanup. A protocol requiring external confirmation cannot rely solely on Drop; expose an explicit close/commit operation when errors matter.
challenge: Put a guard in an inner scope and print before and after that scope.
question: What does std::mem::drop do?
correct: Consume the owner so cleanup can happen now
wrong: Guarantee all cyclic graphs are freed
Return a reference to the destroyed value
reasoning: a is consumed before work; b stays owned until the end of main.

title: Modules, visibility, and API boundaries
body: Modules organize names and privacy inside a crate. pub exposes an item to allowed external callers; pub(crate) limits it to the crate. use brings a path into scope, and pub use can present a chosen public facade.

crate starts at the current crate root, super refers to the parent module, and self refers to the current one. Separate files are a source organization convention; a module is not itself a separately linked package.
Design visibility from invariants: keep fields and implementation details private, expose operations that preserve valid states, and avoid unintentionally committing helper types to your public API.
challenge: Re-export the public function at the crate root and call the shorter path.
question: Does use make a private item publicly callable?
correct: No; importing a path does not bypass privacy
wrong: Yes, for all callers
Only when the name is short
reasoning: The public function can use a private helper inside its module, while main calls the exposed boundary.

title: Tests, assertions, and contracts
body: A test checks behavior against a contract. Unit tests can access private implementation details from their module; integration tests exercise the public crate API. Documentation tests keep examples connected to compiled behavior.

assert checks a condition; assert_eq and assert_ne compare values and report useful differences. Result-returning tests can use ?. A test expecting a panic should identify the intended failure rather than accepting any unrelated panic.

Test boundaries, invalid input and ownership consequences as well as happy paths. A passing test is evidence for those inputs, not proof of all possible behavior. Concurrency tests must avoid assuming a particular scheduler order.
challenge: Test a function returning Option for division by zero and valid division.
question: What does one passing example establish?
correct: That example’s checked behavior, not universal correctness
wrong: Every possible input is correct
The code cannot leak under any workflow
reasoning: Both normal and failure branches are checked explicitly; neither claim depends on printed output alone.

title: Read and write interfaces with Result
body: The Read and Write traits abstract byte streams. A function using impl Read can accept a file, an in-memory cursor or another adapter. This keeps the algorithm testable without requiring the filesystem.

I/O can return partial work or errors. read_to_string and write_all handle their respective loops, while text decoding and size policy still matter. Never assume one read fills a buffer or one write consumes it all.

Separate parsing from resource acquisition. A bounded reader policy is needed for untrusted large input, and buffered I/O can reduce repeated system calls. Paths are platform values, not necessarily Unicode strings.
challenge: Read at most four bytes from an in-memory source using take.
question: Does one Read::read call guarantee the whole buffer is filled?
correct: No; handle the returned count or use an appropriate helper
wrong: Yes on every platform
Only if the buffer is on the heap
reasoning: take limits bytes consumed before read_to_end. A separate policy is needed to decide whether truncation is acceptable.

title: Threads, move, and scoped borrowing
body: std::thread::spawn creates concurrent execution. Its closure must satisfy Send and a static lifetime bound because it can outlive the caller’s local scope. move transfers captured ownership; join waits and reports a panic as an error.
Scoped threads may borrow local data because the scope ensures its threads finish before borrowed storage disappears. This avoids cloning an entire input merely to satisfy an unscoped lifetime bound.

Concurrency order is nondeterministic. Collect results through joins or channels before printing deterministic summaries, and make synchronization protect a real invariant rather than a hoped-for ordering.
challenge: Spawn an owned String with an unscoped thread and return its length through join.
question: Why can a scoped thread borrow local values?
correct: The scope guarantees completion before those values expire
wrong: Scoped threads ignore lifetimes
Borrowed values are automatically static
reasoning: The first thread finishes inside scope, so numbers remains available afterward.

title: Arc, Mutex, and lock guards
body: Arc shares ownership using atomic reference counting; it does not automatically make the payload’s operations synchronized. Mutex protects a value with exclusive access through a lock guard.

A guard releases its lock when dropped. Keep lock scopes short, avoid holding a synchronous lock across await, and adopt one lock ordering when several locks must be acquired. Poisoning reports a prior panic while locked, not necessarily irreparable corruption.

Send describes moving ownership between threads; Sync describes sharing references safely. These properties propagate through types subject to their fields and implementation contracts. Rc is not a substitute for Arc across threads.
challenge: Have four threads add two each to the protected total, then join all of them.
question: Does Arc<T> alone synchronize mutation of any T?
correct: No; ownership sharing and mutation synchronization are separate
wrong: Yes, because its count is atomic
Only when it has two owners
reasoning: The mutex serializes the updates; joins ensure all updates finish before reading the total.

title: Channels, closure, and backpressure
body: A channel transfers values from senders to a receiver. Ownership moves with each sent value. A receiver’s iterator ends after all senders are dropped and queued messages are consumed.

An unbounded queue can grow when producers outrun consumers. sync_channel supplies a capacity and blocks sending when full; capacity zero is a rendezvous. Define what should happen under overload rather than assuming unlimited buffering.

Keep sender lifetimes deliberate. An unnoticed sender clone can prevent receiver shutdown forever. When cancelling a pipeline, close channels or communicate shutdown so every worker has a way to stop and be joined.
challenge: Use a bounded channel of capacity one to send 4 and 6 from a worker.
question: When does a channel receiver’s iterator finish?
correct: After every sender is dropped and buffered messages are drained
wrong: After any one sender is cloned
After exactly one message by default
reasoning: The worker owns the only sender. It drops on return, allowing the receiver to finish.

title: Atomic operations and memory ordering
body: An atomic operation accesses one atomic location without a data race. Relaxed ordering guarantees atomicity for that location but does not publish arbitrary adjacent non-atomic data. A statistics counter may need only this guarantee.

Release/acquire ordering can establish visibility through a correctly designed synchronization relation. SeqCst additionally supplies a single order for those operations. Stronger ordering cannot repair a logically incorrect protocol or unsafe storage access.

Start with a lock unless a measured need justifies a lock-free protocol. Write the invariant and publication relation before choosing ordering; compare_exchange loops also need to handle contention and possible ABA-style state reuse.
challenge: Use compare_exchange to change an atomic state from 0 to 1, then attempt the transition again.
question: Does Relaxed publish arbitrary non-atomic payload data?
correct: No; it guarantees this atomic operation without that publication relation
wrong: Yes, always
It turns the value into a mutex
reasoning: The scope joins the counter updates. The state transition succeeds only when the observed value equals zero.

title: Future, poll, wake, and await
body: Calling an async function creates a future; it does not complete the computation immediately. An executor polls futures. Ready carries a result; Pending means the future must arrange an appropriate wakeup when progress may be possible.

await suspends the current future until the awaited one is ready. It does not create an OS thread or guarantee parallel work. Blocking I/O inside async can stall an executor thread; use the runtime’s appropriate asynchronous or blocking boundary.

The demonstration polls an immediately ready future once, with a no-op waker. It is intentionally not a production executor: a genuinely pending future needs wakeup scheduling, cancellation and resource management. A runtime such as Tokio supplies those policies separately from the Rust language.
challenge: Compose two immediately ready async operations using await and return their sum.
question: Does calling an async function alone execute it to completion?
correct: No; it constructs a future that must be driven
wrong: Yes, on a new OS thread
Yes, through implicit busy waiting
reasoning: The helper explicitly polls. Both awaited values are immediately Ready, so this bounded demonstration completes.

title: Pin, Unpin, and address-sensitive state
body:
Pin

restricts moving the pointee through its safe interface when the target is not Unpin. It does not pin every variable globally. Pointer ownership and the promise about the pointee’s address are distinct.

Some futures can hold references into their own state after polling, making movement unsafe. Box::pin owns pinned heap storage; pin! pins a local value within a controlled scope. Unpin types do not require that address guarantee.

Unsafe pin construction/projection requires a lasting invariant, including destruction and which fields are structurally pinned. Prefer safe constructors and a well-reviewed projection abstraction rather than assuming every field may be moved out.
challenge: Pin a local i32 with pin!, mutate through get_mut, and explain why it is allowed.
question: Why is safe get_mut available for the i32 example?
correct: i32 is Unpin
wrong: Pin removes all borrowing rules
Every future is Unpin
reasoning: For an Unpin payload there is no address-sensitive invariant to preserve, so safe mutable access is permitted.

title: Cancellation is dropping owned work
body: Dropping a future cancels further polling of that future and drops its owned state. It does not undo external effects already performed, and it may not stop a detached worker or remote request by itself.

Cancellation safety asks what remains true if suspension ends at any await point. Keep partial updates behind transactional boundaries, use explicit task ownership and join policies, and make resource guards release reliably when the future is dropped.

A future that returns Pending must arrange wakeup if it is intended to progress. This example intentionally remains pending and is then dropped; it demonstrates resource release rather than an executor or remote-job cancellation guarantee.
challenge: Store the pending task in Option and cancel it exactly once with take.
question: Does dropping a local future automatically undo an already committed remote effect?
correct: No; external cancellation and transaction policies are separate
wrong: Yes, all remote operations are rolled back
Only if the future used async fn
reasoning: The owner drops once. Taking the empty Option again has no payload to release.

title: Async trait methods and opaque futures
body: Stable Rust supports async methods in traits for static dispatch. The returned future is an opaque implementation type. The public trait contract must deliberately address Send and other requirements needed by consumers.

An async method does not automatically make a trait dyn-compatible. Erased APIs often return Pin<Box<dyn Future<Output = T> + appropriate bounds>> or use an adapter, with allocation and lifetime tradeoffs.

Do not assume every async result is safe to send between threads. Captured values and state held across await determine the future’s auto traits. Document the execution context and test the bounds required by your API.
challenge: Add a generic async function that reads a Source and doubles the result.
question: Does an async trait method automatically support dyn Trait?
correct: No; dyn compatibility needs a suitable interface
wrong: Yes, without any tradeoffs
Only if its output is i32
reasoning: The example uses a concrete type and generic static dispatch; no erased future interface is required.

title: macro_rules, repetition, and hygiene
body: A declarative macro matches token patterns and expands Rust syntax. Fragment kinds such as expr and ident constrain what a matcher accepts. Repetition can generate code for a variable number of inputs.

Macros are not ordinary functions: expansion happens before the resulting code is type checked. Keep a clear reason for syntax generation; a generic function is usually easier to debug when syntax itself need not change.

Hygiene controls name resolution, and exported helpers often need $crate to refer to their defining crate. Match delimiters and optional trailing separators intentionally, and make invalid invocations produce useful diagnostics.
challenge: Write a macro that creates a Vec from a comma-separated sequence, including a trailing comma.
question: When is generated macro code type checked?
correct: After expansion into Rust syntax
wrong: Only when the macro is called at runtime
Never
reasoning: The repetition generates ordinary additions or vector elements; those expressions still obey Rust’s types.

title: Unsafe code and explicit safety invariants
body: unsafe permits specified operations such as dereferencing raw pointers; it does not disable the whole type system. A safe wrapper must establish every precondition of its unsafe implementation for every safe caller.

Raw pointers do not automatically carry ownership, validity, alignment or aliasing proof. Document where a pointer came from, which allocation is alive, what memory is initialized, and whether access conflicts with other references.

Keep unsafe blocks small and place a precise safety argument beside each one. A pointer that is non-null can still be dangling or misaligned. Passing tests is valuable evidence but cannot by itself establish soundness for all callers.
challenge: Create a raw mutable pointer to a live local, update it once, and document exclusive access.
question: Does unsafe remove the requirement to avoid invalid aliasing?
correct: No; the author must uphold the safety contract
wrong: Yes, all pointer accesses become defined
Only for non-null pointers
reasoning: The local outlives the dereference and no conflicting access overlaps it. Those facts justify this particular block.

title: C ABI, extern blocks, and boundary ownership
body: FFI connects Rust with another language’s calling conventions and representations. extern "C" chooses a C ABI, not an ownership protocol. Check widths, layout, lifetimes, allocator ownership and error conventions on both sides.

Edition 2024 requires unsafe extern blocks; declarations inside describe functions the compiler cannot inspect. A foreign function can be marked safe only when all its uses meet a genuinely unconditional contract. Variadic interfaces add ABI-specific promotion requirements.

Do not unwind through an ABI boundary that forbids it. Use compatible unwind contracts where intended, or catch/translate failures. A Rust-facing safe wrapper should validate inputs and ensure foreign resources are released by the correct owner.
challenge: Call abs on -12 while excluding the unrepresentable absolute value of c_int::MIN.
question: Does extern "C" specify who frees a foreign allocation?
correct: No; ownership must be defined separately
wrong: Yes, Rust always frees it
Yes, the C library always frees every pointer
reasoning: abs has no allocation, but even this small boundary requires a matching ABI and valid value range.

title: Representation, padding, and serialization
body: Rust’s default struct layout is not a stable serialization format. repr(C) follows a C-compatible field layout policy, while repr(transparent) supports a wrapper with the specified representation constraints.

Size includes padding and depends on the target and representation. Alignment requirements apply to references and raw accesses. Packed structs can create unaligned fields; taking an ordinary reference to such a field is not a safe way to access it.

Encode a network/file format explicitly with byte-order conversions and fixed-width fields. Do not transmute a struct into bytes and assume it is portable, fully initialized or free of sensitive padding.
challenge: Round-trip a u16 through explicit little-endian bytes.
question: Is a default Rust struct layout a portable wire format?
correct: No; explicitly encode fields and byte order
wrong: Yes on every architecture
Yes when fields are public
reasoning: The byte conversion names the endianness and avoids depending on unspecified field order or padding.

title: MaybeUninit and initialization responsibility
body: MaybeUninit<T> can hold storage that is not yet a valid T. It is useful for low-level initialization and FFI out-parameters, but moving the wrapper does not prove the contents are initialized.

write initializes a value; assume_init is unsafe because the author must prove validity. An arbitrary bit pattern is not valid for every type. For example, references and many enums have representation constraints beyond byte count.

Cleanup is also your responsibility when partially initializing many elements. Track the initialized prefix and drop it on failure; prefer safe constructors such as Vec when they already express the operation. ManuallyDrop likewise changes cleanup obligations rather than making them disappear.
challenge: Initialize an owned String in MaybeUninit and extract it with a documented validity proof.
question: What must be proved before assume_init?
correct: The storage contains a valid initialized T
wrong: Only that its address is non-null
Only that enough bytes were allocated
reasoning: write creates the valid value. The extracted String becomes an ordinary owner and is subsequently dropped.

title: const fn and compile-time evaluation
body: A const fn can be evaluated in a const context when its operations satisfy constant-evaluation rules. The same function can also run at runtime. const does not mean every call is automatically evaluated during compilation.

Compile-time evaluation has restrictions involving effects, allocations, traits and generic computations. These restrictions evolve; consult the target version rather than copying nightly syntax into a stable project.
Use constants for fixed tables or invariant parameters, and check edge cases such as overflow deliberately. A compile-time calculation still needs a meaningful mathematical/domain contract.
challenge: Use a const fn to produce a three-element lookup array at compile time.
question: Can a const fn also be called in ordinary runtime code?
correct: Yes
wrong: No; its body never runs at runtime
Only from unsafe code
reasoning: ANSWER and TABLE require compile-time evaluation. The other square call can be used in a runtime context.

title: Higher-ranked lifetimes and reusable borrowed calls
body: A higher-ranked bound such as for<'a> Fn(&'a str) -> usize says the callable must work for every appropriate input lifetime. That is different from choosing one particular lifetime for the entire surrounding function.
This is useful when an algorithm creates short-lived borrows and passes them to a callback. A callback tied to only one longer lifetime would not necessarily accept those temporary views.

Read the binder as a quantified contract. Lifetimes still describe borrow validity; they do not allocate, clone or extend the referent. Type variance then governs which lifetime substitutions are permitted inside a type.
challenge: Call a higher-ranked callback on two independently owned temporary strings.
question: What does for<'a> in this callback bound mean?
correct: The callable accepts borrows for every suitable input lifetime
wrong: The referent lives forever
The callback chooses one fixed global lifetime
reasoning: The callback only reads each current borrow; it does not store a reference beyond its call.

title: A lending interface with a generic associated type
body: A generic associated type can express an output whose type depends on a borrow lifetime. A lending view trait can return a reference into self without pretending each output has a static lifetime.

The bound where Self: 'a states that Self is valid for the lifetime used by the associated output. The implementation chooses the output representation for that lifetime, and the method ties it to the receiver borrow.

This pattern is useful for parsers and reusable buffers. It is also a reminder that an interface with lifetime-dependent outputs can have different dyn-compatibility and combinator constraints from ordinary Iterator.
challenge: Implement the same lending view contract for a Vec<i32> returning &[i32].
question: What does this GAT make explicit?
correct: The output type depends on the receiver’s borrow lifetime
wrong: Every returned reference is static
The output is always heap-allocated
reasoning: The view borrows the stored buffer and cannot outlive its valid owner relationship.

title: Sized, ?Sized, and dynamically sized types
body: A generic type parameter is Sized by default. ?Sized relaxes that default, allowing a reference-based API to accept str, slices or trait objects in addition to sized values.

A dynamically sized type needs pointer metadata: a slice view carries its element count; a trait object carries metadata used for dynamic dispatch. This does not make an unsized value an ordinary stack-local value of known size.

Borrowing APIs can often be more general with T: ?Sized because the reference itself remains sized. Type aliases merely rename a type; a newtype introduces a distinct type and can enforce a separate interface.
challenge: Write a generic Debug printer that accepts both a str and a slice.
question: What does T: ?Sized do?
correct: Relax the implicit Sized bound
wrong: Force every T to be unsized
Erase all type information
reasoning: The references remain sized even when their targets need runtime metadata.

title: LazyLock, OnceLock, and initialization
body: A static value has program lifetime, but shared mutable state still needs synchronization. LazyLock defers initialization until first use; OnceLock supports a value established once by a caller or initializer.

Initialization policy is part of the API: who supplies configuration, what happens if initialization panics, and how repeated requests behave? Do not hide per-user state in a permanent global merely for convenience.
Long-lived caches can intentionally retain memory; distinguish that policy from abandoned ownership. Bound their contents or choose a scoped owner when the app/session should release them.
challenge: Use OnceLock to set a value once and report a rejected second set.
question: Does static storage remove synchronization requirements?
correct: No; storage duration and concurrent access rules differ
wrong: Yes for all mutable values
Only when the type contains a String
reasoning: OnceLock accepts the first value and leaves it unchanged when the second set fails.

title: Pattern binding modes and guarded cases
body: Patterns appear in let bindings, function parameters, match arms and loop bindings. Destructuring names fields and alternatives; a wildcard ignores a value, while a named binding may move or borrow it according to context.

Matching a borrowed value often uses match ergonomics to infer reference bindings. Explicit ref, ref mut and reference patterns need particular care under edition 2024 rules. Prefer clear borrowed inputs and verify the resulting binding types.

@ binds a value while testing a subpattern. Or-patterns cover alternatives with compatible bindings, and guards add Boolean conditions. Exhaustiveness still needs an unguarded fallback for uncovered values.
challenge: Destructure a borrowed pair and print its text without moving the String.
question: Does a match guard alone usually establish exhaustive coverage?
correct: No; uncovered cases still need handling
wrong: Yes, every guard is exhaustive
Only for integers larger than zero
reasoning: The 1..=9 fallback covers odd small values; the wildcard covers all remaining integers.

title: From, TryFrom, and error-preserving conversions
body: From expresses an infallible conversion; implementing it also supplies Into through the standard blanket implementation. TryFrom/TryInto report a conversion that can fail, including range validation.

A custom newtype can require construction through a validated conversion rather than expose an unrestricted field. The error should identify the rejected condition and give callers an explicit recovery path.
as is useful for defined low-level conversions but is not a general validation boundary. Parsing textual input with FromStr and narrowing an already parsed integer with TryFrom are separate checks.
challenge: Implement TryFrom<i32> for a positive integer newtype and reject zero.
question: Which trait should represent a conversion that can reject input?
correct: TryFrom
wrong: From with hidden panics
Deref for every conversion
reasoning: The narrowed or validated type is created only when its explicit domain condition holds.

title: Panic strategy and failed invariants
body: panic reports a failure outside an ordinary Result path. Unwinding can run destructors while it walks the stack; a panic-abort build terminates without that unwinding. The selected build strategy matters to recovery and cleanup.

catch_unwind catches an unwinding panic with the required unwind-safety contract. It does not catch every abort or turn an arbitrary unsafe operation into defined behavior. Keep it at a deliberate boundary rather than replacing typed validation.

Custom panic hooks and error reporting may expose context. Avoid logging secrets, and distinguish a programmer invariant failure from expected input errors so callers can recover without interpreting text messages.
challenge: Replace a potentially panicking arithmetic case with checked_div and handle its failure.
question: Can catch_unwind recover from a panic-abort termination?
correct: No
wrong: Yes, by converting it to Result
Yes, only when the output is an integer
reasoning: A recoverable validation policy uses the checked operation directly rather than depending on panic strategy.

title: Newtypes, blanket impls, and coherence
body: A newtype has a distinct identity even if it wraps an existing representation. It can prevent confusing units and gives you a local type for trait implementations. A type alias does neither; it is another name for the same type.

Coherence prevents incompatible overlapping trait implementations. Blanket implementations can constrain which more-specific implementations are available. Before promising an extension point, examine the current and future implementation space.

Variance describes which subtype/lifetime substitutions a type allows. Shared references and mutable references differ in their treatment of the referent type, and UnsafeCell-based interior mutation affects variance. PhantomData can express ownership/variance relationships but does not allocate a value.
challenge: Define Seconds as a distinct wrapper with its own Display implementation.
question: Does a type alias create a distinct local wrapper for trait coherence?
correct: No; use a newtype for a distinct type
wrong: Yes, always
Only if its name starts with a capital
reasoning: The local wrapper allows custom formatting and prevents accidental interchange of different units.

title: Edition 2024 migration and compatibility
body: Edition 2024 changes compatibility rules, including unsafe extern blocks and unsafe attributes, some temporary scopes, match ergonomics constraints, and return-position impl Trait lifetime capture. New crates should choose the edition deliberately.

cargo fix --edition can perform eligible migrations, but it is not a substitute for testing behavior and public interfaces. Review warnings, macro expansion and foreign boundaries. Dependencies can use different editions because a crate’s edition is local to its compilation.

The minimum supported Rust version is a separate policy from the edition. Put rust-version in Cargo.toml and test it; a feature stabilized after the edition’s initial compiler still needs its own newer minimum.
challenge: Express a precise empty lifetime/type capture for a return-position impl Iterator.
question: Are edition and minimum compiler version the same setting?
correct: No; edition selects compatibility rules, rust-version states a compiler minimum
wrong: Yes, both are release dates
Yes, every dependency must use both identically
reasoning: The precise capture use<> states that no generic parameters are captured by this opaque return type.

title: Rust 1.99: owned buffers and current APIs
body: Rust 1.99.0 is the stable release verified on 14 October 2026. Its additions include boxed-array iteration, owned lossy UTF-8 conversion, NonNull-based ownership conversions, and stable C-variadic definitions. These APIs require the corresponding compiler rather than merely edition 2024.

Owned lossy UTF-8 conversion turns a byte vector into a String, replacing invalid sequences. This is a policy choice: use strict String::from_utf8 when corrupt text should be rejected, and lossy conversion only where replacement is intended.

Release notes also include library contracts, lints and compatibility changes. When upgrading, check your code against the exact release and rerun behavioral tests; a successful build alone does not detect every changed edge case.
challenge: Consume a boxed [4, 5, 6] by iteration and compare strict versus lossy conversion of one invalid byte.
question: What policy does lossy UTF-8 conversion apply to invalid sequences?
correct: Replace them, rather than report a decoding error
wrong: Prove the original bytes were valid
Preserve invalid bytes inside str
reasoning: The strict conversion reports failure; the lossy one produces the replacement character.

title: Rust 1.99: recovering NonNull-owned storage
body: A NonNull pointer proves that the address is not zero; it does not prove live storage, alignment, initialization or exclusive ownership. Converting an owner into a pointer transfers cleanup responsibility to your protocol.

Box::into_non_null and Box::from_non_null provide a NonNull ownership round trip. Recover the same allocation exactly once with matching type/allocator assumptions; do not also drop a second fabricated owner.

Vec::into_parts and Vec::from_parts likewise carry allocation metadata that must remain correct. These APIs are advanced ownership tools for a justified boundary, not a faster replacement for ordinary safe iteration.
challenge: Round-trip an owned Vec through its NonNull pointer, length and capacity.
question: Is NonNull by itself a proof that dereferencing is safe?
correct: No; validity, alignment, lifetime and aliasing still need proof
wrong: Yes for every non-zero address
Yes if the pointer was printed
reasoning: The safety proof relies on the originating owner and unchanged metadata, not just the pointer’s non-null property.

title: Capstone: a validated expression calculator
body: Build a small parser as a composition of checked boundaries: syntax, numeric conversion, operation selection and arithmetic overflow. Return a typed result rather than panic for expected invalid input.

For this deliberately small grammar, exactly three whitespace-separated tokens form one operation. A larger grammar would need tokenization, precedence and a syntax tree; do not stretch split_whitespace into an undocumented language.

Acceptance is observable: valid addition/subtraction works, malformed tokens and unsupported operations fail, overflow is rejected, and all these cases have tests. Explain each failure branch before expanding the grammar.
challenge: Add checked multiplication and tests for valid multiplication and an unsupported operator.
question: Where should expected malformed input be handled?
correct: At the parsing boundary through a typed failure
wrong: Through an unexplained unwrap panic
Only after unsafe arithmetic
reasoning: Each stage validates its own condition and propagates failure. Arithmetic uses checked operations.

title: A complete procedural-macro workspace
body: Procedural macros run at compilation and transform token streams. Function-like, derive and attribute macros have distinct entry attributes. Their implementation belongs in a proc-macro crate and is used from a separate consuming crate.

This complete dependency-free workspace generates the expression 42 from answer!(). It rejects nonempty input with a compile_error diagnostic. The macro consumes syntax; the resulting expression is still checked in the caller’s context.

Create the files below with their exact relative paths, then run cargo run --offline -p guide-demo. A single-file runner cannot build this workspace. For real syntax analysis, choose a parser/token library deliberately, preserve useful spans, and test accepted and rejected syntax.
challenge: Change the expansion from 42 to 64, and verify the consuming program prints 64. Then try answer!(unexpected) and verify the diagnostic rejects it.
question: Where does a procedural-macro implementation belong?
correct: In a separate proc-macro crate
wrong: Inside the same ordinary binary that first invokes it
Only inside main as a runtime callback
reasoning: The compiler builds the macro crate before expanding its invocation in guide-demo. The provided project prints 42; changing its expansion produces the requested 64.

[workspace]
members = ["lesson-macros", "demo"]
resolver = "3"

[package]
name = "lesson-macros"
version = "0.1.0"
edition = "2024"
rust-version = "1.99"
[lib]
proc-macro = true

[package]
name = "guide-demo"
version = "0.1.0"

[dependencies]
lesson-macros = { path = "../lesson-macros" }

title: Project: a tested text-search CLI
body: Build this after the ownership, Result, lifetime, iterator, module and testing lessons. Cargo turns one package into a reusable library crate and a small executable crate: src/lib.rs exports policy, while src/main.rs owns the operating-system boundary. The binary can use minigrep::Config without exposing private implementation details. No third-party crate or network fetch is required.

Config::parse accepts an iterator of owned UTF-8 arguments and returns either a fully valid configuration or a specific error. The process adapter uses args_os and fallible conversion so a non-UTF-8 argument becomes a usage error rather than an args() panic. The -- marker ends option interpretation, allowing a query beginning with a dash. Exactly two positional arguments are required; unknown flags and extra values are rejected. This version deliberately accepts UTF-8 file paths only; a production path interface could preserve OsString separately from the textual query.

search returns Vec<&str> borrowing the contents, not a set of copied lines. The explicit lifetime relates only the input text to the output, so a temporary query can disappear while the selected lines remain usable. The contents String in main therefore must stay alive until all selected lines are printed. Replacing the owned file buffer with a temporary inside search would make these references invalid and the borrow checker must reject that design.

The insensitive mode normalizes the query once, then normalizes each candidate line before testing contains. The output still borrows the original line, preserving its spelling. This is Unicode lowercase comparison, not locale-aware collation, normalization or full case folding: document that contract rather than claiming every human spelling is equivalent. lines() removes CRLF separators and omits the final empty line; an empty query selects every line actually yielded, while an empty file yields no lines.

The binary prints matches to stdout. Usage/argument errors go to stderr with status 2; file/UTF-8 decoding errors use status 1; a successful search with no matches uses status 0 in this teaching contract. Returning ExitCode lets ordinary Rust destructors run. Unlike process::exit in the middle of a function, the return does not skip cleanup of still-live local values. Broken-pipe handling and a streaming BufRead version are further design exercises, not established by these tests.

Run unit, integration and documentation tests. Five library tests isolate parsing, end-of-options, case behavior, CRLF/Unicode, and independent query/text lifetimes. Three integration tests spawn the actual compiled binary and check fixture output, usage failure and a missing file. The rustdoc example is also compiled and run. For the practice solution, add inversion without breaking search callers, then prove both library behavior and executable wiring. A passing quiz alone is not completion of these engineering exercises.
challenge: Beginner: predict the exact output for rust with and without --ignore-case, then run every supplied test. Intermediate: add --invert; it must print precisely the lines not selected by the existing matcher, combine with --ignore-case, respect --, and preserve the existing search API. Add unit and executable tests before revealing the solution. Advanced: design a streaming implementation with numbered/context lines and explicit broken-pipe handling; explain why borrowing lines from a reused BufRead buffer cannot return the same Vec<&str> interface. The advanced design is an open extension, not part of the supplied answer.
question: Why may selected lines remain valid after the query String is dropped?
correct: The output lifetime is tied to the contents buffer; the function does not return references into the query.
wrong: Vec<&str> owns independent copies of every selected line.
All string references automatically have a static lifetime.
The query and file contents must always have exactly the same lifetime.
reasoning: Keep the file contents owner alive while consuming borrowed lines. The worked inversion answer adds a Config field and flag, a separate search_inverted function, and conditional selection in main. It preserves the existing search signature and adds a sixth unit test plus a fourth integration test. Check that inversion of an empty query selects nothing, case-insensitive inversion excludes both Rust and rust, and diagnostics still use stderr with the documented status. For the fixture, --ignore-case rust prints the first two lines; adding --invert prints only OCaml is expressive. The streaming extension needs a callback borrowing each line only during the call, an ordinary iterator yielding owned lines, or a lending iterator with a lifetime-aware interface; an ordinary Iterator cannot yield references into its own reused buffer.
expectedStdout:
Rust is fast
rust is safe

title: Project: Cargo features, generated code and a workspace
body: Work through the basic Cargo, modules, cfg, constant and error lessons first. This complete workspace contains two packages: feature-engine owns an arithmetic policy, and feature-demo is a command-line client through a local path dependency. A package may contain several crates; workspace membership is a separate Cargo organization level. One virtual root manifest supplies resolver version 3 and shared edition, Rust-version, version and lint settings. Each member explicitly opts into inherited package/lint fields; declaring a workspace value alone does not apply it everywhere.

Run the default example and predict wrapping: 4 from the explicit u8 wrapping_add policy. Enable the demo checked feature to forward feature-engine/checked, rebuilding the dependency and returning checked: overflow. Cargo features select compiled capabilities and are unified for a given dependency in the relevant resolution context; they are not ordinary runtime booleans or an arbitrary mutually-exclusive choice system. Design library feature combinations to work together. Resolver 3 affects dependency resolution/MSRV behavior; it does not make every conflicting feature combination valid.

The engine build script runs on the build host before the target crate is compiled. It observes Cargo's CARGO_FEATURE_CHECKED variable, declares the custom engine_checked cfg name to the compiler, conditionally enables it, and writes mode.rs under OUT_DIR. include! reads that generated Rust source at compile time. Generated files belong in OUT_DIR, not src or the dependency registry. Cross compilation can run the script on one architecture while compiling its output for another: do not mistake a build-host probe for a target property.

cargo::rustc-check-cfg makes the custom cfg recognized; unexpected_cfgs=deny then catches spelling errors rather than silently selecting the wrong branch. cfg! expands to a boolean expression, so both branches of an ordinary if still need to type-check; #[cfg] removes a declaration/block from this compilation. The example uses #[cfg] for the arithmetic implementation and cfg! inside tests where both assertion branches are valid Rust. Shared unsafe_code=forbid rejects unsafe blocks, but does not prove the whole dependency graph or all logic correct.

The .cargo/config.toml verify alias runs workspace tests, including both packages and the library rustdoc example. A root cargo run without -p uses the configured default member; selecting -p feature-engine targets the library package instead. Test default and checked separately, and also --all-features so feature-unified builds cannot quietly escape testing. Profiles, target triples, build-script rerun inputs and environment overrides are independent configuration dimensions; this small project demonstrates the stated feature/build/lint contracts, not every Cargo setting.

For practice, make the CLI default to checked arithmetic while keeping the engine library's default policy unchanged. Add default=["checked"] only to demo/Cargo.toml. Then ordinary demo runs report overflow, --no-default-features on the selected demo opts back into wrapping, and direct engine tests still cover its wrapping default. Feature unification can enable checked when testing both members together; that is expected. A deployed project must commit and verify its lockfile and toolchain policy once external dependencies are introduced; this dependency-free project resolves offline.
challenge: Beginner: run the wrapping and checked commands, and explain where MODE is generated and who owns it. Intermediate: make only the demo default to checked; prove the ordinary command prints checked: overflow, --no-default-features restores wrapping: 4, and direct engine tests still pass without defaults. Advanced: introduce a second independent additive feature, test every supported combination, and deliberately misspell engine_checked to inspect the unexpected_cfgs diagnostic. Document host-versus-target behavior before proposing cross-compilation probes. The provided worked answer implements the intermediate requirement; the additional feature/probe design remains your extension.
question: Where should the checked default be declared to change the CLI without changing the library default?
correct: In demo/Cargo.toml as default = ["checked"], forwarding the existing engine feature.
wrong: In engine/Cargo.toml, enabling the feature for every library consumer.
In a runtime environment variable named CHECKED, which always changes compiled cfg blocks.
In workspace.package, because all arbitrary fields automatically propagate to members.
reasoning: The solution changes just demo/Cargo.toml. Its default feature enables the already-declared forwarding feature; the engine package retains no default features. After the change, run the normal demo, the selected demo with --no-default-features, workspace tests and direct engine tests. Remember that --no-default-features disables defaults for the selected package; it cannot turn off a dependency feature another selected consumer has enabled. Build-script output/cfg values and MODE must agree in each invocation. The answer is verified with actual Cargo rebuilds, not by reading manifest text alone.

title: Project: a bounded HTTP server and owned thread pool
body: Build this after the I/O CLI, ownership, FnOnce, Send, channels, mutex, threads and Drop lessons. The six-file package separates transport/framing, response policy, worker ownership and process entry. It reworks the Rust Book final server as a bounded, dependency-free teaching project. TCP supplies an ordered byte stream, not HTTP request boundaries: one read may return part of a header or several messages. HTTP framing belongs above that stream. This project intentionally handles one small request per connection and announces Connection: close.

Read through the complete request header terminator, preserving bytes across reads. Enforce an 8,192-byte header limit before extending the buffer and compute one absolute read deadline with Instant. A client sending tiny chunks must not get a fresh whole-second budget after every read. Set each socket read timeout to the remaining budget. Incomplete EOF, expiry and oversized input return errors and close the connection in this version; they are not promised a formatted HTTP error response. The parser separately rejects unsupported framing, duplicate/missing Host, invalid UTF-8 and nonzero Content-Length.

reply builds status, CRLF-separated headers, the blank separator and body bytes. Content-Length counts bytes, not Unicode characters. The baseline supports GET / and a 404 route; other methods receive 405 with Allow: GET. A body or transfer encoding is outside this deliberately small subset. It is not a general HTTP parser, TLS server, persistent-connection implementation or replacement for a maintained protocol stack. Tests establish the stated subset, not arbitrary malformed-request robustness.

Pool uses sync_channel with a fixed queue capacity and try_send: a full queue rejects work immediately rather than creating unbounded retained closures or blocking the accept loop. serve closes a rejected connection when its dropped closure releases the moved TcpStream; it does not send 503. Workers share a Receiver through Arc<Mutex<_>>. Crucially, the receive guard is released in a separate expression before a job runs. Holding that guard around execution would serialize the workers even though several threads exist. The overlap regression requires two jobs to start before either is released.

Each job is FnOnce because it consumes its captured socket, Send because it crosses threads and static because the worker can outlive the submission stack. Static does not mean the allocation lives forever; it prevents borrowed stack data from escaping. A worker catches an unwinding job panic and accepts later jobs, but cannot recover a process abort or guarantee shared application state survived the panic. The queue and receiver hold no strong reference back to Pool. The self-owner regression also handles a job releasing the final Arc<Pool> without trying to join its own thread.

Shutdown first drops the final sender. The receiver can drain accepted jobs and then wakes with disconnection; Drop joins worker handles. Joining before closing the sender would deadlock idle receivers. Moving each JoinHandle out with drain avoids attempting to consume a borrowed handle. If destruction runs on a worker, all handles are detached after the sender closes. Joining even a peer could block the current callback from signaling that peer. Workers then drain/disconnect after their callbacks finish; this destructor does not synchronously wait for them. Outside the pool, destruction joins all workers. Generic jobs must eventually finish: this pool cannot preempt an infinite closure. The supplied network jobs have bounded reads and fixed responses with a socket write timeout.

The demonstration accepts exactly two connections before draining and joining, matching the Book shutdown progression. That limit counts accepted connections, including rejected jobs or malformed requests, rather than successful responses. It can wait indefinitely for the next client while accepting; that is listener waiting, not a worker leak. Ctrl-C is process termination and is not the graceful shutdown mechanism implemented here. A future cancellation-aware accept loop needs an explicit wakeup/shutdown design and a dependency/runtime policy.

Run the pure parser/pool tests, then actual loopback integration tests and the self-check executable. Tests cover concurrent overlap, a full queue, draining, panic recovery, final-owner release, status/length/framing, incomplete reads, maximum size and actual TCP responses. For the intermediate exercise, add HEAD while keeping the corresponding GET representation length and returning no body for success, 404 or recognizable HEAD validation errors. The answer replaces only http.rs and the integration tests; the pool and transport ownership remain unchanged. Further HTTP parsing, load tests, shutdown signaling and production async are separate projects.
