after writing through both halves: [10, 2, 30, 4, 5, 6]
empty split: 0 and 0
packed field = 0xdeadbeef, tag = 7, align = 1, size = 5
tag stored in the pointer = 0b101
value through the cleaned pointer = 0xabcd
offset_from within one array = 5
challenge: Implement pair_mut<T>(items: &mut [T], i: usize, j: usize) -> Option<(&mut T, &mut T)> that returns mutable references to two different elements, or None when i == j or either index is out of range. Do it with safe code only, using split_at_mut, and test swapping two elements through the references.
question: Why is it undefined behaviour to create two overlapping &mut references to the same data, even if you never use one of them?
correct: A &mut asserts exclusive access, and the compiler optimises on that promise; two live ones violate the aliasing rules by existing
wrong: The borrow checker rejects it at run time with a panic, so the program stops before any data can be corrupted
Because &mut references are slower than raw pointers, and the compiler forbids the slower option in unsafe code
It is only a problem if both references are written through, since unused references make no claims
reasoning: Aliasing rules are about what the references claim, not what they are used for. The compiler may reorder or cache reads and writes assuming exclusivity.

quiz.question: Why is the manual split_at_mut sound?
quiz.correct: The ranges do not overlap, both stay inside the slice, and the original &mut borrow lasts as long as the results, so no other access exists
wrong: Because raw pointers are always valid, so converting a slice into pointers and back cannot break any rule
Because unsafe turns off the aliasing rules inside the block, so overlapping ranges would also have been fine
Because from_raw_parts_mut checks for overlap at run time and panics if the two ranges ever intersect
quiz.reasoning: The proof lives in the safety comment. Unsafe lets you assert the invariants; it does not check them.

quiz.question: Why use ptr::addr_of!(p.value) on a repr(packed) struct instead of &p.value?
quiz.correct: A reference to a possibly misaligned field is invalid (E0793); addr_of! produces a raw pointer without creating a reference
wrong: addr_of! makes the field aligned by copying it to a temporary, so reading it through a reference becomes valid
&p.value works but is slower than addr_of!, because the compiler adds a runtime alignment check
Packed structs cannot have u32 fields, so the example only compiles because addr_of! hides the field type
quiz.reasoning: References must always be aligned. A raw pointer plus read_unaligned handles the misaligned case.

quiz.question: What does map_addr preserve that casting a pointer to usize and back does not?
quiz.correct: Provenance: the right to access the original allocation stays attached to the pointer
wrong: The numeric value of the address, which an integer round trip would change by moving it to a new allocation
The alignment of the pointee, which a cast through usize would otherwise reset to one byte
The size of the pointee, which the integer form of a pointer does not record and map_addr stores
quiz.reasoning: Strict provenance APIs change only the address. Integer round trips make it unclear which allocation the resulting pointer may touch.

quiz.question: Why is tagging the low three bits of a Box<u64> pointer legitimate?
quiz.correct: u64 has alignment 8, so the low three address bits are zero and can carry a tag, if cleared before dereferencing
wrong: All pointers have free low bits regardless of type, so any pointer can carry a three-bit tag safely
The tag survives dereferencing automatically, because the hardware ignores the low bits of an address
Because Box is not a real pointer but an integer handle, so changing its low bits has no effect
quiz.reasoning: Alignment guarantees zero low bits. The tag must be removed with map_addr before the pointer is used or freed.

title: A typed bump arena: stable references and wholesale deallocation
body: An arena (or bump allocator) trades individual deallocation for speed and simplicity. Allocation is just a push onto storage you already own, and everything is released together when the arena is dropped. That is exactly the lifetime of many compiler passes, request handlers and graph builders: build a lot of small interlinked objects, use them, then discard them all at once. The payoff in Rust is that objects allocated from the same arena can hold plain references to each other (&'a Node<'a>) with no Rc, no Box and no ownership puzzles, because they all share the arena's lifetime.

The trick is that alloc takes &self yet hands out &mut T. A normal Vec cannot do this: pushing may reallocate and move every element, which the borrow checker correctly forbids while references exist. The arena avoids reallocation instead of preventing the borrow. Elements live in chunks, each a Vec with a fixed capacity; when the last chunk is full a new, larger one is started and the old one is never touched again, so no element ever moves. A RefCell around the chunk list gives the interior mutability for alloc(&self), and one small unsafe block turns the pointer to the fresh element into a reference. The safety comment is the proof: stable addresses, unique elements so no aliasing, and the arena outliving the borrow.

Know the costs. Memory is not reclaimed until the arena is dropped, so a long-lived arena fed by a long-running loop is a leak by design. Values with destructors are dropped only when the arena drops, in an unspecified order that must not matter. The arena is not Sync, because RefCell is not, so each thread needs its own. Resetting needs &mut self (clear), and that requirement is the proof that no reference into the arena is still alive; the borrow checker enforces it. The demo links nodes into a list with Cell<Option<&'a Node<'a>>>, allocates a thousand more to force several chunks, and shows the early references still work.

Ensure no element ever moves after a reference is handed out, justify the unsafe block in a comment, document that memory is freed only on drop or clear, reset through &mut self, and keep the arena confined to one thread.
expectedStdout:
allocated 1003 nodes in chunks of capacity [4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512]
walked the early list after many more allocations: sum = 6
first values are intact: 1 2 3
drops while the arena is alive: 0
drops after the arena is dropped: 10
challenge: Add Arena::clear(&mut self), which drops every value but keeps the largest chunk's capacity for reuse. Explain in a comment why it must take &mut self, and show that after clearing you can allocate again and that all earlier values were dropped exactly once.
solutionStdout:
len 0 after clear, 20 values dropped, chunk capacities [4, 8, 16] -> [16]
total drops after reuse and drop: 21
question: Why can Arena::alloc take &self and still return a &mut T that stays valid while more values are allocated?
correct: Each call returns a distinct element in a chunk that is never resized or moved, so the references never alias and their addresses stay stable
wrong: Because RefCell makes any reference it hands out safe, since it re-checks every borrow at run time and panics on a conflict
Because the Vec reallocates in place without moving elements, so earlier addresses are preserved across pushes
Because the compiler proves it without unsafe, since lifetimes tied to &self already forbid aliasing
reasoning: Safety comes from the chunk design: a full chunk is left untouched and a new one started. RefCell only supplies the interior mutability for the chunk list; the unsafe block depends on the no-move invariant.

quiz.question: Why must a chunk never be pushed to once it is full?
quiz.correct: Pushing past capacity would reallocate and move its elements, leaving previously returned references dangling
wrong: It would make the arena slower, because each push into a full chunk copies the chunk's elements twice
Vec cannot hold more than its initial capacity, so pushing past it returns an error that the arena ignores
It would change the drop order, which must stay identical to the allocation order for the values
quiz.reasoning: The no-reallocation rule is the invariant behind the unsafe block, so alloc starts a new chunk exactly when len equals capacity.

quiz.question: What do you give up by using an arena?
quiz.correct: Individual deallocation: memory is released only when the arena is dropped or cleared
wrong: The ability to hold references to the allocated values, since the arena's contents move whenever it grows
The ability to drop values, since an arena never runs destructors for anything that it holds
Memory safety, because values allocated in an arena are not checked by the borrow checker
quiz.reasoning: A bump arena has no free list per object. Its simplicity and speed come from freeing everything together.

quiz.question: Why does clear take &mut self?
quiz.correct: Exclusive access proves that no reference into the arena is still alive, so dropping the values cannot create dangling references
wrong: Because RefCell cannot be borrowed otherwise, so clearing needs the exclusive borrow to release its flag
To make clear faster, since exclusive access lets the compiler skip the destructors of the stored values
Because clear needs to allocate a fresh chunk, which requires exclusive access to the arena's list
quiz.reasoning: The borrow checker turns "no outstanding references" into a compile-time fact. alloc(&self) hands out borrows of self, which would conflict with a &mut self call.

quiz.question: Why is Arena<T> not Sync?
quiz.correct: It uses RefCell for interior mutability, which is not thread safe, so each thread should use its own arena
wrong: Because chunks are Vec values, and Vec<T> is not Sync, so any struct containing one cannot be shared
Because unsafe code is never Sync, so the unsafe block inside alloc removes the marker automatically
Because it implements Drop, and a type with a destructor can never be shared between threads
quiz.reasoning: RefCell checks borrows at run time without synchronisation, so sharing &Arena across threads would race on the borrow flag.

title: Generational slab: O(1) handles that cannot dangle
body: Many systems keep large collections of objects that refer to each other and come and go: resting orders in a book, sessions, entities in a simulation. References are awkward (lifetimes, self-referential structures) and Rc<RefCell<..>> is heavy. The alternative is an index into a Vec. A slab stores values in a Vec of slots and hands out small Copy keys; insertion and removal are O(1) because freed slots are threaded into a free list and reused. Keys have no lifetime, no borrow, and can be stored, copied, sent between threads and serialised.

Plain indices have one nasty flaw, the ABA problem. Insert A at slot 0, remove it, insert B which reuses slot 0, and a stale index that was meant for A now silently reaches B: a use-after-free expressed in safe code. The fix is a generation counter. Every slot has one, a key carries the generation it was created with, and removing a value increments the slot's generation. A lookup compares generations and returns None for a stale key. The free list is intrusive: freed entries store next_free pointers, so no extra allocation is needed to track free space.

There are edge cases worth stating. A u32 generation can wrap after about four billion removals of the same slot, after which a very old key could match again, so the slab retires an exhausted slot instead of recycling it (checked_add), trading a few bytes for correctness. get returns Option because a key can be stale; there is no panic path in normal use. The demo compares the slab with a HashMap model over 5,000 random inserts, removals and lookups, including operations with stale keys, and checks that every stale key is rejected and len always matches.

Use generations to defeat ABA, thread the free list through the slots, make every lookup fallible, retire slots whose generation is exhausted, and test against a simple map model with deliberately stale keys.
expectedStdout:
a = Key { index: 0, generation: 0 }, b = Key { index: 1, generation: 0 }, len = 2
remove a -> Some("order A")
c reuses slot 0 with generation 1
stale key a -> None
fresh key c -> Some("order C")
removing a stale key again -> None
b -> Some("order B (amended)")
key from nowhere -> None
matches the HashMap model over 5000 random operations with stale keys: true
slots allocated 64 for 45 live values
challenge: Add iter(&self) -> impl Iterator<Item = (Key, &T)> yielding every live entry with its key, and check that the number of items equals len(), that each yielded key resolves through get to the same value, and that removed entries do not appear.
question: What problem does the generation counter solve?
correct: The ABA problem: after a slot is freed and reused, a stale key would otherwise reach the new, unrelated value
wrong: It makes insertion faster, because a fresh generation lets the slab skip searching for a free slot in the Vec
It lets two keys share a slot safely, because each generation reserves its own copy of the value
It stores the number of values in the slab, so len() can be answered without walking the entries
reasoning: Without generations an index is only a position. The generation turns it into an identity for one particular occupant of the slot.

quiz.question: Why does get return Option<&T> instead of &T?
quiz.correct: A key may be stale or foreign, so lookup can legitimately fail and the caller must handle it
wrong: Because slots can be empty only before the first insert, so get must report that one early case
To allow returning mutable references, which a plain &T return type would not be able to express
Because Option is cheaper than a reference, so returning it avoids a bounds check on every lookup
quiz.reasoning: Removal invalidates keys without notifying their holders. A fallible lookup makes that visible instead of causing a panic or a wrong answer.

quiz.question: How does the slab find a free slot in O(1)?
quiz.correct: Freed entries form an intrusive linked list through their next_free fields, headed by free_head
wrong: It scans the Vec from the start for an empty entry, which is fast because freed slots are usually early
It sorts the entries by generation after every removal, so the lowest generation is always reused next
It allocates a new Vec each time and moves the live entries into it, leaving the old slots behind
quiz.reasoning: Threading the list through the free slots needs no additional storage and makes both insert and remove constant time.

quiz.question: What happens when a slot's generation reaches u32::MAX?
quiz.correct: The slot is retired and never reused, so a very old key can never match a recycled slot after the counter would have wrapped
wrong: The generation wraps to zero and reuse continues, which is safe because wrapped generations are compared by identity
The slab panics immediately, since a generation counter that overflows is treated as a corrupted slab
The slab stops accepting inserts entirely, because one exhausted slot makes every other key ambiguous
quiz.reasoning: checked_add detects exhaustion. Retiring costs one slot of memory and removes any chance of a false match.

quiz.question: Why are slab keys better than references for objects that refer to each other?
quiz.correct: Keys are small Copy values with no lifetime, so they avoid borrow conflicts, cycles of ownership and dangling pointers
wrong: References cannot be stored in a Vec, so a slab must hand out keys even for objects that never refer to others
Keys make cloning the object free, because a key copies the pointed-to value only when it is first read
Keys guarantee the object is never removed, so every lookup with a valid key is certain to succeed
quiz.reasoning: A key is only a name for a slot. The slab remains the single owner, and a stale name is detected rather than followed.

title: Trait objects: fat pointers, vtables and dyn compatibility
body: A trait object, written dyn Trait behind a pointer, lets one collection hold values of different concrete types and call their methods through a shared interface. The price is a different pointer layout. A normal reference &T is one machine word, the address of the value. A reference to a trait object &dyn Trait is a fat pointer of two words: a data pointer to the value, and a pointer to a vtable for the pair (concrete type, trait). Box<dyn Trait>, Rc<dyn Trait> and *const dyn Trait have the same shape, and so do slices and &str, whose second word is a length. The program prints these sizes to make the layout concrete.

The vtable is a static table the compiler generates for each concrete type used as a given trait object. It holds the type's drop glue, its size and alignment, and one function pointer per method. A method call on a trait object loads the function pointer from the vtable and calls it indirectly, which blocks inlining; generic code with a T: Trait bound is instead monomorphised, one copy per type, with direct calls the optimizer can inline. Prefer generics on hot paths and trait objects where you need heterogeneity or want to limit code size. size_of_val and align_of_val read the concrete size from the vtable, which is how a Vec<Box<dyn Pricer>> can hold a zero-sized, an 8-byte and a 24-byte implementation side by side.

Not every trait can be made into an object. A trait is dyn compatible only if the compiler can build a vtable for it: methods cannot return Self or take generic type parameters (the concrete type is unknown, so the size or the set of instantiations is unknown), and the trait cannot require Self: Sized. dyn Clone fails with E0038, because clone returns Self. Two escape hatches matter. Adding where Self: Sized to a generic method exempts that method from the rules; it still exists for concrete types, and calling it through a trait object is rejected ("the g method cannot be invoked on a trait object"). And since Rust 1.86 trait upcasting is stable: with trait Pricer: Named, a &dyn Pricer coerces to &dyn Named.

Know the two-word layout, the vtable contents and the cost of an indirect call, choose generics for hot paths, check dyn compatibility (no Self returns, no generic methods without where Self: Sized), and use boxed_clone-style methods when you need cloning of boxed trait objects.
expectedStdout:
&u8 = 8 bytes, &[u8] = 16, &str = 16
&dyn Pricer = 16 bytes, Box<dyn Pricer> = 16, Box<Linear> = 8
  flat: concrete size  0, align 1, price(2) = 100
linear: concrete size  8, align 8, price(2) = 6
 table: concrete size 24, align 8, price(2) = 7
static dispatch total = 24, dynamic dispatch total = 24
generic helper on a concrete type: [5, 9, 13]
upcast to Named: flat
challenge: Make Box<dyn Pricer> cloneable. Add fn boxed_clone(&self) -> Box<dyn Pricer> to the trait, implement it for each type, and write impl Clone for Box<dyn Pricer> using it. Clone a Vec<Box<dyn Pricer>>, change the original, and show the clone is unaffected.
solutionStdout: clones keep their own state: [2, 6] vs [10, 30]
question: Why is &dyn Trait twice the size of &T on a 64-bit machine?
correct: It is a fat pointer: one word for the data pointer and one for the pointer to the vtable
wrong: It stores the value inline next to the pointer, so the second word holds the first bytes of the data
It carries the full type name as a string, which the runtime uses to find the right method each call
Because trait objects are always heap allocated, so the extra word is the allocation's size
reasoning: The reference must find both the value and the methods for its unknown concrete type. The vtable pointer is what makes dynamic dispatch possible.

quiz.question: What does a vtable contain?
quiz.correct: The concrete type's drop glue, size and alignment, and one function pointer per trait method
wrong: The values of all the type's fields, copied once so that every method call can read them directly
The source code of the methods, which the runtime interprets when a call goes through the trait object
A list of every type that implements the trait, searched at each call to find the matching method
quiz.reasoning: The size and alignment are why size_of_val and Box deallocation work on a trait object, and the method pointers are what calls go through.

quiz.question: Why can a trait with fn duplicate(&self) -> Self not be used as dyn Trait?
quiz.correct: The concrete type is unknown behind the trait object, so the size of the returned value is unknown (the trait is not dyn compatible, E0038)
wrong: Because methods cannot return values from a trait object, since the vtable has no slot for return types
Because Self is a keyword reserved for structs, so a trait that mentions it can only describe struct types
Because trait objects have no methods of their own, so any trait that returns Self is rejected by the parser
quiz.reasoning: Returning Self by value needs a known size at the call site. A boxed_clone method returning Box<dyn Trait> sidesteps it.

quiz.question: What does `where Self: Sized` on a generic method do?
quiz.correct: Exempts that method from dyn compatibility: it exists for concrete types but cannot be called through a trait object
wrong: It makes the method callable on trait objects, by giving the vtable a special entry for generic calls
It forces the trait to be implemented only by structs, which rules out enums and primitive types
It makes the method static, so it must be called as Trait::method with no receiver at all
quiz.reasoning: A generic method would need one vtable entry per instantiation, which is impossible. The bound opts it out and the compiler rejects trait-object calls to it.

quiz.question: When is generic (static) dispatch usually preferable to dyn dispatch?
quiz.correct: In hot paths, where monomorphisation allows inlining and direct calls instead of an indirect call through a vtable
wrong: When the collection must hold different concrete types, because a generic can store only one type
When code size must be minimised, since a generic function has only one copy for all of its types
Never: dyn dispatch is always faster, because the vtable lookup is cached by the CPU on every call
quiz.reasoning: Heterogeneous collections and smaller binaries favour trait objects. Tight loops favour generics.

title: Cow, Borrow and AsRef: designing APIs that avoid needless allocation
body: Cow<'a, B>, "clone on write", is an enum with two states: Borrowed(&'a B) and Owned(B::Owned). It lets a function return its input untouched when nothing needs changing and allocate a new value only when it must. normalize_symbol trims and upper-cases tickers: most inputs from a clean feed are already "AAPL", and for them the function returns Cow::Borrowed(input) with zero allocation; only " aapl " or "msft" produce an owned String. The caller treats both uniformly through Deref to str, and can call into_owned() or to_mut() when it needs ownership. to_mut clones a borrowed value on the first call and returns a mutable reference to the owned copy; later calls are free.

AsRef and Borrow look similar and are not interchangeable. AsRef<T> is a cheap reference-to-reference conversion with no extra promises: fn count_upper<S: AsRef<str>>(s: S) accepts String, &str and Box<str> alike, and sum_all<T: AsRef<[i64]>> accepts Vec<i64>, arrays and slices. Borrow<T> makes a stronger contract: the borrowed form must behave identically for Eq, Ord and Hash. That contract is what lets HashMap<String, V>::get accept a &str: get<Q>(&self, k: &Q) where String: Borrow<Q>, Q: Hash + Eq. The program verifies that a String and its &str hash to the same value. A wrapper that compares case-insensitively must not implement Borrow<str>, because lookups would find the wrong buckets; it can implement AsRef<str> safely.

A short guide to parameter types. To only read text, take &str, or impl AsRef<str> when callers hold varied owned types and you want to spare them conversions. To keep the value, take impl Into<String> so the caller can pass an owned String without a copy or a &str that will be allocated. To return something that is often unchanged, return Cow. Using Cow in a hot parsing or normalisation path removes an allocation per record without complicating callers, which is the point of the lesson.

Return Cow when the common case needs no change, accept AsRef for read-only generic inputs, accept Into<String> when you will own the data, and implement Borrow only when Eq, Ord and Hash really agree with the owned form.
expectedStdout:
"AAPL" -> AAPL  (borrowed)
" aapl " -> AAPL  (owned)
"msft" -> MSFT  (owned)
"GOOG" -> GOOG  (borrowed)
"  XOM" -> XOM   (owned)
3 of 5 inputs needed an allocation
before to_mut: borrowed
after to_mut: owned -> buy 100
AsRef<str> accepts &str, String, Box<str>: 2 2 2
AsRef<[i64]> accepts Vec, array, slice: 6 30 15
HashMap<String, _>::get("AAPL") through Borrow<str>: Some(300)
String and &str hash identically (the Borrow contract): true
HashMap<Vec<u8>, _>::get(&[u8] slice): Some("pair")
challenge: Write normalize_all(symbols: &[&str]) -> (Vec<Cow<str>>, usize) returning the normalised tickers and how many needed allocation, and join_ids<I, S>(ids: I) -> String for any IntoIterator whose items are AsRef<str>, joined with commas. Check that a clean feed performs zero allocations and that join_ids accepts a Vec<String>, an array of &str and a slice.
solutionStdout: clean feed allocations: 0, mixed feed allocations: 2
question: What does returning Cow<'_, str> let normalize do?
correct: Return the borrowed input unchanged when no edit is needed, and allocate an owned String only when it had to modify the text
wrong: Always allocate a new String, so the caller owns the result and never has to track the input's lifetime
Mutate the input string in place, avoiding both the allocation and the copy for every kind of edit
Avoid ever returning an owned value, which is why the function can promise it never allocates
reasoning: Cow is "borrowed or owned". For already-clean data the function costs no allocation, and callers use the result through Deref either way.

quiz.question: What does Borrow promise that AsRef does not?
quiz.correct: Equality, ordering and hashing of the borrowed form agree with the owned type, which HashMap lookups rely on
wrong: That the conversion never allocates, which AsRef is allowed to do when it builds a temporary
That the borrowed form is always shorter, so a lookup compares fewer bytes than the owned type
That the type is Copy, so the borrowed and owned forms can be compared without taking any reference
quiz.reasoning: AsRef is just a cheap reference conversion. Borrow adds a semantic contract so a key can be looked up by its borrowed form.

quiz.question: Why does HashMap<String, V>::get("AAPL") compile with a &str argument?
quiz.correct: String implements Borrow<str>, and get accepts any Q where K: Borrow<Q> and Q: Hash + Eq
wrong: Because &str is automatically converted to String first, which costs one allocation for each lookup
Because HashMap stores &str internally, so a String key is only a convenient way to build one
Because get is defined only for str keys, and String is treated as a str by deref coercion
quiz.reasoning: The generic bound lets the lookup use the borrowed form without allocating a temporary String.

quiz.question: What does Cow::to_mut do to a Borrowed value?
quiz.correct: It clones the data into an owned value on the first call and returns a mutable reference to it; later calls are free
wrong: It mutates the original borrowed data in place, so the source string changes for every other reader too
It panics because borrowed data is read-only, so callers must check is_owned() before every call
It always clones, even for owned values, so repeated calls keep allocating a fresh copy each time
quiz.reasoning: This is the "clone on write" behaviour: pay for the allocation only when you actually modify.

quiz.question: Which parameter type fits a function that will store the string it receives?
quiz.correct: impl Into<String>, so the caller can hand over an owned String without copying, or a &str that is allocated once
wrong: impl AsRef<str>, because it accepts every string type and the function can keep the borrowed value
&str, which always allocates inside the function when it keeps the text, so callers lose nothing
&mut String, so the function can take the caller's buffer and keep it without asking for ownership
quiz.reasoning: If you need ownership, asking for it in the signature lets callers avoid a redundant copy. AsRef is for read-only use.

title: Writing iterator adapters: size_hint, DoubleEnded, ExactSize and extension traits
body: Iterator is the most reusable trait in the standard library, and writing your own adapter shows how the pieces fit. An adapter is a struct that wraps another iterator and implements Iterator itself, doing its work lazily inside next. Pairwise yields each consecutive pair of items, which is exactly what you need to turn a price series into changes: [100, 101, 99, 105] becomes (100, 101), (101, 99), (99, 105). It stores the wrapped iterator and the previous item (cloned, so the item type must be Clone), and it never collects anything, so it works on unbounded sources like (0..) and processes one element at a time.

The required method is next; the optional methods are where quality lives. size_hint returns (lower, upper) bounds on the remaining item count. collect and Vec::from_iter use it to preallocate, and a correct, exact hint makes ExactSizeIterator::len available. Pairwise has a subtle hint: before the first call it has not read the first item, so n inner items yield n - 1 pairs; after priming, each remaining inner item produces one pair. The code tracks a primed flag and adjusts both bounds with saturating subtraction, so an empty iterator gives (0, Some(0)) and an infinite one gives (0, None) or a huge lower bound without underflow. Implementing DoubleEndedIterator (next_back) adds .rev() and lets ends be consumed from both sides, which the Doubled adapter does by forwarding to the inner iterator. Not every iterator can promise an exact length: the compiler rejects .len() on a doubled RangeInclusive<i64>, because ranges over 64-bit integers are not ExactSizeIterator (their length might not fit in usize), so the demo uses a Vec iterator where it needs len().

To make adapters read fluently, add an extension trait with a blanket implementation: trait IterExt: Iterator + Sized { fn pairwise(self) -> Pairwise<Self> where Self::Item: Clone } and impl<I: Iterator> IterExt for I {}. Now any iterator has .pairwise(), and it chains with map, filter and the rest. A wrong size_hint is a logic bug, not memory unsafety in safe code, but callers and std rely on it for performance, and the unsafe TrustedLen marker is reserved for the standard library, so test your hints against the real counts.

Keep adapters lazy, implement size_hint correctly (use saturating arithmetic), add DoubleEndedIterator and ExactSizeIterator when they are truthful, expose the adapter through an extension trait, and test against the real item counts.
expectedStdout:
changes of [100, 101, 99, 105] = [1, -2, 6]
pairs: [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3)]
size_hint before the first item: (3, Some(3)), len = 3
size_hint after one item: (2, Some(2)), len = 2
empty: (0, Some(0)), single: (0, Some(0))
infinite source stays lazy: [(0, 1), (1, 2), (2, 3)]
infinite size_hint: None
doubled len = 3, reversed = [6, 4, 2]
from both ends: Some(2) Some(10) 3
size_hint brackets the real count for every length 0..8: true
challenge: Write a Dedup adapter that skips consecutive duplicate items (for example 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 3, 1, 1 gives 1, 2, 3, 1) for Item: PartialEq + Clone, with an honest size_hint (lower bound 0 or 1, upper bound from the inner iterator) and a dedup() extension method. Check it against Vec::dedup on random vectors.
solutionStdout: deduped: [1, 2, 3, 1]; matches Vec::dedup and honours size_hint on 500 random vectors
question: Why does collect() benefit from a correct size_hint, and what does an exact hint enable?
correct: It preallocates capacity from the lower bound, and an exact hint lets ExactSizeIterator::len report the remaining count
wrong: It makes next() run in parallel, using the bounds to split the iterator across the available threads
It sorts the items before collecting, because the bounds tell the collector the order of the elements
It allows the iterator to be cloned cheaply, since the bounds record where to restart from
reasoning: size_hint is advice for consumers. Preallocation avoids repeated growth, and equal bounds mean the length is known without consuming the iterator.

quiz.question: Why does Pairwise::size_hint subtract one before the first item is read?
quiz.correct: Nothing has been read yet, so n inner items will make only n - 1 pairs; once primed, each remaining item makes exactly one pair
wrong: Because pairs are always one fewer than the iterator length, so the same subtraction applies at every step
Because the first item is discarded when the adapter is created, so it never takes part in a pair
Because size_hint counts bytes rather than items, and a pair needs one byte fewer than its source
quiz.reasoning: The adapter's state changes the arithmetic. Tracking primed lets both bounds stay correct at every step.

quiz.question: Why add an extension trait with a blanket impl for every Iterator?
quiz.correct: It gives every iterator the new method so adapters chain fluently, like iter.pairwise().map(..)
wrong: It is required to implement Iterator, because every adapter must expose its own constructor method
It makes the adapter faster, since the blanket impl lets the compiler skip bounds checks entirely
It lets the adapter mutate the source iterator after it has been consumed by a for loop
quiz.reasoning: impl<I: Iterator> IterExt for I {} attaches the method everywhere without modifying std types.

quiz.question: What does implementing DoubleEndedIterator add?
quiz.correct: next_back, which enables .rev() and consuming the iterator from both ends
wrong: Parallel iteration, because both ends can be consumed by different threads without locking
Random access by index, so the iterator can be read at any position without consuming items
Cloning of the iterator, which the second end needs to remember where the first one stopped
quiz.reasoning: Adapters that can preserve order from the back, such as Doubled, forward the call to the inner iterator.

quiz.question: What is the consequence of a wrong size_hint in safe code?
quiz.correct: A logic error with poor performance or surprising len() results, but not undefined behaviour; unsafe code must not trust it
wrong: Undefined behaviour in safe code, because the standard library trusts the hint when it allocates the buffer
A compile error, since the trait checks that the lower bound never exceeds the real item count
The iterator stops being lazy, because collecting must now read every item before it can continue
quiz.reasoning: The hint is advisory. Only the unsafe TrustedLen trait, reserved for the standard library, promises exactness.

title: Error design without dependencies: typed enums, source chains and boundaries
body: Good error handling is part of an API. A library should expose a typed error enum so callers can match on the failure and decide what to do. OrderError has one variant per way an order line can be wrong, and each variant carries the data that explains it: the offending text, the field name, or the underlying ParseIntError. To work with ?, `std::error::Error`, and error reporting, implement Display for a one-line description of this error alone, and Error with a source() method that returns the underlying cause when there is one. This is what the thiserror crate generates; writing it by hand once shows how little magic it contains.

Chains compose across layers. LineError wraps an OrderError with the line number, and its source() returns the OrderError, whose source() returns the ParseIntError. A reporter walks the chain with a loop over source() and prints "line 2 <- caused by: bad quantity `abc` <- caused by: invalid digit found in string". The rule that makes this work: an error's Display should describe only itself, not repeat its source, because the reporter prints the cause separately and duplicated text becomes noise. Use map_err to attach context at the layer that knows it (the line number lives in load, not in parse_order) and ? to propagate unchanged.

Choose the type for the boundary. Libraries return concrete enums, and mark public enums #[non_exhaustive] so that adding a variant later is not a breaking change, since downstream matches must include a wildcard arm. Applications often return Box<dyn Error> at the top level, where the only goal is to report and exit; ? converts any error into it through From, and downcast_ref::<LineError>() recovers the concrete type when the program does need to inspect one. Avoid stringly-typed errors (Err(String)): they lose the structure, the source chain and the ability to match.

Give each failure its own variant with data, implement Display (this error only) and source (the cause), add context with map_err where it is known, return typed errors from libraries and Box<dyn Error> at application edges, and mark growing public enums #[non_exhaustive].
expectedStdout:
parsed 2 orders, notional cents = 3951250
missing price: line 1 <- caused by: missing field `price`
bad side: line 1 <- caused by: unknown side `HOLD` (expected BUY or SELL)
bad quantity: line 2 <- caused by: bad quantity `abc` <- caused by: invalid digit found in string
bad price: line 1 <- caused by: bad price `142.1`: expected exactly two decimals
through Box<dyn Error>: line 2 <- caused by: bad quantity `-1` <- caused by: invalid digit found in string
downcast recovered the line number: 2
source chain depth for a bad quantity: 1
a missing field has no source: true
challenge: Change load to collect every bad line instead of stopping at the first: return Result<Vec<Order>, Vec<LineError>>. Print how many lines failed and the full chain of the first failure, and show that a file of only valid lines still returns Ok.
solutionStdout:
2 of 4 lines failed
first failure: line 2 <- caused by: bad quantity `x` <- caused by: invalid digit found in string
last failure: line 3 <- caused by: unknown side `HOLD` (expected BUY or SELL)
question: Why does OrderError::BadQuantity implement source() and keep its Display short?
correct: So reporters can walk the chain to the root cause without the outer message repeating it
wrong: Because Display cannot contain data, so the details of the failure must live in the source instead
Because source() replaces Display, so the error's own message is never printed when a cause exists
To make the error Copy, since a short Display message lets the compiler duplicate the value cheaply
reasoning: Display describes this error alone; source() exposes the underlying cause. A reporter joins them, so repeating the cause in Display would print it twice.

quiz.question: When should a function return Box<dyn Error> instead of a typed enum?
quiz.correct: At application edges where the caller only reports the failure; libraries return typed errors so callers can match and react
wrong: Always, because enums are slower than trait objects when the compiler has to match on their variants
Never: Box<dyn Error> is deprecated, and every function should return its own typed enum instead
Only in code that uses threads, since trait objects are the only error type that is safe to send
quiz.reasoning: Typed errors give callers structure to act on. Boxing is convenient at the top of a program, where errors are logged and the process exits.

quiz.question: What does #[non_exhaustive] on a public enum accomplish?
quiz.correct: Downstream crates must include a wildcard arm when matching it, so adding a variant later is not a breaking change
wrong: It prevents the enum from being matched at all outside its own crate, so callers use methods instead
It makes every variant optional, so a value can be built without choosing any variant at all
It removes the Debug implementation, because extensible enums cannot be printed without a wildcard arm
quiz.reasoning: The attribute affects other crates, so the library keeps the freedom to grow the enum.

quiz.question: What does ? do with a LineError in a function returning Result<_, Box<dyn Error>>?
quiz.correct: It converts the error into the box with From and returns early; downcast_ref can later recover the LineError
wrong: It prints the error and continues, so the function keeps running after the failing line is reported
It unwraps the error and panics, because Box<dyn Error> cannot carry a LineError through a return
It discards the source chain, so only the outermost message survives the conversion into the box
quiz.reasoning: Any type implementing Error converts into Box<dyn Error>. The source chain stays attached to the boxed value.

quiz.question: Where should the line number be attached to an OrderError?
quiz.correct: In load, which knows the line, using map_err; parse_order only knows about one line of text
wrong: Inside every variant of OrderError, so each parse failure records the line it came from itself
In main, by parsing the error message string to find the number that the lower layer mentioned
It cannot be attached, because an error value is immutable once the lower layer has created it
quiz.reasoning: Context should be added by the layer that has it. Wrapping in LineError keeps the lower layer reusable.

title: Panics, unwinding and ABI boundaries: catch_unwind, poisoning and C-unwind
body: A panic is Rust's response to a bug or an impossible state. With the default panic strategy (unwind) it runs destructors for every value on the way up the stack, then either ends the thread or is caught. With panic = "abort" it terminates the process immediately and no destructors run. Unwinding is what makes RAII cleanup work during a panic: the Guard in the program prints "cleanup" while the stack unwinds. std::panic::catch_unwind stops an unwind at a chosen point and returns Result<T, Box<dyn Any + Send>>; the payload is a &str for panic!("literal") and a String for a formatted message, so downcast_ref recovers the text. Catching panics is for isolation boundaries such as a worker thread pool or a plugin call, not for ordinary error handling, which belongs to Result.

Two things guard against observing half-finished state. A closure that captures &mut data is not UnwindSafe, because after a caught panic the data might violate its invariants; AssertUnwindSafe is the explicit statement that you have considered it. And Mutex poisoning applies this idea to locks: if a thread panics while holding the guard, the mutex is marked poisoned, lock() returns Err(PoisonError), and you decide whether the data is still usable; into_inner on the error gives the guard back. Thread::join similarly returns Err when the thread panicked. All of these assume the unwind strategy; under panic = "abort" there is nothing to catch.

The ABI boundary is the sharp edge. Unwinding out of a function declared extern "C" is not allowed to continue into a caller that cannot handle it, and since Rust 1.81 the runtime aborts the process instead: running the check for this lesson on 1.99, a panic in a plain extern "C" fn printed "before" and then killed the process with SIGABRT. If the caller can unwind (Rust code calling through the C ABI, or C++ built with exceptions that you control), declare extern "C-unwind" so the panic may propagate, and catch it on the other side. Never let a panic cross into C code that does not expect it.

Use Result for expected failures and panics for bugs, catch panics only at isolation boundaries, wrap captured state in AssertUnwindSafe consciously, handle poisoned locks on purpose, and declare "C-unwind" (never plain "C") on functions that may panic across an ABI boundary.

wrong: The panic is converted into a returned error code, which the C caller receives as the function's result

The panic is silently ignored and the function returns its default value to the caller instead

quiz.correct: A thread panicked while holding the guard, so the data may be half-updated; into_inner on the PoisonError recovers it
wrong: Mutexes poison whenever a thread exits while it still has a clone of the Arc, and the data is then lost

quiz.question: Why is AssertUnwindSafe needed for a closure that mutates captured state?
quiz.correct: After a caught panic the state might violate its invariants, so the compiler requires an explicit assertion that you have considered it
wrong: Because closures cannot be called twice after a panic, so the wrapper marks the call as consumed
To make the panic message shorter, since the wrapper replaces the payload with a one-line summary
Because mutable references cannot be sent between threads, and catch_unwind runs the closure on another thread

wrong: Never: a panic skips destructors, which is why resources must be released with explicit cleanup calls
Only for values in the panicking function, because the frames above it are discarded without cleanup

quiz.reasoning: Unwinding drops each live value on the way up the stack. Aborting terminates immediately.

title: IEEE 754 floating point: what f64 really stores
body: An f64 is a 64-bit pattern: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits and 52 fraction bits. For normal numbers the value is (-1)^sign * 1.fraction * 2^(exponent - 1023), where the leading 1 is implicit. to_bits exposes the pattern, so 1.0 has exponent field 1023 and an all-zero fraction. Because the fraction has finite length, only numbers of the form m * 2^k are exact. 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 are not, so each is stored as the nearest representable neighbour, and arithmetic on those neighbours then rounds again.

That is why 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 is false: the rounded sum lands one unit in the last place (ulp) away from the rounded literal 0.3. The gap between adjacent doubles grows with magnitude. Near 1.0 it is f64::EPSILON, about 2.2e-16, but near 1e16 neighbours are 2 apart, so adding 1.0 is absorbed and 1e16 + 1.0 == 1e16 is true. Subtracting nearly equal numbers causes catastrophic cancellation: (1 + x) - 1 for x = 1e-15 should be x, yet the leading digits cancel and what remains is mostly the rounding error of 1 + x, giving a relative error above 10 percent.

Equality on computed floats is therefore the wrong question. Compare with a tolerance scaled to the magnitude of the operands, or avoid floats for exact quantities and use integers. Subnormal numbers fill the gap below f64::MIN_POSITIVE with reduced precision, which keeps tiny results from flushing to zero but can be slow on some CPUs. Summing many values accumulates rounding error, so summation order and compensated algorithms matter; the next lessons return to that.

Check which quantity is exact (prices, quantities and counts should be integers), compare floats with a relative tolerance and never with ==, watch for absorption when mixing very large and very small magnitudes, and avoid subtracting nearly equal values when a rearranged formula exists.

question: Why does 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 evaluate to false in Rust?
correct: None of 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 is exactly representable in binary, and the rounded sum lands one unit in the last place from 0.3
wrong: Rust compares floats by their decimal string forms, and "0.30000000000000004" is a different string from "0.3"
Floating-point addition is only inexact in debug builds, so the same comparison is true in a release build
The literal 0.3 is stored as an integer, so comparing it with the float sum always converts and then fails
reasoning: The behaviour comes from IEEE 754 binary representation, which Rust follows in every build mode. The values are doubles, == compares their bit-level values (with NaN and zero special cases), and no string comparison is involved.

quiz.question: How are the 64 bits of an f64 divided?
quiz.correct: 1 sign bit, 11 exponent bits and 52 fraction bits, with an implicit leading 1 for normal numbers
wrong: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits and 23 fraction bits, with an implicit leading 1 for normal numbers
1 sign bit and 63 fraction bits, with the exponent kept in a separate field stored beside the number
11 sign bits and 53 fraction bits, so the exponent is implied by the position of the first set bit
quiz.reasoning: That layout is IEEE 754 binary64. The 8 and 23 split is f32. The implicit leading 1 gives 53 bits of precision.

quiz.question: Why is 1e16 + 1.0 == 1e16 true for f64?
quiz.correct: Near 1e16 adjacent doubles are 2 apart, so adding 1.0 rounds back to the same value
wrong: f64 saturates at 1e16, so any larger sum is clamped back to that value instead of growing
== ignores the lowest bit of the mantissa, so values that differ by one bit compare as equal
The addition overflows to infinity, and infinity compares equal to 1e16 under IEEE rules
quiz.reasoning: The gap between doubles scales with magnitude. A change smaller than half the gap is absorbed by rounding.

quiz.question: What is the right way to compare two computed prices stored as f64?
quiz.correct: Use a tolerance relative to their magnitude, or store prices as integer ticks and compare exactly
wrong: Use == because Rust floats are exact to 15 digits, so equal-looking computed prices are always equal
Convert both to strings and compare, since the printed form hides the last bits of rounding error
Round both to an integer number of dollars, which removes the error without losing the cents
quiz.reasoning: Computed floats carry rounding error, so exact equality is brittle. Integers avoid the issue for quantities with a natural unit.

quiz.question: What is catastrophic cancellation?
quiz.correct: Subtracting nearly equal numbers cancels the leading digits, leaving mostly the rounding error of earlier steps
wrong: An overflow caused by subtracting a large number from a small one, which wraps the result around
A panic raised when two floats are equal, because their difference would be exactly zero
Rounding that always makes the result of a subtraction zero, whatever the operands were
quiz.reasoning: The subtraction itself is exact, but it exposes error that was already in the operands, so relative accuracy collapses.

title: NaN, signed zero and total ordering of floats
body: Floating point reserves a family of bit patterns for NaN (not a number), produced by operations such as 0.0 / 0.0 or inf - inf. NaN is unordered: it is not equal to anything, including itself, and partial_cmp against any number returns None. That is why f64 implements PartialOrd and PartialEq but not Ord or Eq, and why a Vec<f64> has no sort() method and a BTreeMap<f64, _> does not compile. The language is protecting you from containers whose invariants would break when a NaN arrives.

There are also two zeros. 0.0 == -0.0 is true under ==, yet they have different bits and 1.0 / -0.0 is negative infinity. f64::total_cmp implements the IEEE totalOrder predicate, a genuine total order on all bit patterns: negative NaN, negative infinity, finite negatives, -0.0, +0.0, finite positives, positive infinity, positive NaN. Use sort_by(f64::total_cmp) to sort safely. The common alternative, sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap()), panics the first time it compares a NaN.

To use floats as keys, wrap them in a newtype whose Eq, Ord and Hash are all built from the same notion of identity. Here equality is total_cmp == Equal, which holds exactly when the bit patterns are equal, so hashing to_bits is consistent with it, as the Hash contract requires. min and max follow a different rule: f64::max returns the non-NaN operand, so NaN can silently vanish from a running maximum. In trading code the best defence is to reject NaN at the boundary where data enters, and to use integer ticks for prices so the question rarely arises.
Check that no NaN can reach a sort, key or comparison unexpectedly, choose total_cmp when you need an order, keep Eq/Ord/Hash consistent in a key wrapper, and remember that max and min ignore NaN.

question: Why does Rust give f64 PartialOrd but not Ord?
correct: NaN is unordered, so f64 comparisons are only a partial order, without the total order that sorting and BTreeMap need
wrong: Floating-point values cannot be compared at all, so == and < are rejected by the compiler for f64
Ord is reserved for integer types in the standard library, because floats have no meaningful size
NaN compares equal to every other value, so no ordering of f64 values could ever be consistent
reasoning: Ord requires every pair of values to be comparable and consistent. NaN breaks that. f64 comparisons work, but only as a partial order.

wrong: NaN, because any operation with NaN returns NaN

quiz.question: Where does total_cmp place -0.0 and NaN?
quiz.correct: -0.0 sorts below +0.0, and positive NaN sorts above positive infinity
wrong: -0.0 equals +0.0 and NaN is rejected with an error before sorting begins
NaN sorts first of all and -0.0 sorts last, after every positive finite number
NaN equals infinity under total_cmp, and both zeros are treated as the same value
quiz.reasoning: total_cmp follows the IEEE totalOrder predicate, which distinguishes zeros by sign and orders NaN beyond the infinities according to its sign.

quiz.question: Why is hashing to_bits consistent with an Eq based on total_cmp == Equal?
quiz.correct: total_cmp is Equal exactly when the bit patterns are identical, so equal keys always hash the same
wrong: Because hashing floats ignores the sign bit, so -0.0 and 0.0 always land in the same bucket
Because to_bits normalises NaN payloads, so every NaN hashes the same regardless of its bits
Because HashSet never compares keys, so the hash alone decides whether two floats are equal
quiz.reasoning: The Hash contract requires k1 == k2 to imply equal hashes. Bit-identical values hash identically.

quiz.correct: partial_cmp returns None for a NaN comparison and unwrap panics
wrong: It silently puts NaN first in the sorted output and keeps going
It sorts correctly but slowly, because NaN forces extra comparisons
It removes the NaN values from the slice before sorting begins
quiz.reasoning: The comparator must produce an Ordering for every pair it sees. None cannot be unwrapped.

title: Fixed-point money: exact integer arithmetic with checked operations
body: Money and prices are decimal quantities with a natural smallest unit, so store them as integers of that unit. Here a Money(i64) counts units of 1/10,000 (a scale of four decimal places). Integer addition and subtraction are exact, so ten additions of 0.1000 equal 1.0000 exactly, which f64 cannot promise. The type is a newtype: it prevents mixing raw integers and amounts, lets you implement Display once, and gives one place to put overflow policy.

Parsing must be explicit, not "parse an f64 and multiply by 10,000". The f64 parse has already rounded the decimal, so a price such as 1.0005 may arrive as 1.00049999..., and a later round turns the wrong way. The parser here splits at the decimal point, validates digits, rejects more than four decimals instead of silently rounding, pads the fraction to four digits and combines the parts with checked_mul and checked_add so a huge input becomes an Overflow error instead of wrapping.

Multiplication and scaling are where bugs hide. price * quantity can overflow i64 for large positions, so use checked_mul and surface None. Scaling by a ratio (price * numerator / denominator) can overflow in the intermediate product even when the final answer fits, so the code widens to i128, divides, rounds half away from zero on the magnitude and only then narrows with try_from. Display formats the integer part and a four-digit zero-padded fraction from unsigned_abs, which also handles i64::MIN without overflow.

Check that amounts are integers of a documented unit, parsing rejects excess precision rather than rounding silently, every arithmetic operation that can overflow is checked, and any division states its rounding rule.

question: Why store amounts as integers of a fixed scale instead of f64?
correct: Integer addition and subtraction are exact, so repeated sums such as ten times 0.1 equal 1.0 exactly
wrong: Integers are always faster than floating point, so the choice is about speed rather than exactness
f64 cannot represent any decimal fraction at all, so every money amount in f64 is already wrong
Rust forbids floating point for currency, and the compiler rejects f64 in money types
reasoning: Binary floating point cannot represent most decimals exactly, and errors accumulate. Fixed-point integers make the unit explicit and arithmetic exact. Speed is not the reason, f64 can represent some fractions exactly, and Rust has no such rule.

quiz.question: Why does the parser split the text instead of parsing an f64 and multiplying by 10,000?
quiz.correct: The f64 parse has already rounded the decimal, so the scaled integer can be off by one unit
wrong: Splitting is required by the Rust grammar, which does not allow a decimal point in a number literal parse
f64::from_str cannot parse a decimal point, so the text has to be split before any parsing
Multiplication by 10,000 is not allowed on floats, because it changes the exponent bits
quiz.reasoning: A decimal like 1.0005 may become 1.00049999... as a double. Parsing the digits directly keeps the exact decimal value.

quiz.question: Why does scaled() widen to i128 before dividing?
quiz.correct: price * numerator can exceed i64 even when the result fits, and i128 avoids a wrong or panicking intermediate
wrong: i128 division is always exact, so no rounding rule is needed once the intermediate is wide enough
It makes rounding unnecessary, because a wider integer type never produces a remainder in a division
It lets the function accept a zero denominator, since i128 division by zero returns zero
quiz.reasoning: The product is formed before the division, so its range matters. Rounding still has to be chosen explicitly, and zero denominators are rejected separately.

quiz.question: What does Money(-5).scaled(1, 2) produce, with 5 units halved and rounded half away from zero?
quiz.correct: -3 units, because the magnitude 2.5 rounds up to 3 and the sign is restored
wrong: -2 units, because the magnitude 2.5 rounds down to 2 and the sign is restored
-2.5 units, because the result keeps the fraction and is stored as a float
0 units, because a negative value halved by one is rounded toward zero
quiz.reasoning: The code rounds the magnitude (2 * 5 + 2) / 4 = 3 and then reapplies the negative sign.

quiz.question: Why format with unsigned_abs instead of abs?
quiz.correct: abs overflows for i64::MIN, while unsigned_abs returns a u64 that can hold it
wrong: unsigned_abs is faster because it skips the sign check that abs performs at run time
abs is not defined for i64, so only unsigned_abs compiles for signed integer types
abs rounds toward zero for negative values, while unsigned_abs rounds away from it
quiz.reasoning: i64::MIN has no positive i64 counterpart. unsigned_abs returns the magnitude as u64 without overflow.

title: Rounding modes and tick sizes for prices
body: Exchanges list prices on a grid: the tick size is the smallest allowed price increment, so every order price must be an integer multiple of it. Converting a computed value onto the grid is integer division with a rounding rule. The rule is a business decision: a buy limit must never be rounded up past the trader's limit, so buys floor to the tick; a sell limit must never be rounded below, so sells ceil. Round-to-nearest is for display and marks, not for protecting a limit.

Integer division in Rust truncates toward zero and % takes the dividend's sign, which makes floor logic wrong for negative numerators. div_euclid and rem_euclid give the floor quotient and a non-negative remainder when the divisor is positive, so q + 1 is the ceiling whenever the remainder is non-zero. From that, five modes follow: Floor, Ceil, TowardZero (truncate), HalfUp (ties go toward positive infinity) and HalfEven (ties go to the even neighbour). A tie means the remainder is exactly half of the divisor.

Why bother with half-even? Rounding ties always up adds a small upward bias to a long sum. The program rounds half-units 0.5, 1.5, 2.5, 3.5: the exact sum is 8, half-up gives 10 and half-even gives 8, because the ties split evenly up and down. Whenever many rounded values are added, bias accumulates linearly while the unbiased error grows more slowly. Decide the mode once, in one function, and test it on negative values and exact ties.
Check that every price sent to a venue is a multiple of the tick, buys floor and sells ceil, ties are handled by a documented mode, and negative numerators are tested.

correct: 100.35, which floors the limit so the buyer never pays more than the stated limit
wrong: 100.40, the nearest tick above the limit, because a buyer should always round up to be filled

quiz.question: Why use div_euclid and rem_euclid instead of / and % when flooring?
quiz.correct: / truncates toward zero and % takes the dividend's sign, which gives the wrong floor for negative numbers
wrong: / and % are not defined for negative numbers, so negative values must use the euclid methods
Euclidean division is always faster than / and %, so it is the better default for every case
They round to nearest instead of truncating, which is what the tick conversion needs
quiz.reasoning: For d > 0, div_euclid is the floor quotient and rem_euclid is in 0..d, which makes floor and ceiling logic straightforward.

quiz.question: What does round_div(-5, 2, HalfUp) return, where HalfUp sends ties toward positive infinity?
quiz.correct: -2, because -2.5 is a tie and ties go toward +infinity
wrong: -3, because -2.5 is a tie and ties always go away from zero
-2.5, because a tie keeps its fractional part when rounded
0, because ties between two negative integers collapse to zero
quiz.reasoning: The floor quotient is -3 with remainder 1. A remainder of half the divisor is a tie, so HalfUp returns q + 1 = -2.

quiz.question: Why is half-even preferred when many rounded values are summed?
quiz.correct: Ties go up and down equally often, so the systematic upward bias of always rounding ties up disappears
wrong: It is the only mode that never needs a remainder, so it is cheaper than the others on large sums
It produces a smaller average error for non-tie values than any other mode, so the total drifts less
It guarantees the result is a multiple of the tick, which the other modes cannot do
quiz.reasoning: Non-tie values round identically in both modes. Only ties differ, and alternating them removes the bias.

quiz.question: A sell limit of 100.37 with a 0.05 tick should be sent at which price?
quiz.correct: 100.40, which ceils the limit so the seller never receives less than the stated limit
wrong: 100.35, which floors the limit so the seller gives up a little less than the stated limit
100.37, because off-grid prices are accepted and rounded by the venue at the match
100.45, one tick of safety margin above the next grid price, to make sure the order fills
quiz.reasoning: Sell limits are floors on proceeds, so they round up to the next grid price.

title: Streaming mean and variance with Welford's algorithm
body: A stream of prices or returns is too long to store, so mean and variance must be updated one observation at a time. The textbook shortcut keeps a running sum and a running sum of squares and computes variance as (sum of squares - sum^2 / n) / (n - 1). It is algebraically right and numerically dangerous: when the mean is large and the spread small, both terms are huge and nearly equal, and subtracting them is catastrophic cancellation. With values near 1e9 and a true variance of 30, the squares are near 1e18, where adjacent doubles are 128 apart, so the answer is mostly rounding error.

Welford's algorithm tracks the count n, the mean and m2, the sum of squared deviations from the current mean. For each x it computes delta = x - mean, updates mean += delta / n, then m2 += delta * (x - mean), using the old and the new mean. Nothing large is ever subtracted from something nearly equal, so accuracy holds even at 1e9. The sample variance is m2 / (n - 1), known as Bessel's correction: the mean is estimated from the same data, so dividing by n would underestimate the population variance. After a single observation the sample variance is undefined, so the method returns None.

Two partial results can be combined exactly with Chan's formula: n = na + nb, mean = mean_a + delta * nb / n and m2 = m2a + m2b + delta^2 * na * nb / n, where delta = mean_b - mean_a. That makes the statistic parallel and distributable: compute one Welford per chunk or per thread, then merge. The program checks that merging two halves matches a single pass to within 1e-9.

Check that no large nearly equal quantities are subtracted, that n - 1 is used for samples and undefined cases return None, and that partial accumulators are merged with the exact formula rather than averaged.

true variance = 30
welford variance = 30.000000
naive variance is off by more than 1: true
merged mean matches single pass: true

challenge: Write streaming_zscores(values) that returns, for each value, its z-score against the Welford statistics of all earlier values (None for the first two points, or when the earlier variance is zero). Print the z-score of the last point of [10, 11, 9, 10, 30].
question: Why is the sum-of-squares variance formula unreliable for prices near 1e9 with a spread of a few units?
correct: It subtracts two huge nearly equal numbers, so catastrophic cancellation leaves mostly rounding error
wrong: Squaring a price always overflows f64, so the sum of squares becomes infinity for large inputs
The formula is wrong for any data with a non-zero mean, so it only works for centred data
f64 cannot store numbers above 1e8, so squares of prices near 1e9 are rounded to the nearest 1e8
reasoning: The formula is algebraically valid, and f64 reaches about 1.8e308. The problem is precision: near 1e18 adjacent doubles differ by 128, which swamps a true difference of 90.

quiz.question: Why does the sample variance divide by n - 1?
quiz.correct: The mean was estimated from the same data, so dividing by n would underestimate the population variance
wrong: To keep the result an integer whenever the observations are integers, which dividing by n would not
Because the first value is always discarded as a warm-up, leaving n - 1 usable observations
To avoid division by zero when n = 1, which is the only reason the correction exists
quiz.reasoning: Bessel's correction gives an unbiased estimator of the population variance. With one sample the variance is undefined, which is why the code returns None.

quiz.question: What does merge allow that a plain average of two variances does not?
quiz.correct: Combining partial statistics from separate chunks into the exact result of a single pass
wrong: Skipping the final sample in each chunk so that the chunks do not overlap when combined
Computing variance without storing a count, because merge works on the means alone
Estimating variance for infinite streams without any error, since the chunks are merged exactly
quiz.reasoning: Chan's formula adds the between-group term delta^2 * na * nb / n, which averaging the variances would miss.

quiz.question: What should variance() return after exactly one observation?
quiz.correct: None, because a sample variance needs at least two observations
wrong: 0.0, because one observation has no spread around its own mean
NaN, because dividing by n - 1 = 0 gives an undefined result
The observation itself, because a single value is its own variance
quiz.reasoning: Returning Some(0.0) would claim certainty that one point cannot give. An Option forces callers to handle the undefined case.

quiz.question: In the streaming z-score solution, why is the new point scored before it is pushed?
quiz.correct: Including the point in its own history would shrink its z-score and hide outliers
wrong: Because push mutates the mean in a way that a z-score calculation cannot read afterwards
To avoid dividing by zero on the first value, where the standard deviation is undefined
Because Welford cannot be queried after a push, only before the first value arrives
quiz.reasoning: An outlier changes the mean and spread when it is included, making it look less extreme. Scoring against prior history gives the signal a trader would have had.

title: Rolling windows and exponential moving averages in O(1) per update
body: A rolling statistic summarises the last w observations. Recomputing it from scratch costs O(w) per tick; maintaining running totals costs O(1). Keep the window in a VecDeque, which supports push_back and pop_front in constant time, plus the running sum and sum of squares. On each new value, if the window is full, pop the oldest and subtract it, then add the new one. The mean is sum / w and the sample variance is (w * sum_sq - sum^2) / (w * (w - 1)).

Floating-point running sums drift: every subtract-and-add leaves a rounding residue that accumulates, and the squared form suffers cancellation. When inputs are integer ticks, avoid the problem entirely by accumulating in i128. The totals are then exact, adding and removing a value restores the state bit for bit, and only the final division becomes floating point. The program checks every window against a brute-force recomputation. Warm-up semantics matter too: until the window holds w values the statistic is not defined, so the methods return None instead of a misleading partial answer.

An exponential moving average (EMA) needs no window at all: ema = alpha * x + (1 - alpha) * previous, with alpha = 2 / (span + 1), so the weight of an observation k steps old is alpha * (1 - alpha)^k. The first value seeds the average. Choosing alpha through a half-life h instead, alpha = 1 - 0.5^(1/h), makes the memory interpretable: an observation loses half its weight every h steps. Rolling windows forget abruptly, an observation counting fully until it falls off the end, while EMAs forget smoothly, which is why they produce fewer jumps.
Check that the window length and warm-up rule are explicit, that integer inputs use exact integer accumulators, that updates are O(1), and that alpha is derived from a stated span or half-life.

question: Why does the rolling statistic accumulate integer ticks in i128 instead of using f64 running sums?
correct: Integer totals are exact, so adding and later removing a value restores the state exactly with no rounding drift
wrong: i128 arithmetic is faster than f64 on current CPUs, so the running sums cost fewer cycles
f64 cannot represent prices above 1000, so larger ticks would lose their low digits
It lets the window length change at run time without recomputing any of the stored totals
reasoning: Each f64 add/subtract rounds, and the residues accumulate over millions of updates. Integers carry exact totals; only the final division is floating point. Speed and range are not the reason.

quiz.question: What should mean() return before the window has w observations?
quiz.correct: None, because a partial window is a different statistic and returning a number would mislead
wrong: 0.0, because the missing observations count as zero and the mean is taken over the window length
The mean of whatever has arrived, labelled as complete so the caller cannot tell the difference
It should panic, because asking for a statistic before the window is full is a programming bug
quiz.reasoning: The warm-up rule is part of the definition. An Option makes callers decide how to treat the first w - 1 ticks.

quiz.question: How is alpha related to the span of an EMA?
quiz.correct: alpha = 2 / (span + 1), so a larger span gives a smaller alpha and a longer memory
wrong: alpha = span / 2, so a larger span gives a larger alpha and a faster reaction
alpha = 1 / span^2 for every EMA, so memory shrinks quadratically with the span
alpha is always 0.5, and the span only sets the number of values used to seed it
quiz.reasoning: The span convention matches the centre of mass of a simple window, so a span of 3 gives alpha 0.5 and a span of 19 gives 0.1.

quiz.question: What does an EMA half-life of h steps mean?
quiz.correct: An observation loses half of its weight after h steps, because (1 - alpha)^h = 0.5
wrong: The EMA is recomputed from scratch every h steps, which resets all accumulated weights
The window holds exactly h observations, each with the same weight as the others
alpha equals 1 / h, so a half-life of 5 gives a smoothing factor of 0.2 per step
quiz.reasoning: The half-life parametrisation fixes the decay rate directly: alpha = 1 - 0.5^(1/h).

quiz.question: What is the cost of a rolling update with running totals compared with recomputing the window?
quiz.correct: O(1) per tick versus O(w) per tick
wrong: O(w) per tick for both approaches
O(log w) per tick versus O(w) per tick
O(1) per tick versus O(w^2) per tick
quiz.reasoning: Popping the oldest value and adding the newest changes the totals in constant time, while recomputation touches every element of the window.

title: Reproducible Monte Carlo with a seeded xorshift generator
body: Monte Carlo estimates a quantity by averaging random samples. Two properties matter more than raw speed: reproducibility and a known error. A reproducible run uses an explicit seed so the same inputs produce the same stream, which lets you rerun a failing test, compare two code versions and audit a result. Operating-system randomness gives none of that. Here the generator is xorshift64*, a few shifts, xors and a multiply on a u64 state. It is fast and statistically adequate for simulation, it must start from a non-zero state, and it is not cryptographically secure: its outputs let an observer predict the rest.

To turn 64 random bits into a uniform f64 in [0, 1), keep the top 53 bits (next_u64() >> 11) and divide by 2^53. An f64 has a 53-bit significand, so every such value is exactly representable and the result can never equal 1.0. The program estimates pi by sampling points in the unit square and counting how many fall inside the quarter circle: pi is about 4 times the hit fraction. With p the hit probability and N samples, the standard error is 4 * sqrt(p * (1 - p) / N).

That formula is the heart of the method. Error shrinks as 1 / sqrt(N), so 100 times more samples buy only 10 times more accuracy; a 2.5 sigma interval around the estimate is a statement about the estimator, not a guarantee about one run. Always report the estimate with its standard error. For independent streams in parallel work, derive each stream's seed from a master seed and an index with a mixing function such as splitmix64, rather than seeding with consecutive integers, which produce correlated starts.
Check that every random source takes an explicit seed, state is never zero, floats are built from the top 53 bits, results carry a standard error, and parallel streams have mixed independent seeds.
