projectChecks.name: JSON round trip and rejections

quiz.question: What does #[serde(deny_unknown_fields)] do?
quiz.correct: Deserialization fails when the input contains a field the struct does not declare, catching typos and version drift
wrong: It deletes unknown fields from the input file, so a later save writes the cleaned version
It stores unknown fields in a hidden map so they can be written back unchanged on output
It makes serialization skip fields that are None, so the output stays free of null values
quiz.reasoning: By default serde ignores extra keys. The attribute turns them into errors, which is stricter and often safer for configuration and protocol messages.

quiz.question: What do default and skip_serializing_if = "Option::is_none" do for the venue field?
quiz.correct: A missing key becomes None on input, and a None value is omitted from the output
wrong: They make venue mandatory on input and output, so a missing key is reported as an error
They serialize None as the string "None", which keeps the key present in every record
They convert venue into a number, with None mapped to zero in the JSON
quiz.reasoning: default supplies a value when the key is absent and skip_serializing_if suppresses the key when the predicate is true, so the optional field round-trips cleanly.

quiz.question: Why are JSON numbers risky for money amounts?
quiz.correct: Many consumers parse JSON numbers as f64, so decimal values can lose exactness; strings or integer ticks stay exact
wrong: JSON cannot contain numbers with decimals, so every price needs to be written as an integer
serde_json refuses to write numbers above 100, so larger prices must be stored as text
JSON numbers are always integers, so a decimal price is silently truncated when written
quiz.reasoning: The JSON grammar allows decimals, but the receiver decides how to parse them. A string with fixed decimals is unambiguous.

quiz.question: Why does Deserialize for Price read a String instead of a &str?
quiz.correct: A borrowed &str works only when the input can lend the text without unescaping; String works with every deserializer
wrong: Because &str cannot hold digits, so a numeric text must be copied into an owned String first
Because String is faster to parse than a &str, since parse can reuse the allocation
Because the Deserialize trait forbids borrowed data, so every field must be an owned type
quiz.reasoning: Zero-copy deserialization is possible with the right lifetime bounds, but it only works when the input is available unchanged. Owned data is the portable default.

title: Benchmarking honestly: warm-up, black_box and medians
body: A benchmark answers one question: how long does this exact work take on this machine under these conditions? Rust compiles with an optimizer that is very good at noticing that a result is never used, or that an input is a constant, and then deleting or pre-computing the work. A loop that merely calls a pure function and discards the answer can time as zero nanoseconds. std::hint::black_box is the standard tool: it returns its argument unchanged but asks the compiler to treat the value as if it came from and went to somewhere unknown. Wrap both the input that would otherwise be a visible constant and the result that would otherwise be unused. The documentation calls it best effort, so a surprisingly fast number is a reason to inspect the machine code, not a reason to celebrate.

A trustworthy harness has three parts. Warm-up runs execute the work before recording so caches, branch predictors, lazily initialised statics and page tables are in their steady state. Repeated samples are each timed with Instant, a monotonic clock that is safe for measuring durations, whereas SystemTime can jump when the operating system adjusts the wall clock. Finally the samples are summarised with robust statistics. A median ignores the occasional sample inflated by a context switch or a page fault, while a mean lets one bad run distort the answer. Reporting the minimum and maximum next to the median shows how noisy the machine was.

Build mode matters as much as method. A plain cargo run builds without optimization, so iterator chains are not inlined, bounds checks are not hoisted and costs that disappear in release builds dominate the profile. Measure with cargo run --release (or the bench profile) and remember that the numbers describe one CPU, one compiler version and one load level. The program below keeps its printed output deterministic by timing internally but printing only the checksum of the work and the ordering facts it asserts, so it can be a reliable example while the real timings stay on your machine.

Check what you measured: use the result (accumulate a checksum and print it), keep inputs behind black_box, record several samples after warm-up, compare release builds only, and treat any difference under the observed min-to-max spread as noise.
expectedStdout:
one run = 333383335000
checksum over 3 warm-up + 11 timed runs = 4667366690000
min <= median <= max: true
challenge: Write checksum_of_runs(runs, f) that returns the wrapping sum of f() over that many calls, passing each result through black_box. Use it to show that doubling the number of runs doubles the checksum of sum_squares(1_000).
question: Why do benchmark inputs and results go through std::hint::black_box?
correct: It hides the data flow from the optimizer so the work cannot be folded into a constant or removed as unused
wrong: It moves the computation onto a separate thread so timing is not disturbed by the work itself
It forces the function to be inlined into the timing loop so call overhead is not measured
It pins the CPU to a fixed clock frequency for the duration of the run, so timings repeat
reasoning: black_box returns its argument unchanged, but the compiler must assume the value may be observed or produced elsewhere. Without it a pure computation on constants can be evaluated at compile time or deleted. It does not spawn threads, force inlining or touch CPU frequency, and its effect is best effort rather than a hard guarantee.

quiz.question: Why report the median of the samples instead of the mean?
quiz.correct: A few samples disturbed by scheduling or page faults inflate the mean but barely move the median
wrong: The median is guaranteed to equal the minimum, so it reports the best case the machine could achieve
Integer nanosecond counts cannot be averaged, because the sum of the samples would overflow
The median removes the need for warm-up runs, because cold-start samples fall away automatically
quiz.reasoning: Noise on a general-purpose machine is mostly one-sided: interruptions only add time. The median is robust to a minority of such outliers. It is not equal to the minimum, integers average fine, and warm-up serves a different purpose.

quiz.question: Why can timing a plain cargo run (debug) build mislead a performance decision?
quiz.correct: Debug builds skip most optimizations, so inlining, bounds-check removal and vectorization that drive release speed are absent
wrong: Debug builds cannot call Instant::now, so timing code has to be compiled out of unoptimized binaries
Debug builds always run slower by the same constant factor, so relative comparisons stay valid
Debug builds run on a different instruction set, so their timings cannot be compared with release ones
quiz.reasoning: Optimization changes relative costs, not just absolute speed: abstractions that are free in release can be expensive in debug. The slowdown is not a constant factor and the clock and CPU are the same.

quiz.question: Which clock should a benchmark use to measure elapsed time?
quiz.correct: std::time::Instant, because it is monotonic and cannot jump backwards
wrong: std::time::SystemTime, because it is the most precise wall clock
A counter incremented once for each loop iteration of the work
The date printed by the shell before and after the run
quiz.reasoning: Instant is designed for measuring durations. SystemTime follows the adjustable wall clock and can move backwards or jump, which would corrupt a measurement.

quiz.question: What is the purpose of the warm-up runs before the timed samples?
quiz.correct: To bring caches, branch predictors and lazily initialised state to steady state before recording
wrong: To make the compiler re-optimize the function with profile data gathered from the first runs
To discard the checksum produced by the first runs so it cannot leak into the final result
To increase the resolution of Instant::now, which improves as the clock is read repeatedly
quiz.reasoning: The first executions pay one-off costs such as cold caches and page faults. Rust is compiled ahead of time, so there is no runtime re-optimization, and warm-up does not change clock resolution.

title: Memory layout: array of structs versus struct of arrays
body: A struct is laid out in memory as its fields plus padding so that every field sits at an address that satisfies its alignment, and the struct is rounded up to a multiple of its largest alignment. A record with an i64, a u32 and a u8 holds 13 bytes of data but occupies 16, because 8-byte alignment forces three padding bytes. size_of and align_of report this, and the default Rust representation is allowed to reorder fields to shrink padding, which is why #[repr(C)] exists: it fixes declaration order and C-style padding when layout must be stable, for example across FFI or when reading a wire format.

A Vec of such records is an array of structs (AoS). Reading one record touches its fields together, which is ideal when an operation uses most of the record. A struct of arrays (SoA) stores each field in its own Vec instead. A loop that needs only price and quantity then streams through two dense arrays and never loads the side byte or the padding. CPUs fetch memory in cache lines, commonly 64 bytes on x86_64 and 128 bytes on Apple silicon (sysctl hw.cachelinesize reports 128 here), so the number of lines a loop touches is a good first estimate of its memory cost. The program computes that estimate for 1,000 rows both ways using a 64-byte line; the ratio between layouts, not the absolute count, is the point.

Neither layout is universally better. AoS wins when code handles a whole record at a time, such as matching one order, because one or two cache lines hold everything. SoA wins for scans over one or two fields of many records, such as computing notional across a day of ticks, and it also lends itself to vectorization because consecutive elements of one field are adjacent. Converting between the two is cheap, so measure the real access pattern in release mode before restructuring a hot type.

Check the access pattern before the layout: count how many fields each hot loop reads, print size_of for the record, and remember that the default representation is unspecified, so never rely on a particular padding unless the type is repr(C).
expectedStdout:
notional = 405697012
row size = 16, align = 8
payload = 13, padding = 3
repr(C) = 24, default = 16
cache lines read: rows = 250, columns = 188
side column left unread: 1000 bytes
challenge: Add a venue: u8 field to TickRow. Predict, then print, the new size_of the row, its padding, and the bytes per row that a column layout stores. Explain why the row did not grow.
solutionStdout:
row size = 16
payload = 14, padding = 2
column bytes per row = 14
question: A loop sums price * qty over a million ticks and never reads the side field. Why can a struct-of-arrays layout touch fewer cache lines than an array of structs?
correct: The loop reads only the price and qty arrays, so unused side bytes and padding never occupy cache lines
wrong: Struct-of-arrays values are kept in CPU registers instead of memory, so no cache lines are used
Struct-of-arrays removes every bounds check from the loop, which is where an AoS loop loses time
An array of structs cannot be iterated sequentially, so its loop jumps between unrelated cache lines
reasoning: Cache lines are loaded whole. In AoS each 16-byte row drags the unused side byte and padding through the cache along with the useful fields. SoA keeps the hot fields dense. Bounds checks and sequential iteration are unrelated, and columns still live in memory.

quiz.question: What is size_of for a struct with an i64, a u32 and a u8 under the default representation?
quiz.correct: 16 bytes: 13 bytes of data rounded up to the 8-byte alignment
wrong: 13 bytes: the exact sum of the field sizes, with no padding added
12 bytes: the u8 shares the slot of the u32, so only 12 are needed
24 bytes: each field takes its own 8-byte slot in the struct
quiz.reasoning: The size must be a multiple of the struct alignment, which is that of i64. 13 rounds up to 16. Fields can share space, but the total is still padded to the alignment.

quiz.question: When does an array of structs beat a struct of arrays?
quiz.correct: When an operation reads or writes most fields of one record together, so a record fits in one or two cache lines
wrong: When a loop reads a single field from every record, because the other fields then stay out of the cache
Never, because struct-of-arrays is always faster, whatever the access pattern of the program
Only when records are larger than a memory page, since smaller records always favour columns
quiz.reasoning: Handling a whole record at a time (for example matching one order) wants its fields adjacent. Single-field scans are the SoA case, and there is no universal winner.

quiz.question: What does #[repr(C)] guarantee that the default Rust layout does not?
quiz.correct: Fields stay in declaration order with C padding rules, so the layout is stable for FFI and wire formats
wrong: Fields are packed with no padding at all, so the struct is always as small as its data
Fields are reordered to minimise the struct size, which the default layout never does
The struct is allocated on the heap, so its address stays stable for foreign code
quiz.reasoning: repr(C) fixes order and padding, which is what an external consumer needs. The default representation may reorder fields and makes no promise. repr(C) does not pack or move anything to the heap.

title: Cache-aware loops: loop order and tiling for matrix multiply
body: Matrix multiply does the same arithmetic however you order the loops, yet the order decides how memory is read. A matrix stored row-major in a flat Vec has element (row, col) at row * n + col. The textbook i-j-k loop walks b down a column, jumping n elements (n * 8 bytes for i64) between reads, so almost every read lands on a different cache line and most of each line is wasted. Swapping to i-k-j keeps a[i][k] in a register and makes the inner loop sweep b and c along rows with stride one, so every byte of every loaded line is used. Nothing about the answer changes, only the traffic to memory.

Tiling (blocking) goes one step further. For matrices too large to stay in cache, even row sweeps evict data before it is reused. A tiled algorithm cuts each dimension into blocks and finishes all the work that touches a small block of a, b and c before moving on, so those blocks are reused while still cache resident. Three tile-by-tile blocks of i64 with tile = 32 occupy 3 * 32 * 32 * 8 = 24,576 bytes, a size that can sit in a typical 32 KiB L1 data cache. The last block along each edge may be short when the tile does not divide n, which the code handles with min(n).

With integers all three orders give identical results because addition is associative, as long as nothing overflows. With f64 the sums are grouped differently, so results can differ in the last bits, and a test that compares floating-point outputs needs a tolerance rather than equality. Production code usually calls a tuned BLAS-style kernel, but writing the loops once teaches you to read a hot loop by asking what addresses it touches, in what order, and how many times each is reused.

Check stride before cleverness: the innermost loop should move through memory contiguously, tile edges must be clipped, and compare against a simple reference implementation on awkward sizes such as n = 10 with tile = 4.
expectedStdout:
checksum = -2078
naive: b is read with a stride of 80 bytes
ikj: b is read with a stride of 8 bytes
tile blocks per dimension = 3
tile = 32 working set = 24576 bytes
challenge: Write transpose(b, n) and matmul_bt(a, bt, n) that multiplies using a transposed copy of b so the inner k loop reads both operands along rows. Check it equals the naive result on a 5 by 5 example.
question: Why is the i-k-j loop order usually faster than i-j-k for row-major matrices?
correct: Its inner loop walks b and c along rows with stride one, so each loaded cache line is fully used
wrong: It performs fewer multiplications than i-j-k, since the middle loop skips zero entries
It removes the bounds checks from the indexing, because the inner index is always in range
It is the only order that produces the correct product, because the others reorder the sums
reasoning: All orders do the same n cubed multiply-adds and all are correct. The difference is access pattern: i-j-k jumps n elements through b on every step, wasting most of each cache line, while i-k-j reads contiguous memory.

quiz.question: What does tiling add on top of a good loop order?
quiz.correct: It reuses a small block of each matrix while it is still in cache, cutting trips to slower memory
wrong: It reduces the number of multiply-add operations, because blocks of zeros are skipped entirely
It makes floating-point results exact, since each small block accumulates without rounding
It lets the code skip rows that are zero, because a tile can be checked for zeros first
quiz.reasoning: Tiling does not change the operation count or the exactness of arithmetic; it reorders the work so data is reused before eviction.

quiz.question: The naive, ikj and tiled versions produce identical i64 results. Why?
quiz.correct: Integer addition is associative, so regrouping the sums cannot change the result when nothing overflows
wrong: Tiling changes rounding but only in the last digit, which the equality check tolerates
They only agree when the tile size divides n, because ragged tiles change the sums
They only agree in release builds, because debug builds skip the tiled loop order
quiz.reasoning: Exact integer arithmetic is order independent (without overflow). The tile does not need to divide n because the edges are clipped with min(n), and build mode does not change semantics.

quiz.question: If the same loops used f64, which statement is true?
quiz.correct: Different loop orders can differ in the last bits because floating-point addition is not associative
wrong: All orders are always bit-identical, since floating-point addition gives the same result in any order
Tiling always makes the answer more accurate, because it adds smaller numbers together first
f64 matrices cannot be tiled, because a tile must hold whole integer values
quiz.reasoning: Regrouping floating-point sums changes intermediate rounding, so compare with a tolerance. Accuracy may go up or down and tiling works for any element type.

quiz.question: For n = 10 and tile = 4, how many blocks does (0..n).step_by(tile) visit along one dimension?
quiz.correct: 3: blocks of 4, 4 and a clipped block of 2
wrong: 2, because 10 / 4 rounds down to two blocks
4, because 10 / 4 rounds up and adds one
10, one block for each element
quiz.reasoning: step_by(4) yields starts 0, 4 and 8. The last block covers only indices 8 and 9, which is why the inner ranges use min(n).

title: SIMD on aarch64: NEON intrinsics with a portable fallback
body: SIMD (single instruction, multiple data) executes one operation on several lanes at once. On Apple silicon and other aarch64 CPUs the baseline vector unit is NEON with 128-bit registers, so one instruction can multiply four i32 lanes. Rust exposes the instructions as intrinsics in std::arch::aarch64, for example vld1q_s32 to load four i32 values, vmlaq_s32 to multiply and accumulate lanes, and vaddvq_s32 to add the lanes together. Because intrinsics belong to one architecture, the code is wrapped in #[cfg(target_arch = "aarch64")] and a portable function with the same name is compiled everywhere else, so the crate builds and behaves the same on every target.

Intrinsics that dereference pointers are unsafe and the safety comment is a real proof obligation. Here the loop runs len / 4 times and each vld1q_s32 reads four elements starting at index i * 4, so the last load ends at 4 * (len / 4), which never passes the end of either slice. The remaining len % 4 elements, the tail, are handled with ordinary safe indexing. Always test the SIMD path against the scalar reference on lengths that are not multiples of the lane count, including zero and lengths below one vector.

NEON is part of the aarch64 baseline, so no detection is needed for it. Optional extensions are different: x86_64 code that uses AVX2 must check is_x86_feature_detected!("avx2") at runtime and call a function marked #[target_feature(enable = "avx2")] only when the check passes, and aarch64 has the matching is_aarch64_feature_detected! macro for extensions such as dot-product instructions. Calling an instruction the CPU lacks is undefined behaviour, not a catchable panic. Many simple loops over slices are auto-vectorized by LLVM in release builds, so reach for intrinsics only after measuring that the compiler did not.
Check four things: a scalar reference exists and is compared in tests, loads stay in bounds, the tail is processed, and any optional CPU feature is detected at runtime before it is used.
expectedStdout:
dot = 190
tail elements for len 19 with 4 lanes = 3
fast path matches scalar for every tested length: true
challenge: Write sum_fast(values: &[i32]) -> i32 using vld1q_s32, vaddq_s32 and vaddvq_s32 on aarch64, with a portable fallback on other targets and a scalar tail. Check it against iter().sum() for several lengths.
question: Why is the NEON code guarded by #[cfg(target_arch = "aarch64")] with a portable function for other targets?
correct: The intrinsics exist only for that architecture, so without a portable fallback the crate would not compile elsewhere
wrong: NEON intrinsics are always slower than scalar code, so the cfg gate keeps them off other targets
The cfg attribute makes the intrinsics safe to call, so no unsafe block is needed on aarch64
The scalar version is needed to detect integer overflow, which the NEON version cannot report
reasoning: std::arch is organised per architecture. Items for aarch64 are absent on x86_64, so a cfg gate plus a fallback keeps one code base portable. The cfg attribute changes what is compiled, not safety, and speed is the reason to use intrinsics in the first place.

quiz.question: Why is the pointer arithmetic in the NEON loop sound?
quiz.correct: The loop runs len / 4 times, so every four-element load ends within both slices, and the tail uses safe indexing
wrong: Raw pointer arithmetic is always in bounds, so the loop needs no length reasoning of its own
NEON loads ignore bounds and wrap around, so an out-of-range load just reads the first lane again
unsafe turns off the borrow checker, so any pointer offset in the block is acceptable
quiz.reasoning: Soundness comes from the arithmetic proof stated in the safety comment. Raw pointers are not checked and unsafe does not make an out-of-range read valid.

quiz.question: How should code use an instruction-set extension that only some CPUs of an architecture support, such as AVX2 on x86_64?
quiz.correct: Detect it at run time with is_x86_feature_detected! and call a #[target_feature] function only when true
wrong: Compile for it and rely on catch_unwind to recover if the CPU lacks the instruction
Check cfg!(debug_assertions) before calling, because release builds select the right instructions
Call it unconditionally; unsupported instructions simply return zero without any error
quiz.reasoning: Executing an unsupported instruction is undefined behaviour or a hardware trap, not a recoverable panic. Runtime detection gates the call.

quiz.question: Why might a plain iterator loop match the intrinsic version in release builds?
quiz.correct: LLVM can auto-vectorize simple counted loops over slices, so intrinsics matter mainly where it does not
wrong: Iterators always emit SIMD instructions at run time, whatever the optimization level
Auto-vectorization works at opt-level 0 too, so debug builds are vectorized like release ones
Scalar code never uses vector registers, so only intrinsics can make use of the vector unit
quiz.reasoning: Auto-vectorization is a compile-time optimization that needs optimization enabled and a vectorizable loop shape. Measure before hand-writing intrinsics.

quiz.question: With 4 lanes per vector and a slice of 19 elements, how many elements does the scalar tail process?
quiz.correct: 3, because 19 = 4 * 4 + 3
wrong: 4, because the tail is one vector
0, because NEON handles any length
19, because the tail does everything
quiz.reasoning: len / 4 gives 4 full vectors covering 16 elements; the remaining 19 % 4 = 3 elements are summed with ordinary code.

title: Data parallelism with scoped threads and ordered reduction
body: std::thread::spawn requires a closure that is 'static, which forces Arc and cloning for data that already lives on your stack. std::thread::scope removes that requirement. Inside scope(|s| ...) every thread started with s.spawn is guaranteed to be joined before scope returns, so the compiler allows those threads to borrow local variables: the borrow cannot outlive the data because the scope cannot end first. This turns "split a slice among workers" into ordinary borrowing, with no reference counting and no unsafe.

Splitting is done with slice methods. chunks(n) yields shared sub-slices, so several threads can read different regions, and chunks_mut(n) yields non-overlapping &mut sub-slices, so each thread gets exclusive access to its own region and no lock is needed. The borrow checker accepts this because the pieces are disjoint by construction. The chunk length is len.div_ceil(parts), clamped to at least one so an empty or tiny slice does not ask for chunks of size zero, which panics.

Parallel code must also be reproducible. Each thread returns a partial result through its join handle, and the caller combines the partials in chunk order, not in the order threads happen to finish. For integers the order does not matter, but floating-point addition is not associative, so a fixed combination order makes the answer identical from run to run for a given number of parts. If one thread panics and its handle was not joined by you, scope panics after all threads finish, so failure is never silently lost.

Check that the work per chunk outweighs thread start-up and join cost, that chunk size is never zero, that partial results are combined in a fixed order, and that a thread panic is handled on purpose rather than ignored.
expectedStdout:
sum = 500500
sum of squares = 333833500
repeatable with a fixed chunk order: true
empty slice sum = 0
challenge: Write parallel_max(data: &[i64], parts: usize) -> Option<i64> using scoped threads that returns the largest element, or None for an empty slice. Compare it with iter().max() for several part counts.
question: Why can threads started inside std::thread::scope borrow local variables without Arc?
correct: The scope joins every spawned thread before it returns, so a borrow cannot outlive the data it points to
wrong: Scoped threads copy the borrowed data into their own stacks, so the original can be dropped early
Borrow checking is switched off inside scoped threads, so the programmer must guarantee safety
Scoped threads run on the calling thread, never in parallel, so no sharing actually occurs
reasoning: thread::spawn needs a 'static closure because the thread may outlive the caller. scope bounds the threads' lifetime by the scope itself, which lets the compiler accept shorter borrows. The borrow checker still runs and the threads do run concurrently.

quiz.question: Why combine partial sums in chunk order instead of in the order threads finish?
quiz.correct: f64 addition is not associative, so a fixed order gives reproducible sums while completion order varies run to run
wrong: Threads always finish in chunk order, so there is no difference between the two approaches
Integer sums need a fixed order but floats do not, because floats are always rounded the same way
Combining in completion order is impossible with join handles, because they hide the thread's finish time
quiz.reasoning: Different groupings of f64 additions can round differently, and the scheduler decides who finishes first. Joining handles in the order they were created fixes the grouping.

quiz.question: What does chunks_mut allow that makes lock-free parallel mutation possible?
quiz.correct: It yields non-overlapping mutable sub-slices, so each thread has exclusive access to its own region
wrong: It wraps every element in a Mutex automatically, so each thread locks the elements it touches
It copies the data and merges the copies afterwards, so each thread works on a private copy
It disables the aliasing rules for the slice, so overlapping writes are allowed between threads
quiz.reasoning: Disjoint &mut regions satisfy the aliasing rules by construction, so no synchronisation is required for the mutation itself.

quiz.question: What happens if a scoped thread panics and you never joined its handle?
quiz.correct: scope waits for all threads and then panics, so the failure is not silently lost
wrong: The process aborts immediately without joining the other threads, so their work is lost
The panic is silently discarded, because the handle was never joined to receive it
All other scoped threads are killed instantly, and the scope returns without waiting
quiz.reasoning: The scope joins automatically on exit and propagates a panic from any thread whose handle was not joined manually.

quiz.question: When is splitting work across threads a bad idea?
quiz.correct: When the work per chunk is small compared with the cost of starting and joining threads
wrong: When the element type is Copy, because copying the elements into each thread costs too much
When the program is built in release mode, since optimized code is already fast enough
When the threads only borrow data, because borrowed data cannot be processed in parallel
quiz.reasoning: Thread creation costs microseconds. Tiny chunks lose to a single-threaded loop. Copy types, release builds and borrowing are not reasons to avoid parallelism.

title: False sharing and cache-line padding
body: Cores do not share individual variables; they share cache lines, blocks of 64 or 128 bytes that the coherence protocol moves between cores. When one core writes to a line, copies in other cores are invalidated. Two threads that write two different variables stored in the same line therefore take turns owning that line even though they never touch each other's data. This is false sharing: the program is correct, but a counter per thread can run several times slower than it should because the line ping-pongs between cores.

The cure is layout. Give each independently written value its own line by padding and aligning it. #[repr(align(128))] on a wrapper struct raises the alignment to 128 and, because size must be a multiple of alignment, rounds its size up to 128, so consecutive array elements start on different lines. This machine reports a 128-byte line (sysctl hw.cachelinesize), and well-known libraries such as crossbeam pad to 128 bytes on aarch64 and x86_64, so 128 is a safe default; padding to 64 on hardware with 128-byte lines would leave neighbours sharing.

The lesson avoids printing times, which vary, and instead proves the layout: size_of and align_of of the wrapper, and the byte distance between adjacent elements. Two threads then increment their own AtomicU64 with Relaxed ordering. Relaxed is enough for an independent counter because only the atomicity of each increment matters, not ordering relative to other memory. Padding spends memory to buy speed, so apply it only to hot, per-thread, frequently written data.

Check that the hot fields are written by different threads, that padding matches the target's line size, and that you confirmed the slowdown with a release-mode measurement before spending the memory.
expectedStdout:
AtomicU64: size 8, align 8
Padded<AtomicU64>: size 128, align 128
packed distance = 8 bytes
padded distance = 128 bytes
packed totals = 100000 and 100000
padded totals = 100000 and 100000
challenge: Predict and then print size_of and align_of for Padded<u8> and Padded<[u8; 129]> when Padded is #[repr(align(128))]. Explain why the second is larger.
solutionStdout:
Padded<u8>: size 128, align 128
Padded<[u8; 129]>: size 256, align 128
question: What is false sharing?
correct: Threads write different variables that live in the same cache line, so the line bounces between cores
wrong: Two threads write the same variable without synchronization, so the updates overwrite each other
A thread reads stale data because a memory fence is missing, so it sees an old value
Two Arc handles point to the same allocation, so cloning them contends on one counter
reasoning: False sharing is a performance problem caused by the coherence protocol working on whole lines. The data accessed is distinct, so it is neither a data race nor a visibility bug.

quiz.question: What does #[repr(align(128))] do to a wrapper around an AtomicU64?
quiz.correct: It raises the alignment to 128 and rounds the size up to 128, so adjacent array elements start on separate lines
wrong: It shrinks the AtomicU64 to fit a smaller line, so more counters share each cache line
It makes the atomic operations stronger than SeqCst, so the increments are ordered globally
It allocates the value on the heap, so each counter lives in its own separate allocation
quiz.reasoning: Alignment dictates both the start address and, through the size-multiple rule, the size. It does not change the atomic operation semantics or allocation strategy.

quiz.question: Is false sharing a correctness bug?
quiz.correct: No, the counts stay correct; only performance suffers from cache-coherence traffic
wrong: Yes, it loses increments, because both threads overwrite the shared line with stale values
Yes, it is a data race under the Rust memory model, because two threads touch one line
Only when Relaxed ordering is used, since stronger orderings keep the counts correct
quiz.reasoning: Each thread updates its own atomic, so there is no race and no lost update. The cost is invalidation traffic between cores.

quiz.question: Why is Ordering::Relaxed enough for the independent per-thread counters?
quiz.correct: Only the atomicity of each increment matters; no other memory access depends on ordering relative to the counter
wrong: Relaxed makes the increment non-atomic but faster, which is acceptable for a simple counter
Relaxed guarantees the threads run in lockstep, so the counts always end up equal
Relaxed is required whenever threads are scoped, since scoped threads reject stronger orderings
quiz.reasoning: Relaxed still makes each read-modify-write atomic, and joining the scope synchronises the final read. Stronger orderings only matter when other data must be published with the counter.

quiz.question: Why should padding size follow the target hardware instead of always being 64?
quiz.correct: Some CPUs, including Apple silicon, use 128-byte lines, so 64-byte padding could still leave neighbours sharing a line
wrong: Padding to 64 always wastes memory on every target, so smaller padding is better on all CPUs
Line size is the same on every CPU, so only the compiler version decides the right padding
Alignment above 64 is rejected by rustc, so 64 is the largest padding that can be written
quiz.reasoning: Cache line size is a hardware property. Padding to the largest relevant line size avoids sharing at the cost of memory, which is why libraries use 128 on several architectures.

title: Memory ordering in practice: publishing data with Release and Acquire
body: Atomic operations take an Ordering argument because compilers and CPUs reorder memory accesses. Relaxed guarantees only that the operation itself is atomic and that each atomic has a single modification order; it promises nothing about other memory. That is exactly right for an independent counter, and exactly wrong for handing data from one thread to another. For a handoff you pair a Release store with an Acquire load of the same atomic: when the load observes the stored value, everything the writer did before the Release store is visible to the reader after the Acquire load. The pair forms a one-way bridge, called synchronizes-with.

The example publishes the number 42. The writer stores the data with Relaxed and then sets a ready flag with Release. The reader spins on the flag with Acquire and then reads the data with Relaxed. Because the flag load that sees true synchronizes with the flag store, the earlier data store must be visible, so the reader always sees 42. Change the flag store or load to Relaxed and the Rust memory model permits the reader to see true and still read the old zero. On a strongly ordered x86 machine you might never observe it; on weakly ordered aarch64 hardware, or after a compiler reordering, you can. Tests that pass on one machine do not prove an ordering is sufficient.

Read-modify-write operations such as fetch_add are always atomic; their ordering argument controls only the publication behaviour around them. compare_exchange_weak lets you build operations the library lacks. It may fail spuriously, so it sits in a loop that reloads the current value and retries, and the weak form can be cheaper than compare_exchange on some architectures. SeqCst is the strongest ordering and adds a single total order over all SeqCst operations. It is needed in patterns where two threads each write their own flag and then read the other's, because Acquire and Release alone do not forbid both threads reading the old values. Default to the weakest ordering you can justify in a comment and promote only with a reason.

Check every atomic for the claim it needs: independent counter (Relaxed), publication (Release store, Acquire load), read-modify-write retry loop (reload on failure), or a global order across several atomics (SeqCst), and never trust a passing run on one CPU as proof.
expectedStdout:
consumer always saw 42
relaxed counter total = 100000
max from CAS loop = 10006
challenge: Publish a two-field message (price and qty) safely: the writer stores both fields Relaxed and then stores sequence number 1 with Release; the reader waits for sequence == 1 with Acquire and then reads both fields. Run it repeatedly and assert the reader never sees a partial message.
question: What does pairing a Release store with an Acquire load of the same atomic guarantee?
correct: If the load sees the stored value, everything the writer did before the store is visible to the reader after the load
wrong: The two threads run in lockstep, one instruction at a time, with the store always before the load
Only the atomic variable itself is ordered; other memory accesses remain completely unordered
Every atomic operation in the program becomes sequentially consistent, whatever ordering it requested
reasoning: Release/Acquire creates a synchronizes-with edge for that atomic, publishing earlier writes. It does not force lockstep execution, it is not limited to the one variable, and it does not change the ordering of unrelated atomics.

quiz.question: If the flag store were Relaxed instead of Release, what could go wrong in the example?
quiz.correct: The reader could see ready == true yet still read the old data, because nothing orders the data store before the flag
wrong: The program would no longer compile, because Relaxed cannot be used to store a boolean flag
The flag would never become true, since a Relaxed store is not visible to other threads
The data store would become non-atomic, since it was only atomic because of the Release flag
quiz.reasoning: Relaxed provides atomicity only. The memory model permits the data store to be observed after the flag, and weakly ordered CPUs or compiler reordering can expose it. Compilation and atomicity are unaffected.

quiz.question: For which job is Ordering::Relaxed correct?
quiz.correct: An independent counter or statistic where only the atomicity of each update matters and no other data is published through it
wrong: Publishing a buffer to another thread, because a counter ordering covers the buffer's contents too
Implementing a lock that protects other variables, since a Relaxed swap acquires the lock
Establishing one global order across several atomics, because Relaxed operations are ordered together
quiz.reasoning: Relaxed has no synchronising effect on other memory. Publication, locks and cross-atomic ordering need Acquire/Release or SeqCst.

quiz.question: Why is compare_exchange_weak normally used inside a retry loop?
quiz.correct: It may fail spuriously on some architectures, so a loop reloads and retries; the weak form can be cheaper
wrong: It never fails, so the loop only handles integer overflow and the weak name is historical
It is the only compare-and-swap Rust provides, so every update loop has to use it
It automatically upgrades the ordering to SeqCst when the exchange fails, which makes retries safe
quiz.reasoning: Spurious failure is allowed for the weak form. A retry loop is already needed for real contention, so the weak form costs nothing extra there.

quiz.question: When is SeqCst genuinely needed over Acquire and Release?
quiz.correct: When several atomics must be seen in one global order, such as two threads each writing a flag then reading the other
wrong: Whenever threads share any atomic variable, since Acquire and Release never give consistent results
For every simple counter, because Relaxed increments can lose updates under contention
Only on x86_64 targets, because other architectures order every atomic operation globally
quiz.reasoning: Release/Acquire does not forbid both threads reading the old value in the write-then-read-other pattern. SeqCst adds the single total order that does. Counters and ordinary handoffs do not need it.

title: A bounded lock-free single-producer single-consumer queue
body: A single-producer single-consumer (SPSC) ring buffer is the workhorse of low-latency pipelines because exactly one thread writes and exactly one reads, so no locks or compare-and-swap loops are needed. The buffer has a power-of-two capacity. Two monotonically increasing counters, head (next slot to pop) and tail (next slot to push), are reduced to a slot with counter & (capacity - 1). The queue is empty when head == tail and full when tail.wrapping_sub(head) == capacity, so all slots can be used and wrap-around of the usize counters stays correct.

The unsafe core is small. Slots are UnsafeCell<MaybeUninit<T>>, since a slot is uninitialised until pushed. The producer reads head with Acquire to know space is free, writes the value into the slot at tail, then stores tail + 1 with Release. The consumer reads tail with Acquire, reads the value out of the slot at head, then stores head + 1 with Release. The Release/Acquire pairs give two guarantees: the consumer that sees the new tail also sees the written element, and the producer that sees the new head knows the slot has been fully read and may be reused.

Soundness depends on the API, not on the internals alone. channel() returns a Producer and a Consumer that are not Clone and whose methods take &mut self, so at most one thread can push and one can pop at a time. A shared Arc owns the buffer, and Shared implements Sync with a comment explaining the invariant. MaybeUninit never drops its contents, so Drop for Shared must drop exactly the elements between head and tail that were pushed but not popped, or values leak.

Check the invariants: one producer and one consumer by construction, Release on publishing an index and Acquire on reading the other side's index, only the initialised range is dropped, capacity is a power of two, and a single-threaded reference model agrees with the queue on full, empty and wrap-around.
expectedStdout:
capacity = 8
drained after wrap-around = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8]
two-thread FIFO sum = 4999950000
drops after one pop = 1
drops after both ends are gone = 3
challenge: Before trusting the unsafe queue, write the safe single-threaded reference model: RingModel<T> over Vec<Option<T>> with push -> Result<(), T> and pop -> Option<T>. Use it to check FIFO order, full, empty and wrap-around with capacity 4, the same behaviour the concurrent queue must have.
solutionStdout: FIFO preserved across 24 items with capacity 4
question: Why does the producer publish the new tail with Release and the consumer read it with Acquire?
correct: So a consumer that observes the new tail also observes the element the producer wrote into the slot before publishing it
wrong: Release makes the usize store atomic, whereas a Relaxed store of a usize could be torn on aarch64
It stops the producer from overwriting slots the consumer has not read, by blocking until they are read
aarch64 cannot load a usize without Acquire, so every load of an index needs the ordering
reasoning: The pair publishes the slot contents. Atomicity of a usize store holds for any ordering, and preventing overwrite is the job of the head counter (read by the producer with Acquire), not of the tail publication.

quiz.question: Why is `unsafe impl<T: Send> Sync for Shared<T>` justified?
quiz.correct: channel() gives out one Producer and one Consumer, neither Clone, so each slot has one writer and one reader
wrong: UnsafeCell is always Sync, so the impl is only a formality that documents an existing guarantee
Sync only matters for types stored in an Arc, which is not the case for this shared buffer here
MaybeUninit prevents any data race on its contents, so the buffer is safe to share by itself
quiz.reasoning: UnsafeCell is not Sync; the impl is a promise by the author. It holds only because the public API enforces a single producer and single consumer with a correct handoff protocol.

quiz.question: How does the queue distinguish full from empty using monotonic counters?
quiz.correct: tail - head == capacity means full and head == tail means empty, using wrapping arithmetic
wrong: It stores a separate length that both threads update, so full and empty are read directly
It always leaves one slot unused, so the indices are equal only when the queue is empty
It compares each slot with zero, because an empty slot always holds the value zero
quiz.reasoning: Because the counters only grow, their difference is the number of queued items, so no slot has to be sacrificed and no shared length field is needed.

quiz.question: What must Drop for Shared do, and why?
quiz.correct: Drop the elements between head and tail that were pushed but never popped, because MaybeUninit never drops its contents
wrong: Nothing, because MaybeUninit drops its value automatically when the buffer itself is dropped
Drop every slot, including uninitialised ones, so no value is leaked whatever the queue holds
Free the buffer manually with dealloc, because Box cannot release memory that holds MaybeUninit
quiz.reasoning: MaybeUninit<T> has no drop glue, so leftover elements would leak. Dropping uninitialised slots would be undefined behaviour. The Box frees the buffer memory itself.

quiz.question: Why do push and pop take &mut self?
quiz.correct: It enforces one active producer and one active consumer; two threads pushing through shared references could race
wrong: It lets the compiler skip bounds checks, because exclusive access proves the index is in range
It makes the atomics unnecessary, since exclusive access already orders the two threads
It is required by Arc, because Arc can only hand out mutable access to exclusive owners
quiz.reasoning: The exclusive borrow is part of the safety argument for the unsafe code. The atomics are still required for the cross-thread handoff.

title: Zero-allocation hot paths: reuse buffers and prove it with a counting allocator
body: Calling the allocator is not free. It may take a lock, walk free lists, touch cold memory and, for large requests, ask the operating system for pages; the time varies from call to call, which is poison for a latency-sensitive loop. Low-latency systems therefore allocate everything they need up front, and the steady-state path allocates nothing. In Rust the usual sources of hidden allocation are String and Vec growth, collect into a new Vec, format!, to_string, clone of owned data and boxing. Each of them has an allocation-free form: borrow slices with &str, write into a buffer you own, or reuse a collection with clear().

Vec::clear and String::clear drop the elements and set the length to zero but keep the capacity, so a buffer that was grown once is reused for free afterwards. with_capacity (and reserve) pays the growth cost at start-up instead of inside the loop. Parsing is a good example: split_ascii_whitespace and parse::<u32> work on borrowed text and do not allocate, whereas collecting words into Vec<String> allocates the vector and one string per word. Formatting into a reused String with the fmt::Write trait avoids format!'s fresh allocation per message.

Do not guess; count. A global allocator is a type that implements GlobalAlloc and is registered with #[global_allocator]. The wrapper below forwards every call to System and increments an atomic counter in alloc and realloc, so allocations_during(work) reports how many times the closure called into the allocator. The trait is unsafe to implement because the compiler cannot check the contract (valid pointers, matching layouts), and delegating to System preserves it. Keep printing outside the measured closure, since the first use of stdout can allocate its buffer and would distort the count.
Check a hot loop with a counter, not with intuition: pre-size buffers, reuse them with clear(), prefer borrowed slices over owned strings, and assert that steady-state allocations are exactly zero.
expectedStdout:
notional = 52460164, last rendered length = 9
hot path allocations = 0
naive path allocates at least once per line: true
rendered sample = S 1@10999
challenge: A function collects every price into a new Vec<i64> each frame. Show with the counting allocator that growing a Vec from empty allocates repeatedly, that with_capacity allocates once, and that reusing one Vec with clear() across 100 frames allocates zero times after the first frame.
solutionStdout:
grow-from-empty allocates more than once: true
with_capacity allocations = 1
reused buffer allocations over 100 frames = 0
question: Why does clearing a reused Vec or String help a hot path?
correct: clear() drops the elements but keeps the allocation, so later pushes reuse existing capacity without calling the allocator
wrong: clear() returns the memory to the allocator, which makes later allocations cheaper because the free list is warm
clear() converts the Vec into a stack array, so later pushes no longer touch the heap
clear() is the only operation that can allocate without taking the allocator's lock
reasoning: Capacity is separate from length. clear() sets length to zero and drops elements while the heap block stays owned by the Vec. That is why a buffer sized once can serve every later frame without touching the allocator.

quiz.question: Which statement about implementing GlobalAlloc is correct?
quiz.correct: It is an unsafe trait because the compiler cannot verify the allocation contract; a wrapper that delegates to System keeps it intact
wrong: It is safe to implement because the compiler checks every pointer that the allocator returns to callers
It may only be implemented by the standard library, because user allocators cannot be trusted
It must always call malloc directly, since System is not allowed to be wrapped by another allocator
quiz.reasoning: GlobalAlloc has safety requirements (valid, suitably aligned memory, matching layouts on dealloc). A forwarding wrapper preserves System's guarantees. Any type may implement it, and it need not call malloc.

quiz.question: Why is the output printed after the measured closure instead of inside it?
quiz.correct: The first use of stdout can allocate buffers or format arguments, which would distort the allocation count
wrong: println! cannot be called inside a closure, because closures are not allowed to write to stdout
Printing resets the allocation counter, so any count taken before it would be lost
The counting allocator only counts after main returns, so earlier allocations are never seen
quiz.reasoning: Printing is outside the code under test. Including it can add allocations that are not part of the path being measured.

quiz.question: Which parsing approach avoids per-token allocation on a hot path?
quiz.correct: Iterate with split_ascii_whitespace and parse each borrowed &str, without collecting into Vec<String>
wrong: Collect each line into Vec<String> and drop it, because the drop frees every token at once
Call to_string on every token for safety, so each token owns its text before it is parsed
Use format! to rebuild each token before parsing, since format! reuses the line's buffer
quiz.reasoning: Borrowed &str slices point into the input line and parse::<T> reads them in place. Owned String values and format! all call the allocator.

quiz.question: What does Vec::with_capacity(n) change?
quiz.correct: It reserves room for n elements up front, moving the allocation cost to start-up instead of the loop
wrong: It makes the Vec length n, filled with default values that are immediately available to read
It prevents the Vec from ever reallocating, even if you push more than n elements into it
It zero-fills the memory up front so that later reads are faster and need no initialisation
quiz.reasoning: Capacity is not length. Pushing up to n elements will not reallocate, but pushing beyond n still grows the Vec.

title: Cargo build profiles: LTO, codegen units, panic strategy and overflow checks
body: A Cargo profile is a named bundle of compiler settings. The dev profile (used by cargo run and cargo build) favours fast compiles and debuggability; the release profile (--release) favours speed. The same source can behave differently under each: debug assertions are on in dev and off in release, integer overflow panics in dev but wraps in two's complement in release unless overflow-checks is enabled, and optimization level, inlining and vectorization differ enormously. Wrapping on overflow in release is defined behaviour, not undefined behaviour, but it silently changes results, so quant code that must never overflow should use checked or saturating arithmetic regardless of profile.

Three release settings matter most for speed. opt-level = 3 enables the aggressive optimizer. lto = "fat" performs link-time optimization across every crate in the build as one unit, which lets the compiler inline across crate boundaries at the cost of longer builds. codegen-units = 1 stops rustc from splitting the crate into parallel pieces, giving the optimizer more context at the cost of compile time. panic = "abort" removes unwinding: a panic terminates the process, so catch_unwind cannot recover, but code is smaller and the optimizer has fewer landing pads to preserve. Each is a trade between build time, binary size, debuggability and speed, so measure the effect on your own workload.

Profile-guided optimization (PGO) goes further: build an instrumented binary with -C profile-generate, run it on representative input, then rebuild with -C profile-use so the compiler knows which branches and call sites are hot. It needs LLVM tools and a representative workload, so this lesson describes it rather than running it. The project below makes profile effects observable and testable without timing: it prints cfg!(debug_assertions), triggers an overflow, and calls catch_unwind, and the checks assert the different exit codes and outputs under dev, release and a custom profile.

Check which profile you actually shipped, keep correctness independent of overflow-checks by using explicit checked arithmetic, and benchmark one setting change at a time on release builds before keeping it.
challenge: Add a custom profile named lab to Cargo.toml that inherits from release but turns debug-assertions and overflow-checks on and panic back to unwind. Run it with cargo run --profile lab and explain what each argument now prints and why.
question: What does panic = "abort" change about how a Rust program handles a panic?
correct: The process terminates at the panic instead of unwinding the stack, so catch_unwind cannot recover from it
wrong: The panic is turned into a returned Result, so callers handle it like any other error value
Destructors run first, then the program continues running from the point where it panicked
It only affects panic messages, not control flow, so catch_unwind still recovers as before
reasoning: With the abort strategy there is no unwinding, so no destructors run on the way out and catch_unwind never sees the panic. The setting trades recoverability for smaller code and a simpler optimizer problem.

quiz.question: What does lto = "fat" do?
quiz.correct: It optimizes across all crates as one unit at link time, allowing cross-crate inlining at the cost of build time
wrong: It strips debug symbols from the binary at link time, which makes the executable smaller
It compiles each function in parallel to shorten builds, at the cost of slower code
It removes the standard library from the binary, leaving only the code the crate uses
quiz.reasoning: Link-time optimization defers optimization until the whole program is visible. It is a build-time and speed trade, unrelated to symbol stripping or parallel compilation.

quiz.question: What is the trade-off of codegen-units = 1?
quiz.correct: The optimizer sees the whole crate at once and can often produce faster code, but compilation is slower and less parallel
wrong: Binaries become larger but compile faster, because the crate is split into one piece per function
It enables overflow checking, because a single unit lets the compiler insert arithmetic checks
It disables inlining so builds are reproducible, because inlining decisions differ between units
quiz.reasoning: Fewer units mean fewer cross-unit optimization barriers and less compile parallelism.

quiz.question: In a release build without overflow-checks, what does 255u8 + 1 evaluate to at runtime?
quiz.correct: 0, because release wraps in two's complement; this is defined behaviour, not undefined behaviour
wrong: Undefined behaviour with an unpredictable result, because release builds assume overflow never occurs
255, because the addition saturates at the maximum value of u8 instead of wrapping
256, because the value is widened automatically to hold the result of the addition
quiz.reasoning: Rust defines overflow in release as wrapping (when checks are off); it only panics when overflow-checks or debug assertions are enabled. u8 cannot hold 256.

quiz.question: What does profile-guided optimization need?
quiz.correct: A profile recorded from an instrumented run on representative input, fed back to the compiler for a second build
wrong: Only opt-level = 3, because the compiler learns branch frequencies from its own analysis
A nightly compiler and unsafe code, because the profile data cannot be read by stable rustc
A profile of the source file line counts, collected by running a linter over the crate
quiz.reasoning: PGO uses observed branch and call frequencies. A profile from an unrepresentative workload can make hot paths slower.

title: Data parallelism with rayon and pipelines with crossbeam channels
body: Two crates cover most multi-core needs in Rust. rayon turns sequential iterator chains into data-parallel ones: replace iter() with par_iter() and map, filter, sum, max and collect run on a work-stealing thread pool, and the type system still guarantees there are no data races because closures must be Send and Sync. crossbeam-channel provides fast multi-producer multi-consumer channels, including bounded ones. Together they cover "split this array across cores" (rayon) and "connect these stages with queues" (channels). This project pins both crates exactly (rayon 1.12.0, crossbeam-channel 0.5.17) and ships its Cargo.lock so everyone builds the same dependency graph; the first build needs network access to download them.

Parallel does not mean reproducible. Integer sums and maxima give the same answer however the work is split, but floating-point addition is not associative, so a parallel sum can differ in the last bits when the number of threads or the splitting changes. The example fixes the partition with par_chunks(250), collects the chunk sums into a Vec (collecting an indexed parallel iterator preserves order) and adds them sequentially, so the result matches a serial chunked sum bit for bit. It also builds a ThreadPool with two threads and runs the work inside pool.install, which shows how to bound parallelism instead of using the global pool that defaults to one thread per core.

The pipeline connects a producer, three workers and a consumer with two bounded(16) channels. Bounded channels apply back-pressure: when the buffer is full, send blocks until a receiver makes room, so a fast stage cannot flood a slow one with unbounded memory. A channel closes for receivers only when every Sender has been dropped, so the code moves the producer's sender into its thread and explicitly drops the spare receiver and the spare out sender in the owner; otherwise the consumer loop would wait forever on a sender it holds itself. Output order from the workers is not deterministic, so the program reports only totals.

Check that closures capture only what is Send, that floating-point reductions use a fixed partition when reproducibility matters, that every spare Sender is dropped so channels can close, and that bounded channel capacity is chosen on purpose.
challenge: Add word_histogram(text) -> BTreeMap<String, usize> using par_split_whitespace, fold with a private HashMap per task and reduce to merge the maps. Print the histogram of "buy sell buy hold buy sell" and explain why sorting into a BTreeMap makes the output deterministic.
question: Why does the pipeline code explicitly drop the spare raw_rx and out_tx before consuming from out_rx?
correct: A channel closes only when all senders are dropped, so a sender kept by the consumer would make its loop wait forever
wrong: Dropping them returns their buffered messages to the producer so that nothing is lost when the pipeline stops
Crossbeam channels require an explicit close call before a receiver loop is allowed to end
Spare handles make the workers run sequentially, so dropping them restores parallelism
reasoning: Iterating a Receiver ends when the channel is disconnected, which happens when every Sender is gone. An extra clone held by the thread that is waiting prevents that. There is no close method to call, and extra handles do not serialize workers.

title: Statistical benchmarking with Criterion and a correctness test beside it
body: A hand-rolled timing loop gives one number; Criterion gives a measurement. It warms the code up, takes many samples, fits their distribution, reports a confidence interval and compares against the previous run to say whether performance changed. Benchmarks live in a benches/ directory and need harness = false in Cargo.toml, because criterion_main! generates its own main function in place of the default test harness. Criterion belongs in dev-dependencies so downstream users of your library never download or link it. This project pins criterion 0.8.2 with default features off and only the cargo_bench_support feature, which keeps the build small, and ships its Cargo.lock.

The library has two functions that compute the same sum of squares, one by iterating and one with the closed form n(n + 1)(2n + 1) / 6 using u128 intermediates so the multiplication cannot overflow. The unit test asserts that they agree for several sizes, because a faster function that returns the wrong value is worthless; correctness tests and benchmarks belong side by side. The benchmark uses std::hint::black_box on the input so the compiler cannot treat n as a constant, and BenchmarkId to give each size a stable name in the report.

Read results critically. On a typical release build the iterator version takes about the same time for n = 1,000 and n = 100,000, which cannot be true of a loop that does a hundred times more work. LLVM recognised the sum-of-squares pattern and replaced the loop with arithmetic, so the "iterator" benchmark is really measuring a closed form too. Criterion cannot know that; the flat curve is the clue. Use the quick mode (cargo bench --bench sums -- --quick) to smoke-test benchmarks cheaply in CI and the full run for decisions, and remember that a benchmark result describes one machine, one compiler and one input.

Check that each benchmark does real work (flat scaling with size is a warning), that inputs and outputs pass through black_box, that a unit test pins correctness, and that you compare runs on the same quiet machine.
challenge: Add a third implementation sum_squares_chunks that adds four squares per loop step plus a remainder loop, test it against sum_squares for n from 0 to 40 (so every remainder length is covered), and add it to the benchmark group with Throughput::Elements(n).
question: What does harness = false in a [[bench]] section do?
correct: It disables the default test harness so the benchmark file supplies its own main, which criterion_main! generates
wrong: It disables optimization for the benchmark target, so the measured code is not altered by the compiler
It runs the benchmark without compiling it first, using the previous build of the crate
It makes the benchmark single-threaded, so thread scheduling cannot disturb the timings
reasoning: Cargo normally wraps bench targets in the libtest harness. Criterion needs control of the entry point to run its own sampling and reporting, so the section turns the default harness off. The setting does not affect optimization or threading.
