projectInstructions: Rust 1.99 / edition 2024. Create the five files with the displayed paths. Run cargo test --quiet, cargo run --quiet, then cargo bench --bench sums -- --quick. The first build downloads criterion from crates.io (network needed); keep Cargo.lock. On some local toolchain installs rustc prints harmless warnings about rust-objcopy during cargo bench; the benchmark still runs.

projectChecks.name: unit tests prove both implementations agree
quick benchmark run reports every case

quiz.question: The iterator benchmark takes about the same time for n = 1,000 and n = 100,000. What is the most likely explanation?
quiz.correct: The optimizer replaced the loop with a closed-form computation, so the benchmark no longer measures a loop
wrong: Criterion caches results between input sizes, so the second size reuses the first measurement
The CPU executes loops of that size in a single cycle, so the time cannot depend on n
black_box makes the loop run in parallel, so the extra iterations cost no extra time
quiz.reasoning: Work proportional to n cannot take constant time unless the loop was eliminated. LLVM can turn polynomial summations into closed forms. Criterion does not cache across inputs and black_box does not parallelise.

quiz.question: Why is criterion listed under [dev-dependencies]?
quiz.correct: Only benchmarks, tests and examples use it, so library consumers never build or link it
wrong: Dev-dependencies compile faster than normal dependencies, so the benchmark builds are quicker
Criterion cannot be linked into a library, so it has to stay out of the normal dependencies
Cargo requires every crate with a benches directory to declare its harness crate there
quiz.reasoning: Dev-dependencies are built for tests, examples and benches only. They do not become requirements of crates that depend on yours.

quiz.question: How does Criterion produce more trustworthy numbers than one timed run?
quiz.correct: It warms up, collects many samples, analyses their distribution and compares against the saved previous run
wrong: It always reports the fastest single iteration, since that is the least disturbed run
It disables the operating system scheduler while measuring, so no other process can interrupt
It repeats the run until the numbers are identical, then reports that exact value
quiz.reasoning: Statistical sampling with warm-up and change detection reduces the effect of noise. Reporting only the minimum hides variance, and identical numbers would not happen on a real machine.

quiz.question: Why is there a unit test beside the benchmark?
quiz.correct: A faster function that returns a wrong answer is useless, so the test pins correctness while the benchmark measures speed
wrong: The benchmark cannot run unless a test passes first, because cargo runs tests before benches
Tests make the benchmark results more precise, since they warm up the code being measured
Cargo refuses to compile benches without tests, because it needs a baseline for comparison
quiz.reasoning: Benchmarks measure time, not correctness. The assertion that both implementations agree prevents optimizing into a bug.

title: Zero-copy parsing of a binary market-data protocol
body: Exchange feeds such as Nasdaq ITCH are streams of tightly packed binary messages, not text. Each frame starts with a one-byte type, the type fixes the frame length, and numeric fields are big-endian (network byte order). This lesson parses a small ITCH-style protocol: Add (type A, 34 bytes: timestamp u64, order id u64, side byte, shares u32, 8-byte space-padded symbol, price u32), Cancel (X, 21 bytes) and Execute (E, 29 bytes). Reading a field is u32::from_be_bytes on a four-byte slice, which is correct on any host because the conversion defines the byte order explicitly rather than reinterpreting memory.

The parser is safe code with no pointer tricks. It first reads the type byte, looks up the frame length, and compares it with the number of bytes available. If the buffer is shorter it returns Truncated { needed, have } before touching a field, so a slice index can never go out of range. It returns the message and the number of bytes consumed, so the caller can advance through a buffer. The symbol is validated as ASCII and returned as a &str that borrows from the input buffer, so parsing a message allocates nothing; the message type carries the lifetime, Message<'a>.

A network read delivers arbitrary chunks, so a frame can arrive in two pieces. Truncated is therefore not a fault: parse_all stops, returns the messages decoded so far and the unconsumed tail, and the caller appends the next read to that tail and tries again. A different error, such as an unknown type byte or an invalid side, means the stream is corrupt, and the parser reports it along with the offset where it stopped, because guessing a frame boundary after corruption would produce garbage orders.

Check the available length before indexing, define byte order explicitly, return the consumed length, treat truncation as normal and corruption as an error, validate every enumerated byte, and keep borrowed strings tied to the buffer lifetime.
challenge: Write FrameReader, which owns a Vec<u8> buffer, has push(&mut self, chunk: &[u8]), and next_cancel(&mut self) -> Option<(u64, u64, u32)> that returns the next complete Cancel frame (type X, 21 bytes: ts, id, shares) and drains it from the buffer. Feed the same four cancel frames in 7-byte chunks and check that they all come out, in order.
solutionStdout: 4 cancels recovered from 12 chunks, 0 bytes left
question: Before reading any field from a frame, what must the parser check?
correct: That the buffer holds at least the frame length implied by the type byte, so every index stays in range
wrong: That the timestamp is strictly increasing, so a later message can never carry an earlier time
That the host CPU is big-endian, since the fields would otherwise be read in the wrong order
That the symbol is listed on the exchange, because unknown symbols cannot be stored in a &str
reasoning: Bounds are the parser's responsibility. Checking the frame length first turns a short read into a Truncated result instead of a panic or a misread field. Content checks and CPU endianness are separate concerns.

quiz.question: Why does the parser use u32::from_be_bytes instead of casting memory to a u32?
quiz.correct: from_be_bytes fixes the byte order explicitly, so the result is correct on any host CPU and alignment does not matter
wrong: Casting memory is not allowed in Rust at all, so reading a wire format must go through a conversion
from_be_bytes is the only way to read a u32 from a slice, since slices cannot be indexed
Big-endian is always faster than little-endian, so converting to it saves a byte swap on every CPU
quiz.reasoning: Reinterpreting bytes depends on host endianness and alignment. from_be_bytes performs a defined conversion. Unsafe casts are possible but unnecessary here.

quiz.question: A read ends in the middle of a frame. What should parse_all do?
quiz.correct: Return the decoded messages and the unconsumed tail without an error, so the caller can append the next read
wrong: Return an error and drop the partial frame, because a short read means the stream is corrupt
Panic because the data is corrupt, since a frame that stops early can never be completed
Pad the frame with zeros and parse it, so a message is always produced for each read
quiz.reasoning: TCP delivers byte streams, not messages, so partial frames are normal. Corruption is a different case that is reported as an error.

quiz.question: Why does the Add message hold stock: &str rather than String?
quiz.correct: The symbol borrows from the input buffer after ASCII validation, so parsing allocates nothing
wrong: Because String cannot hold ASCII text, so a symbol read from the wire must be a &str
Because &str values are copied by the compiler automatically, so no lifetime ties them to the buffer
Because the exchange sends the symbol as a pointer, so the parser can only keep a reference to it
quiz.reasoning: A borrowed slice avoids a heap allocation per message. The cost is that the buffer must outlive the message, which Message<'a> expresses.

quiz.question: Why is an unknown type byte treated as a hard error rather than skipped?
quiz.correct: The frame length is unknown, so the next frame boundary cannot be trusted and continuing would decode garbage as orders
wrong: Unknown types are always heartbeat messages, so they carry nothing that the parser needs to keep
Skipping one byte is always correct, because the next frame must start right after the bad type byte
Rust cannot skip bytes in a slice, so the only option is to stop the whole program with an error
quiz.reasoning: Without a known length the parser cannot find the next frame. Resynchronising requires an out-of-band mechanism such as a session restart or sequence request.

title: A limit order book with BTreeMap price levels and FIFO queues
body: A limit order book lists resting buy orders (bids) and sell orders (asks). Orders at the same price form a level, and within a level the earliest order has priority: price-time priority. Two data-structure choices follow directly. Price levels live in a BTreeMap<Price, Level>, which keeps keys ordered, so the best bid is the largest key (last_key_value) and the best ask the smallest (first_key_value), both in O(log n). Orders inside a level live in a VecDeque, because new orders go on the back and the oldest order is taken from the front, which is FIFO in O(1).

Cancelling needs an id lookup, otherwise every cancel would scan every level. A HashMap<OrderId, (Side, Price)> records where each order rests, so a cancel finds its level directly, then scans that one queue for the order. Each Level also keeps a running total quantity, so depth queries and best-price quantity are O(1) per level instead of summing a queue. An empty level must be removed from the map, otherwise best_bid would report a price nobody is quoting.

The invariants are the real specification, and the program checks them after every operation: the best bid is strictly below the best ask (the book is never crossed), no level is empty, each level total equals the sum of its orders, and the id index contains exactly the resting orders. This lesson rests orders without matching. An incoming order that would cross the spread is rejected with WouldCross; the matching engine project later turns such an order into trades. Rejecting duplicate ids and zero quantity at the boundary keeps the internal state valid.
Check that best prices come from the ordered map ends, FIFO order inside levels, cancel by id through the index, empty levels removed, level totals maintained and the book never crossed.
expectedStdout:
best bid = Some((10000, 12)), best ask = Some((10010, 10))
bid depth = [(10000, 12), (9990, 10)]
ask depth = [(10010, 10), (10030, 8)]
spread = 10
cancel 1 -> Some(Order { id: 1, qty: 5 })
best bid after cancel = Some((10000, 7))
cancel 3 -> Some(Order { id: 3, qty: 10 }), bid levels now 1
cancel unknown -> None
front of the 10000 queue is order 2
duplicate: Err(DuplicateId)
zero quantity: Err(ZeroQuantity)
crossing bid: Err(WouldCross)
crossing ask: Err(WouldCross)
invariants hold
challenge: Write volume_to_buy(asks: &BTreeMap<i64, u32>, qty: u32) -> Option<i64>, the total cost of a market buy that walks the ask levels from the lowest price upward, taking as much as needed at each level. Return None when there is not enough depth. Check 10 shares against asks {101: 4, 102: 8, 105: 20}, which cost 4 x 101 + 6 x 102 = 1016.
solutionStdout: 10 shares cost Some(1016), 33 shares cost None
question: Why are the price levels stored in a BTreeMap and the orders at one price in a VecDeque?
correct: The BTreeMap keeps prices ordered, so best bid and ask are its ends; the VecDeque gives O(1) FIFO within a price
wrong: A BTreeMap is faster than a HashMap for every operation, and a VecDeque is safe to share between threads
The BTreeMap stores orders by arrival time and the VecDeque stores prices in sorted order
They are required by the exchange protocol, which fixes how a book keeps its prices and queues
reasoning: Ordered keys give cheap access to the best prices and iteration in price order. A deque pushes new orders to the back and serves the oldest from the front. Neither choice is protocol-mandated, and BTreeMap is not faster than HashMap for point lookups.

quiz.question: Why does the book keep a HashMap from order id to (side, price)?
quiz.correct: A cancel can jump straight to the right level instead of scanning every level of both sides
wrong: It is required to keep the BTreeMap sorted, since the map cannot order its own price keys
It stores the best bid and best ask, so those prices never have to be searched for
It makes duplicate ids possible, since the same id can then rest on both sides of the book
quiz.reasoning: Cancels reference only an id. The index supplies side and price, so the cost is one map lookup plus a scan of a single queue.

quiz.question: What must happen when the last order at a price is cancelled?
quiz.correct: The empty level is removed from the map, otherwise best_bid or best_ask would report a price nobody is quoting
wrong: The level stays so the price can be reused quickly, because removing it would cost an allocation
The next level is merged into it, so the book always keeps a contiguous range of prices without gaps
The book flips side, because an empty bid level turns into an ask level at the same price
quiz.reasoning: Best prices come from the map ends, so a stale empty level would corrupt market data and the spread.

quiz.question: Why does add reject a bid at or above the best ask instead of resting it?
quiz.correct: A resting crossed order would leave bid >= ask; such an order should trade, which the matching engine handles
wrong: Rust forbids equal keys in a BTreeMap, so a bid and an ask at the same price cannot both rest
Bids may never be placed above 10,000, since that is the largest price the book can store
Crossing orders are cancelled by the exchange at random, so the book must not hold them
quiz.reasoning: The no-cross invariant is what makes the best bid and ask meaningful. Crossing flow becomes trades in the matching engine lesson.

quiz.question: Why does Level keep a running total instead of summing its queue on demand?
quiz.correct: Depth and best-price quantity become O(1) per level, and the invariant check can verify the total against the queue
wrong: Because VecDeque cannot be iterated, so the only way to know a level's quantity is a stored total
Because totals are required for FIFO ordering, since the queue cannot tell which order is first
Because summing would overflow, so a stored total with a wider type is the only safe choice
quiz.reasoning: The total is redundant data kept consistent on add and cancel. Redundancy is acceptable when an invariant check ties it to the source of truth.

title: A dense price-array book: O(1) updates and best-price pointers
body: When the price range is bounded and activity clusters near the touch, a dense array beats an ordered map. Prices sit on a tick grid, so a price maps to an index with (price - base) / tick, and the book is two Vec<u64> arrays of quantity, one for bids and one for asks. Adding or removing quantity at a price is one array write, O(1), with no allocation and excellent cache behaviour because neighbouring prices are neighbouring memory. This is the structure behind many L2 (aggregated by price) market-data books built from add and reduce messages.

The best prices need care. Scanning the array for the best bid on every query would be O(range), so the book stores best_bid and best_ask as indices. Adding quantity above the best bid moves the pointer up in O(1). Removing quantity that empties the best level makes the pointer stale, so the code scans downward from it to the next non-empty level. Near the touch that scan is short, which is why the structure works well in practice, and it is also its worst case: a thin book with a large gap behind the best price makes the scan long.

Validity checks are part of the design. A price below the base, above the range, or not on the tick grid must be rejected, because otherwise integer division would silently map it to the wrong level. Reducing by more than the resting quantity is also an error. The trade-offs against the BTreeMap book are the lesson: arrays give O(1) updates and no per-level allocation but use memory proportional to the price range and lose per-order queues, so they suit aggregated depth, not price-time-priority matching. The program proves equivalence by driving both structures with 10,000 pseudo-random operations and comparing the best prices after each one.

Check range and tick alignment on every price, keep best pointers consistent when levels empty, reject over-reduction, document that this is an aggregated book, and test it against a simple ordered-map model.
expectedStdout:
best bid = Some((10000, 5)), best ask = Some((10010, 4))
after the top bid empties: Some((9990, 10))
after the top ask empties: Some((10050, 8))
off tick: Err(OffTick)
below the range: Err(OutOfRange)
above the range: Err(OutOfRange)
over-reduce: Err(Insufficient)
array book agrees with the BTreeMap model after 10000 random operations: true
array memory for 200 levels: 1600 bytes per side
challenge: Add depth(&self, side: Side, n: usize) -> Vec<(i64, u64)> returning the top n non-empty levels in priority order (highest bid downward, lowest ask upward) by scanning from the best pointer. Check a book with bids at 100, 98, 97 and asks at 101, 103.
question: In which situation does the dense price-array book beat the BTreeMap book?
correct: When prices lie in a bounded range on a tick grid and activity clusters near the touch, so updates are O(1) array writes
wrong: When prices are unbounded and sparse, because an array only costs memory for the levels in use
When price-time priority matching needs per-order queues, since arrays keep orders in arrival order
When the book must store individual order ids, because each array slot can hold a whole queue
reasoning: The array trades memory for speed: it needs a bounded range and tick grid, and it stores aggregate quantity. Sparse or unbounded prices waste memory, and per-order queues need a different structure.

quiz.question: Why does the book store best_bid and best_ask as indices?
quiz.correct: Scanning the array for the best price on every query would be O(range), while a maintained pointer answers in O(1)
wrong: Because indices cannot be negative, whereas a price can be, so a pointer is the only option
Because Vec cannot be searched, so the book needs a stored position for each best price
Because the BTreeMap model requires them, and the two books must agree on the representation
quiz.reasoning: The pointer is cached state that must be repaired when the best level empties.

quiz.question: What happens when the best bid level is reduced to zero?
quiz.correct: The best pointer is stale, so the code scans down to the next non-empty level, which is cheap near the touch
wrong: The book flips to the ask side, since an empty best bid means that no buyers remain at all
The array shrinks by one element, so the top of the book is always the last element
The next add automatically repairs it, so nothing needs to be done until a new order arrives
quiz.reasoning: Only the emptied best level invalidates the pointer. The repair scan is the structure's worst case when there is a large gap behind the best price.

quiz.question: Why is an off-tick price rejected instead of rounded to the nearest level?
quiz.correct: Integer division would silently map it to the wrong level, hiding a bug in the sender
wrong: Rounding is not defined for integers, so the book cannot move a price to its nearest level
Off-tick prices can never occur in real markets, so the check only guards against test data
The array cannot be indexed with remainders, because remainders are always negative numbers
quiz.reasoning: The grid defines valid prices. Accepting a bad one corrupts the book, so it is reported at the boundary.

quiz.question: What does the 10,000-operation comparison with the BTreeMap model establish?
quiz.correct: The fast structure matches a simple reference on those sequences: evidence of correctness, not a proof
wrong: That the array book is proven correct for all possible inputs, since the model covers every case
That the BTreeMap model is faster than the array book, since it is used as the reference
That order ids are unique across the two books, since both use the same random sequence
quiz.reasoning: Differential testing against a slow, obviously correct model is a strong check on a fast implementation, but it samples behaviours rather than proving them.

title: A price-time priority matching engine with limit, market and IOC orders
body: A matching engine takes an incoming order, trades it against the opposite side of the book and decides what to do with any remainder. The rules are price-time priority: a buy trades with the lowest-priced asks first, and among orders at one price the oldest goes first. The trade executes at the resting order's price, not the incoming order's, so a buy limit at 105 meeting a resting sell at 100 trades at 100 and the taker keeps the price improvement. The data structure is the one from the order book lesson: a BTreeMap from price to a VecDeque of resting orders per side, plus a HashMap from id to (side, price) for cancels.

Order types differ only in what happens to the unfilled remainder. A limit order is willing to trade at its price or better, so matching stops at the first price the limit does not allow, and a Gtc (good till cancelled) remainder then rests on the book. An IOC (immediate or cancel) limit order keeps what it traded and cancels the rest. A market order has no limit price: it sweeps levels until it is filled or the book is empty, and its remainder is cancelled because there is no price at which it could rest. The Outcome struct reports trades, quantity left resting and quantity cancelled, so no share is ever unaccounted for.

The tests are the specification. Unit tests pin FIFO order within a level, execution at the resting price, an inclusive limit price with better prices first, partial fills that rest, IOC and market remainders, cancels, and rejected zero quantity or duplicate ids (checked against resting orders only: a filled or cancelled id can be reused, whereas a production engine enforces uniqueness for the whole session). An integration test drives 2,000 pseudo-random orders and checks two global invariants after every step: the book is never crossed (best bid below best ask), and quantity is conserved, because every traded share leaves both the taker and a maker, so submitted = 2 x traded + cancelled + still resting. The validation also deliberately breaks the engine: one mutation flips the queue from FIFO to LIFO, another makes the limit exclusive, and the checks require the tests to fail. A test suite that cannot detect a broken rule is not guarding it.

Check execution price, FIFO within a level, what happens to each order type's remainder, that empty levels disappear, that cancel and duplicate ids are handled at the boundary, and that mutation of a core rule makes the tests fail.
challenge: Add Tif::Fok (fill or kill): the order trades its whole quantity immediately or does nothing and reports the whole quantity as cancelled. Compute the quantity available at acceptable prices before matching, and add a test that a too-large FOK leaves the book untouched while a satisfiable one fills completely.
question: A buy limit order at 105 meets a resting sell order at 100. At what price do they trade?
correct: 100, the resting (maker) order's price, so the taker receives price improvement
wrong: 105, the incoming order's limit price, because the taker is the one that caused the trade
102.5, the midpoint of the two prices, so both sides share the price improvement equally
Whichever price belongs to the order with the larger id, because the newer order sets the price
reasoning: Under price-time priority the resting order has already told the market its price. The taker is only constrained by its own limit, so it gets the better price. A midpoint rule would need an explicit auction mechanism.

quiz.question: What happens to the unfilled remainder of an IOC limit order?
quiz.correct: It is cancelled and reported in Outcome::cancelled; it never rests on the book
wrong: It rests at the limit price like a Gtc order, so it can trade later when a seller arrives
It is converted to a market order, so it trades at whatever price is still available
It is held for the next trading session, after which it is cancelled automatically
quiz.reasoning: Immediate-or-cancel means any quantity that cannot trade immediately is cancelled. Only Gtc limit remainders rest.

quiz.question: Why does the random-flow test check submitted = 2 x traded + cancelled + resting?
quiz.correct: Each traded share leaves both a taker and a maker, so the identity detects lost or duplicated quantity
wrong: Because traded shares are counted twice in the exchange fee, once for each side of the trade
Because cancelled shares always equal traded shares, so the two cancel out in the identity
Because resting orders are always empty at the end, so the identity has no resting term
quiz.reasoning: A conservation law like this catches bugs that individual example tests miss, such as a partial fill that forgets to reduce a maker.

quiz.question: Why does a market order that finds no liquidity report its quantity as cancelled?
quiz.correct: A market order has no limit price, so there is no price at which the remainder could rest
wrong: Because market orders are rejected by the exchange when the book has no liquidity at all
Because the book would otherwise become crossed, which the engine must never allow
Because cancelled orders are cheaper to process than orders that rest on the book
quiz.reasoning: Resting requires a price. Without liquidity the order cannot trade, and it is not allowed to wait.

quiz.question: What does the LIFO mutation check demonstrate?
quiz.correct: That the test suite really guards price-time priority: breaking it makes tests fail
wrong: That LIFO is a valid alternative priority rule, so the tests accept either queue order
That VecDeque cannot be used for matching, because only a stack preserves arrival order
That the engine never uses the queue, so changing its end has no effect on any trade
quiz.reasoning: A mutation test deliberately introduces a defect. If the tests still passed, they would not be protecting the rule they claim to.

title: Position and PnL accounting with FIFO lots, flips and fees
body: A position is the net of every fill, and profit and loss (PnL) comes in two kinds. Realized PnL is locked in when a trade closes part of an existing position. Unrealized PnL is the mark-to-market gain on what is still open, computed against a current price. Net PnL is realized plus unrealized minus fees. Everything here is integer arithmetic in price ticks with i128 accumulators, so the books balance exactly and there is no floating-point drift to explain to an auditor.

The account stores open lots as a VecDeque of (signed quantity, price): positive quantity is a long lot, negative a short lot. A new fill first closes lots of the opposite sign in first-in first-out order. Closing c units of a long lot bought at p0 by selling at p1 realizes (p1 - p0) * c, and closing a short lot sold at p0 by buying at p1 realizes (p0 - p1) * c. Whatever quantity remains after the opposite lots are exhausted opens a new lot at the fill price. That one rule handles adding, reducing, closing and flipping through zero: selling 15 against a long of 10 closes the 10 lots and opens a short of 5 at the sell price.

Unrealized PnL for any lot is (mark - price) * signed quantity, which is positive for a long when the mark is above its cost and for a short when the mark is below. Fees reduce net PnL immediately. FIFO is one accounting convention; average cost is another, and they report different realized PnL at different times even though total PnL is identical once the position is flat. Pick one convention, document it, and reconcile against the broker or exchange statement using the same one.

Check that realized and unrealized PnL are tracked separately, signs are tested for shorts and flips, fees are included in net PnL, wide accumulators (i128) are used, and the convention (FIFO or average cost) matches the statement you reconcile against.

Show that after buying 10 @ 100, buying 5 @ 102 and selling 12 @ 105 average cost realizes 52 where FIFO realized 56, but selling the last 3 @ 104 brings both methods to a total of 62.

question: A trader is long 10 and sells 15. How does the accounting treat the extra 5?
correct: It closes the long 10 (realizing PnL) and opens a new short position of 5 at the sell price
wrong: It rejects the sell because it exceeds the position, since the account never goes short
It realizes PnL on all 15 units against the long cost, treating the extra 5 as already owned
It opens a short of 15 and keeps the long 10, so the account holds both at once
reasoning: Only the quantity of opposite sign that exists can be closed. The remainder has nothing to offset, so it becomes a new lot in the opposite direction at the fill price.

quiz.question: How is unrealized PnL computed for a short lot of -5 opened at 103 when the mark is 100?
quiz.correct: (100 - 103) * (-5) = +15, because a short gains when the price falls
wrong: (100 - 103) * 5 = -15, because the quantity is always taken as positive
0, because shorts have no unrealized PnL until the position is closed
103 * 5 = 515, because unrealized PnL is the full value of the lot
quiz.reasoning: Using signed quantity makes one formula work for longs and shorts: (mark - price) * qty.

quiz.question: Why are the accumulators i128 integers instead of f64?
quiz.correct: Integer sums are exact, so PnL reconciles to the tick with no rounding drift, and i128 avoids overflow in price times quantity totals
wrong: Because i128 arithmetic is faster than f64 on current CPUs, so large accounts need fewer cycles per fill
Because f64 cannot represent negative PnL, so losses would have to be tracked in a separate field
Because Rust forbids floating point in finance code, and the compiler rejects f64 in money types
quiz.reasoning: Prices in ticks times quantities stay exact in integers. Floats would introduce small errors that make exact reconciliation impossible.

quiz.question: FIFO and average-cost accounting report different realized PnL after a partial close. What is true when the position is later fully closed?
quiz.correct: Total PnL is identical; the methods differ only in when profit is recognised
wrong: FIFO always reports higher total PnL, because it matches the oldest and cheapest lots first
Average cost always reports higher total PnL, because it smooths every price into one number
The totals can differ by the fees, since each method charges fees at a different time
quiz.reasoning: Over the full life of the position, total PnL is proceeds minus cost regardless of the allocation method.

quiz.question: What does the round trip buy 10 @ 100 then sell 10 @ 100 with no fees show?
quiz.correct: Position 0 and net PnL 0: closing at the entry price realizes nothing and leaves no open lots
wrong: A profit equal to the spread, because the buy and the sell are matched at slightly different prices
A leftover lot of 10, because the sell only closes the lot after the next fill arrives
An error because the fills are equal, since a buy and a sell at one price cancel out illegally
quiz.reasoning: Realized PnL is (price - lot price) * quantity, which is zero, and the lot is removed when its quantity reaches zero.

title: Black-Scholes pricing, Greeks and implied volatility
body: The Black-Scholes model prices a European option on a non-dividend stock when the stock follows geometric Brownian motion with constant volatility and the interest rate is constant. For spot S, strike K, rate r, volatility sigma and time to expiry T in years, d1 = (ln(S/K) + (r + sigma^2/2) T) / (sigma sqrt(T)) and d2 = d1 - sigma sqrt(T). The call is S Phi(d1) - K e^(-rT) Phi(d2) and the put is K e^(-rT) Phi(-d2) - S Phi(-d1), where Phi is the standard normal cumulative distribution function. The standard library has no erf, so the code uses the Abramowitz and Stegun polynomial approximation whose absolute error is below 7.5e-8, which is fine for teaching and for tests with explicit tolerances but not for production pricing.

The Greeks are sensitivities, and each has a closed form here. Delta, the change in price per unit change in spot, is Phi(d1) for a call. Gamma, the change in delta, is the normal density at d1 divided by S sigma sqrt(T). Vega, the change per unit of volatility, is S times the density times sqrt(T); the program reports it per 1.00 of volatility, so a 1 percentage point move is a hundredth of it. Never trust a formula you cannot check: the program recomputes delta and gamma by central finite differences, (C(S+h) - C(S-h)) / 2h and the second difference, and requires agreement to a tolerance.

Markets quote prices, not volatilities, so traders invert the model. The price is strictly increasing in sigma, which makes bisection a robust way to find the implied volatility: bracket sigma between a tiny value and a large one and halve the interval until the model price matches. Newton's method is faster but can diverge when vega is tiny. A price outside the no-arbitrage bounds, for example below the call's intrinsic value S - K e^(-rT), has no solution, so the function returns None. Note that put-call parity C - P = S - K e^(-rT) holds here by construction because Phi(-x) = 1 - Phi(x) in the code; it checks internal consistency, not accuracy, so also compare against a known reference price.

Check inputs (positive vol, time and prices), test the normal CDF approximation against known values, verify Greeks by finite differences, treat prices outside no-arbitrage bounds as errors, and never describe an approximate CDF as exact.

question: Why is bisection a good way to compute implied volatility?
correct: Price is strictly increasing in volatility, so bisection on a bracket converges reliably without needing a derivative
wrong: Because the price is not monotonic in volatility, so only a bracketing method can find the root
Because bisection needs no upper bound on volatility, so it can search every positive value
Because Newton's method cannot be used for options at all, since vega is always exactly zero
reasoning: Monotonicity guarantees a unique solution inside any bracket whose endpoints straddle the target price. Newton works too and is faster, but it can overshoot when vega is small.

quiz.question: What does the put-call parity check in the program establish?
quiz.correct: Internal consistency: Phi(-x) = 1 - Phi(x) makes parity hold by construction, so it does not prove accuracy
wrong: That the normal CDF approximation is exact, because parity could not hold with any error in it
That the model matches market prices, since parity is the relationship the market itself enforces
That the volatility is correctly implied, because parity fixes the call and the put to one sigma
quiz.reasoning: Parity would hold even if the CDF approximation were poor. Accuracy needs a reference value such as 10.4506 for the sample call.

quiz.question: How is vega reported in the program, and what is the practical conversion?
quiz.correct: Per 1.00 of volatility, so a one percentage point move changes the price by about vega / 100
wrong: Per 1 percentage point of volatility, so no conversion is needed for a one-point move
Per day, so multiply by 252 to convert the figure into an annual sensitivity
As a percentage of spot, so a vega of 37 means the price moves by 37 percent of spot
quiz.reasoning: The derivative with respect to sigma is naturally expressed per unit (1.00 = 100 vol points). Desks usually quote per vol point, which is a hundredth of that.

quiz.question: Why verify closed-form Greeks with finite differences?
quiz.correct: An independent numerical derivative catches algebra or sign mistakes in the formulas
wrong: Because closed-form Greeks do not exist for Black-Scholes, so numerical derivatives are the only way
Because finite differences are always more accurate than formulas, so they replace the closed form
Because Rust cannot evaluate exp and ln exactly, so the formulas need an independent check
quiz.reasoning: Two independent routes to the same number agreeing, within a tolerance chosen for the step size, is strong evidence. Finite differences have their own truncation and rounding error, so they are a check, not a replacement.

quiz.question: What should implied_vol return when the target price is below the call's intrinsic value?
quiz.correct: None, because no volatility produces a price outside the no-arbitrage bounds
wrong: 0.0, the lowest volatility in the bracket, because that gives the smallest possible price
The largest volatility in the bracket, because that is the closest value to the target
NaN, which callers can safely ignore because it compares unequal to every number
quiz.reasoning: A call is worth at least max(S - K e^(-rT), 0). A price below that is not explained by any volatility, so inverting it would be meaningless.

title: Monte Carlo option pricing with antithetic variates
body: Monte Carlo pricing applies the risk-neutral valuation principle: the price of a derivative is the discounted expected payoff under a model where the stock grows at the risk-free rate. For a European call on geometric Brownian motion the terminal price is S_T = S exp((r - sigma^2/2) T + sigma sqrt(T) Z) with Z a standard normal, and the estimate is the average of e^(-rT) max(S_T - K, 0) over many draws. The closed-form Black-Scholes price exists for this case, which makes it a perfect test: a Monte Carlo estimate should land within a few standard errors of it.

Normals come from uniforms. The Box-Muller transform turns two independent uniforms u1 and u2 into two independent standard normals, sqrt(-2 ln u1) cos(2 pi u2) and sqrt(-2 ln u1) sin(2 pi u2). The uniform generator here returns values in (0, 1], never exactly zero, because ln(0) is negative infinity and would poison the average. The generator is the seeded xorshift64* from the earlier lesson, so the whole experiment is reproducible, and the standard error is computed from the sample variance, se = sqrt(variance / N).

Variance reduction buys accuracy without more samples. With antithetic variates each draw Z is paired with -Z. Because the call payoff is monotone in Z, the two payoffs are negatively correlated, so their average has lower variance than the average of two independent draws. The comparison must be fair: plain uses 200,000 independent payoffs, antithetic uses 100,000 pairs, so both evaluate the payoff 200,000 times, and each pair average counts as one observation when estimating the standard error. This is the main idea of variance reduction: more information per random number, not more random numbers.

Check that the estimate is reported with its standard error, the seed is fixed, the generator can never return an exact zero to ln, the comparison with the closed form uses a multiple of the standard error, and variance-reduction comparisons use the same number of payoff evaluations.

antithetic: 10.469 +/- 0.023 (200000 payoffs)

Show that its price is below the European call because averaging reduces effective volatility, using the same random numbers for both payoffs.

question: Why is each antithetic pair treated as ONE observation when estimating the standard error?
correct: Only the pair averages are independent, so counting both members of each pair would understate the error
wrong: Because pairs always contain the same number, so the average of a pair has no variance
Because the standard error formula does not apply to averages, only to single payoffs
Because Box-Muller produces exactly two outputs, so each pair is one draw from the generator
reasoning: The standard error formula assumes independent observations. The pair averages are independent across pairs; the members of a pair are deliberately dependent, so counting them separately would give a falsely small error.

quiz.question: Why does the uniform generator return values in (0, 1] instead of [0, 1)?
quiz.correct: Box-Muller takes ln(u1), and ln(0) is negative infinity, which would corrupt the average
wrong: Because [0, 1) cannot be represented in f64 at all, whereas (0, 1] can be written exactly
Because the xorshift generator cannot produce zero, so the lower bound is already excluded
Because 1.0 gives better normals, so the generator is biased towards the top of the range
quiz.reasoning: Using 1 - u maps [0, 1) to (0, 1], so the logarithm is always finite.

quiz.question: Why do antithetic variates reduce variance for a call option?
quiz.correct: The payoff is monotone in Z, so payoffs at Z and -Z are negatively correlated and their average varies less
wrong: They double the number of independent random numbers drawn, which lowers the error as 1/sqrt(N)
They remove the discount factor from the calculation, which is the main source of variance
They make the payoff linear in Z, so the average of a pair equals its expected value exactly
quiz.reasoning: Negative correlation between the paired payoffs reduces the variance of their average without extra random draws.

quiz.question: What is a fair way to compare plain and antithetic Monte Carlo?
quiz.correct: Use the same total number of payoff evaluations for both, so differences come from variance reduction, not more work
wrong: Use the same number of pairs, giving antithetic twice the evaluations of the plain estimator
Use different seeds that happen to give a lower error to antithetic, so the comparison favours it
Compare only the means, not the standard errors, since the means show which one is closer
quiz.reasoning: Cost matters. Antithetic pairs cost two payoff evaluations, so the comparison halves the number of pairs.

quiz.question: A Monte Carlo price differs from Black-Scholes by 1.5 standard errors. What does that suggest?
quiz.correct: Nothing alarming: differences of a couple of standard errors are expected from sampling noise
wrong: The closed form is wrong, because any correct simulation lands within one standard error
The random generator is broken, since a good generator never produces a deviation this large
The simulation must be rerun until the error is zero, because only then is the estimate valid
quiz.reasoning: A correct estimator lands within about 2 standard errors roughly 95 percent of the time, so 1.5 is ordinary.

title: Historical value at risk and expected shortfall
body: Value at risk (VaR) answers: how much could we lose over one period, with a given confidence? Historical VaR makes no distribution assumption. Take the observed profit-and-loss series, sort it, and read off the loss that was exceeded in only (1 - confidence) of the observations. At 95 percent confidence, 5 percent of days were worse than the VaR. The input here is a series of integer PnL values in ticks; VaR is reported as a positive loss, so a VaR of 100 means "we lost at least 100 on the worst 5 percent of days".

The definition hides choices. The nearest-rank method picks the k-th worst observation with k = ceil(n x (1 - confidence)); the rank is computed in integer arithmetic from confidence in basis points so there is no floating-point error deciding between k = 12 and k = 13. Other conventions interpolate between neighbouring observations, which gives slightly different numbers for the same data. State the convention next to every VaR figure. Also state the sample size: with 250 observations, a 99 percent VaR rests on the worst 3 values, and one extra bad day moves it a lot.

VaR says nothing about how bad the tail is beyond the threshold. Expected shortfall (ES, also called conditional VaR) is the average loss across those tail observations, so it is always at least as large as VaR and it reacts to the two big shocks in the sample (-400 and -250) that VaR at 95 percent ignores. Regulators and risk teams increasingly prefer ES for that reason. The program prints both for 90, 95 and 99 percent and checks that the tail averages are ordered the way the theory says.

Check that the convention and sample size are stated, ranks are computed with integers, losses are reported with a consistent sign, ES is reported next to VaR, and a handful of tail observations is never described as a precise estimate.
expectedStdout:
observations = 250, worst = -400, best = 100
90%: tail size 25, VaR = 79, ES = 109
95%: tail size 13, VaR = 91, ES = 131
99%: tail size 3, VaR = 100, ES = 250
ES >= VaR and higher confidence means a larger VaR: true
99% VaR after one more bad day: 100 -> 250
95% VaR after one more bad day: 91 -> 92
n = 100: tail sizes at 90/95/99% = 10/5/1
challenge: Add var_linear(pnls, confidence_bp) that interpolates between the two order statistics around position p = (n - 1) x (1 - confidence) in the sorted series (position 0 is the worst outcome). Return the loss as an f64 and check that it lies between the sorted values at floor(p) and ceil(p), and that for 95% it is no larger than the 99% value.
solutionStdout:
90%: linear VaR = 79.00, nearest rank = 79
95%: linear VaR = 90.55, nearest rank = 91
99%: linear VaR = 100.00, nearest rank = 100
expected shortfall at 95% = 131
question: What does a 95% one-day historical VaR of 100 mean?
correct: In the sample, about 5 percent of days lost at least 100; it is a threshold from observed data, not a worst-case bound
wrong: The most that can ever be lost in a day is 100, because VaR is a hard limit on losses
The average daily loss over the sample is 100, taken across every day in the history
The loss will exceed 100 on exactly 5 days next year, since VaR predicts the number of breaches
reasoning: VaR is a quantile of the loss distribution. It does not bound the loss, does not describe the tail beyond the threshold, and does not predict an exact count of future exceedances.

quiz.question: Why is the tail size computed with integer arithmetic in basis points?
quiz.correct: Floating-point rounding could push ceil(n * (1 - confidence)) to the wrong integer when the product is an exact boundary like 12.5
wrong: Because floats cannot represent 95 percent exactly, so the percentile index would be off by a few ranks
Because the sort only works on integers, so the confidence level has to be an integer count too
Because basis points are required by the exchange for any risk figure that is reported to it
quiz.reasoning: A rank is a discrete choice. Integer arithmetic removes any chance that a rounding error moves a boundary case to a neighbouring observation.

quiz.question: What does expected shortfall add that VaR does not?
quiz.correct: It averages the losses in the tail beyond the threshold, so it reflects how severe the worst days were
wrong: It predicts the date of the next loss, because it tracks how the tail evolves over time
It removes the need to choose a confidence level, since it averages over all possible levels
It is always smaller than VaR, because an average over the tail cannot exceed its threshold
quiz.reasoning: ES at the same confidence is at least as large as VaR, and it responds to extreme observations that a quantile ignores.

quiz.question: Why is a 99% VaR from 250 observations fragile?
quiz.correct: It rests on only the worst two or three observations, so one more bad day can move it substantially
wrong: Because 250 is not divisible by 100, so the tail size at 99 percent cannot be a whole number
Because the series is sorted, and a sorted series amplifies the effect of the largest values
Because 99% VaR cannot be computed historically, only with a fitted normal distribution
quiz.reasoning: With ceil(250 x 0.01) = 3 tail points, the estimate depends on very few values. Longer histories or other methods are needed for stability.

quiz.question: Two teams report 95% VaR for the same data and get 40 and 43. What is the most likely explanation?
quiz.correct: They use different quantile conventions, such as nearest rank or interpolation, so the convention must be stated
wrong: One of them used the wrong programming language, since VaR depends on how floats are rounded
VaR is random and changes on each calculation, since historical data are resampled every time
Interpolation never changes the result, so the teams must have used different data
quiz.reasoning: Several valid definitions exist for the empirical quantile, and small samples make the differences visible.

title: A fixed-size log-linear latency histogram for percentiles
body: Averages hide what matters in a latency-sensitive system; tails do. You need percentiles such as p50, p99 and p99.99, measured on millions of samples per second without slowing the thing you measure. Storing every sample is too expensive, and sorting them later needs unbounded memory. A histogram stores counts per bucket instead, in a fixed array, so recording a value is one index computation and one increment, with no allocation and no branches that depend on the data. The structure below is about 4 KB in total and can sit next to the hot loop.

Bucket layout decides accuracy. Linear buckets of fixed width waste memory on large values and are too coarse on small ones. A log-linear layout, the idea behind HdrHistogram, splits each power of two into 2^k equal sub-buckets. With k = 3 the values 0 to 7 each get an exact bucket, and from 8 upward every doubling range is cut into 8 slices, so a bucket's width is at most 1/8 of its lower bound: the reported value is within 12.5 percent of the truth at any magnitude from nanoseconds to hours. bucket_of finds the leading-one position with leading_zeros and the next three bits select the slice; bucket_range inverts it, and the program checks that every value lands inside the range it maps to.

A percentile query walks the buckets accumulating counts until it reaches the target rank, ceil(total x p), and reports the upper edge of that bucket (clamped to the exact maximum), which errs on the safe side. Histograms also merge by adding counts, so each thread can keep its own and a reporter can combine them without locking. Beware the measurement itself: if a stall delays your load generator, the requests that should have been sent during the stall are never timed, so the stall is under-reported. This is coordinated omission. Record latency from the intended send time, not from when the sender got around to it.

Check the relative error bound, record without allocating, choose percentiles that your sample count can resolve (p99.99 needs at least 10,000 samples), merge per-thread histograms instead of sharing one, and measure from the intended start time to avoid coordinated omission.

exact below 8: true, value 100 -> range (96, 104)
samples = 10010, min = 100, max = 5000000

p99.99 = 5000000

p100 is the exact maximum: true

challenge: Add fraction_at_or_below(&self, value) -> f64 (the empirical CDF at the bucket resolution): the fraction of samples recorded in buckets whose upper edge is at most value + 1. Check that it is non-decreasing in value, is 0.0 before the minimum, and is 1.0 at the maximum.
question: Why does the histogram use log-linear buckets instead of equal-width buckets?
correct: They keep a bounded relative error at every magnitude with few buckets, where equal widths waste memory or lose small values
wrong: They sort the samples as they are recorded, so a percentile is just an index into the buckets
They allow storing every individual sample exactly, because each bucket keeps its own list of values
They make the percentile query O(1), because the buckets are indexed directly by percentile
reasoning: Latency spans many orders of magnitude, so accuracy should be relative. Splitting each power of two into equal slices gives that with a few hundred buckets. The histogram is lossy and a percentile query still walks the buckets.

quiz.question: With 3 sub-bucket bits, what is the worst relative error of a reported value?
quiz.correct: About 12.5 percent, because a bucket is at most 1/8 as wide as its lower bound
wrong: About 1 percent, because 3 bits of precision correspond to a hundred buckets per octave
Exactly zero for values above 8, because every such value has a bucket of its own
About 50 percent, because each bucket covers a whole power of two of values
quiz.reasoning: Each power-of-two range is cut into 8 slices, so a slice width is 2^e / 8 over a lower bound of at least 2^e.

quiz.question: Why does record() use a fixed array instead of a Vec of samples?
quiz.correct: Recording is then one index computation and one increment with no allocation, so it is safe on a hot path
wrong: Because Vec cannot hold u64 values, so a fixed array is the only container that fits
Because arrays are always faster to sort, and percentile queries need the samples sorted
Because Rust forbids heap allocation in structs, so a Vec field would not be allowed
quiz.reasoning: Constant memory and constant work per sample keep measurement overhead predictable.

quiz.question: Why is p99.99 reported as the maximum when only about 10,000 samples exist?
quiz.correct: At that sample count the 99.99th percentile rests on the last few values, so it cannot be resolved finer
wrong: Because percentile queries always return the maximum, whatever percentile is asked for
Because p99.99 is defined as the average of the top two samples in the histogram
Because the histogram discards the tail beyond p99.9 to save memory in its buckets
quiz.reasoning: A percentile needs about 1/(1-p) samples to be meaningful. With 10,010 samples, p99.99 is determined by one to ten values.

quiz.question: What is coordinated omission?
quiz.correct: Under-reporting latency because a stall delays the load generator, so requests due during the stall are never timed
wrong: Merging histograms from two threads so that one thread's slow samples hide the other's
Rounding latencies up to the nearest bucket, so the largest values are never reported at all
Dropping samples above the maximum trackable value, so the largest delays vanish from the data
quiz.reasoning: Measure from the intended send time. Otherwise the generator coordinates with the stall and hides the backlog.

title: An event-driven backtester with next-bar fills, costs and no look-ahead
body: A backtest replays history through a strategy and reports what would have happened. Its worst failure is a result that looks profitable because the code peeked at information the strategy could not have had. The structure here prevents that by construction. The event loop walks the bars in order. For each bar it first executes any pending order from the previous decision at this bar's open, then marks equity at this bar's close, and only then asks the strategy what position it wants next. A decision made at a bar's close therefore fills at the next bar's open, and a signal produced on the final bar never fills at all.

Costs are part of the model, not an afterthought. Every fill is charged slippage, ticks paid against the trader (buys fill higher, sells lower), and a fixed fee. Money is integer ticks times integer quantity in i128, so equity is exact: cash + position x close - fees. Because the strategy sees only closes and its own position, running the same strategy with and without costs makes identical decisions, so the difference in final equity is exactly the number of fills times (slippage + fee). The demo prints that identity as a check. A strategy is a trait with one method, so the loop does not know whether it is a moving-average crossover or buy and hold.

The SMA crossover compares the average of the last fast closes with the average of the last slow closes without dividing: fast_sum x slow > slow_sum x fast is the same inequality in exact integer arithmetic. The tests state the contract: fills at the next open, buy-and-hold PnL equal to last close minus fill price, costs reducing equity by exactly slippage plus fee, a flat strategy never trading, a last-bar signal never filling, and deterministic results. The validation also breaks the engine on purpose, filling at the close instead of the next open and dropping fees, and requires the suite to fail.

Check that no decision can use a later bar, fills use the next open, costs are explicit and integer, the strategy is injected through a trait, and mutations of the execution rules make the tests fail. A backtest also overfits easily; this project shows mechanics, not a profitable strategy.
challenge: Add Report::max_drawdown(), the largest peak-to-trough fall of the equity curve, and a test: it is 0 for a rising curve, and exactly 20 for buy and hold over closes [100, 90, 80, 95]. Explain why the answer is 20 rather than 25.
question: Why does a decision made at a bar's close fill at the NEXT bar's open in this backtester?
correct: The strategy could not have traded at a price known only after the bar closed; the next open removes look-ahead
wrong: Because open prices are always better than close prices, so the strategy gets a lucky fill
Because Rust requires a one-bar delay between function calls that share mutable state
To make the results smoother, since fills at the next open hide the noise of each bar
reasoning: Information in the close is known only after it prints. Acting on it at that same price would use the future. The one-bar delay is the earliest realistic execution.

wrong: It cannot include transaction costs, because those depend on live market conditions only

quiz.reasoning: Correct mechanics remove look-ahead and cost errors, but they do not remove selection bias from trying many parameter sets.

title: A market-data feed with threads, bounded channels, gap detection and clean shutdown
body: A feed handler sits between the network and the rest of the system. Here a producer thread stands in for the network reader and sends sequence-numbered updates through a std::sync::mpsc::sync_channel(capacity); the consumer owns the book and applies them in order. Bounded channels matter: sync_channel blocks the sender when the buffer is full, so a slow consumer slows the producer instead of letting memory grow without limit, which in a real feed would mean dropping packets at the socket. The test with capacity 1 and 1,000 updates proves that even a one-slot channel delivers everything without deadlock, because the consumer always makes progress.

Exchanges number every message. The consumer remembers the next expected sequence number and compares it with each arrival. A mismatch means messages were lost (or duplicated or reordered), and a book built on top of a hole is wrong, so the gap is recorded as an (expected, received) pair and surfaced in the Summary rather than hidden. Real handlers then request a retransmission or a snapshot; this project stops at detection. Reduce updates that do not match a resting level are counted in bad_reduces, not applied, for the same reason: bad input should be visible.

Shutdown is the other half of correctness. A session ends with a Shutdown message and the consumer reports clean_shutdown = true. If the sender simply disappears, recv returns Err and the summary says clean_shutdown = false, so a crashed producer is distinguishable from an orderly stop. If instead the consumer hangs up first, dropping the Receiver makes the producer's send return Err; the producer treats that as "stop" and returns how many messages it sent, so it neither panics nor spins forever. Ownership does the work: when the last Sender or the Receiver is dropped, the channel closes and the other side finds out.

Check that channels are bounded, every received sequence number is compared with the expected one, a vanished peer is handled on both sides without panics or hangs, and the summary distinguishes a clean shutdown from a disconnect.
challenge: Treat a repeated or old sequence number as a duplicate: count it in a new Summary::duplicates field and do not apply it, while a number greater than expected is still a gap. Add a test with the sequence 1, 2, 2, 3 and explain why a duplicate must not be applied twice.
question: Why does the producer stop quietly when send returns an error?
correct: An error means the receiver was dropped, so nobody is listening; stopping avoids both a panic and an endless loop
wrong: An error means the channel is full, so the producer should wait a moment and retry the send
An error means the message was corrupted in transit and should be resent by the producer
The producer cannot recover from a send error, so it must panic to tell the consumer
reasoning: For a SyncSender, send fails only when the Receiver has been dropped. Blocking on a full channel is not an error, it just waits.

quiz.question: What does a bounded channel give a feed handler that an unbounded one does not?
quiz.correct: Back-pressure: a slow consumer blocks the producer, so memory use is capped instead of growing without limit
wrong: Faster delivery of every message, because a bounded buffer is always kept in the CPU cache
Automatic reordering of out-of-sequence messages, since the buffer sorts them by sequence number
Guaranteed delivery after a crash, because queued messages survive the restart of the process
quiz.reasoning: The buffer size is a fixed budget. Unbounded channels hide a slow consumer until memory runs out.

quiz.question: What does the summary report when the sender vanishes without a Shutdown message?
quiz.correct: clean_shutdown = false, so a crashed producer can be told apart from an orderly end of session
wrong: clean_shutdown = true, because recv returned and the consumer then finished its loop normally
A panic in the consumer, because a missing Shutdown message is treated as a fatal error
The consumer waits forever, because only a Shutdown message can wake it from recv

quiz.question: A message with sequence 5 arrives when 3 is expected. What does the consumer record?
quiz.correct: A gap (3, 5): messages 3 and 4 are missing, which must be repaired before the book can be trusted
wrong: Nothing; sequence numbers are only informational and the consumer applies messages regardless
A duplicate of message 4, because the consumer assumes it skipped one message in between
A clean shutdown, because a jump in sequence numbers is how the producer ends a session
quiz.reasoning: Sequence numbers exist to detect loss. A hole means the book may be missing updates.

quiz.question: Why must a duplicated message not be applied a second time?
quiz.correct: Applying it would double-count the change, for example adding the same quantity to a level twice
wrong: Because duplicates are always corrupted in transit, so applying one would damage the whole book
Because Rust forbids applying a message twice, as the first application moves the update
Because duplicates change the sequence counter, so the next expected number would be wrong
quiz.reasoning: Updates are deltas, not idempotent state. Replays happen after reconnects, so handlers must recognise and skip them.

title: Property-based testing a matching core with proptest
body: Example tests check the inputs you thought of. Property-based testing states a law that must hold for all inputs and lets a library search for a counterexample. With proptest you describe how to generate inputs (a Strategy), write the property as assertions, and the runner executes hundreds of random cases. When one fails it shrinks the input: it repeatedly simplifies the failing case, shorter sequences and smaller numbers, until the minimal counterexample remains. That minimal case is usually what you need to understand the bug. This project pins proptest 1.12.0 with default features off and ships its Cargo.lock; the first build needs network access.

Choosing properties is the skill. For a matching core the laws are: the book is never crossed after any sequence of submits and cancels; quantity is conserved (submitted = 2 x traded + cancelled + resting); every trade price respects the taker's limit (a buyer never pays above its limit, a seller never receives below); and makers at one price are filled oldest first. The strategies generate sequences of operations, with prop_oneof! weighting submits three times as often as cancels, prices in a narrow band so orders collide, and cancel indices wrapped to ids that exist. A narrow input space with lots of collisions finds bugs faster than a wide one.

A property suite is only as good as its sensitivity, so the validation breaks the engine twice: one mutation lets a buyer trade one tick above its limit, another flips FIFO to LIFO. Both must make the suite fail, which proves the properties constrain behaviour. Randomness has practical consequences. Runs normally differ, so a failure can appear in CI and not locally; proptest normally saves failing seeds in a regressions file so a found bug is replayed forever. This project instead fixes the seed (RngSeed::Fixed) and turns persistence off, so its checks are reproducible and never write into the project directory; a real project usually prefers random seeds with persistence on. Use prop_assume! to discard cases that do not meet a precondition, and keep generators tight so few cases are wasted.

Check that each property is a law and not a restatement of the implementation, generators produce collisions, failures shrink to something readable, a seed or regression file preserves found bugs in real projects, and mutations of the core rules are caught.
challenge: Add a property: after any setup, if submitting an order produces no trades then cancelling it returns exactly its quantity and restores the previous book. Add a snapshot() method to compare book states and use prop_assume! to discard cases where the order did trade.
question: What does shrinking do when a property fails?
correct: It repeatedly simplifies the failing input, with shorter sequences and smaller values, until a minimal counterexample remains
wrong: It reruns the same failing case many times until it passes, which rules out flaky failures from the generator
It deletes the failing assertion from the test, so that later runs of the suite are not stopped by it
It reduces the number of cases for later runs, so the suite becomes faster after a failure
reasoning: Shrinking turns a large random failure into a small one that is easy to read and debug. The failure is still reported, never hidden.

projectInstructions: Rust 1.99 / edition 2024. Create Cargo.toml, Cargo.lock, src/lib.rs and tests/props.rs exactly as shown and run cargo test --quiet. The first build downloads proptest and its dependencies from crates.io (network needed). Experiment: change price + 1 to price + 0 or flip front_mut to back_mut and read the shrunk counterexample proptest prints.

projectChecks.name: a buyer paying above its limit is caught

quiz.question: Why are the generated prices limited to 95..=105 instead of the full i64 range?
quiz.correct: A narrow band makes orders collide and trade, so the interesting matching paths are exercised in almost every case
wrong: Because i64 prices cannot be generated by proptest, which only supports small integer ranges
Because wide ranges make the properties false, since large prices overflow the book's arithmetic
Because the book only supports eleven prices, so any other price would be rejected
quiz.reasoning: Random i64 prices would almost never cross, so matching code would rarely run. Good generators target the behaviour under test.

quiz.question: Why does the suite validate that mutations make it fail?
quiz.correct: A passing suite only matters if it can fail; breaking the rules on purpose shows that the properties constrain behaviour
wrong: Mutations make the engine run faster, because the changed rules skip some of the matching checks
Proptest requires mutations to run, because it generates its inputs from the changed source
It replaces the need for any assertions, since a failing mutation proves the code is correct
quiz.reasoning: A weak property can pass on broken code. A mutation check measures the suite's sensitivity.

quiz.question: What does prop_assume! do?
quiz.correct: It discards the current case when a precondition does not hold, so the property is only checked on relevant inputs
wrong: It marks the whole test as passed as soon as one case meets the condition, so the run finishes early
It makes the case fail with a message that names the missing precondition, for easier debugging
It stores the case as a regression, so it is replayed first in every later run of the suite
quiz.reasoning: Rejected cases do not count as passes or failures. Too many rejections make a test inefficient, so generators should be tight.

quiz.question: Why turn off failure persistence in this project's configuration?
quiz.correct: To keep validation from writing regression files into the project; real projects keep persistence to replay bugs
wrong: Because persistence makes proptest unsound, since replayed seeds bias the later random cases
Because failing seeds cannot be stored on disk, so persistence would silently do nothing at all
Because shrinking needs persistence disabled, since the two features write to the same file
quiz.reasoning: The regressions file records failing seeds so later runs retest them first. It is good practice normally and simply unwanted in this controlled check.

title: Capstone: a low-latency trading pipeline with bounded rings, risk checks and golden tests
body: This capstone joins the previous lessons into one pipeline: a binary parser, a dense price-array book, a quoting strategy, a risk gate and an order gateway that serialises approved orders to bytes. The stages are connected by fixed-capacity rings (Ring<T> over a VecDeque that reserves its capacity once and refuses pushes when full). Because every queue is bounded, memory use is known in advance, and a slow stage naturally holds back the stages before it. The pipeline runs on one thread here so the behaviour is deterministic and testable; the same stage boundaries are where the SPSC queue from the performance stage would split it across cores.

The pump loop runs stages back to front and moves an item only when its destination has room. The gateway drains orders first, risk runs only if the order ring has a free slot, and the book and strategy stage runs only if the intent ring can take the two quotes one update can create. This is back-pressure implemented as an invariant, not as locks: no stage ever pushes into a full ring, so there is no dropped data and no blocking call. The risk gate applies simple rules in a fixed order (price must be non-zero, quantity at most 10, total exposure at most 25) and counts rejections by reason, so every intent is approved or rejected exactly once.

Correctness is argued by tests at three levels. Invariants hold for any input: approved plus rejected equals intents generated, outbound bytes equal approved times the frame size, exposure never exceeds the limit, and the rings' reserved capacity does not change while running. A metamorphic test says results must not depend on ring size, so the same 500-update stream through rings of 2, 3, 5, 64 and 1,024 slots must give identical counters, bytes and book. A golden test pins the exact outcome of a recorded 200-update session, 62 intents of which 2 are approved because two 10-lot orders use 20 of the 25 exposure limit; a golden number is a regression alarm, not independent proof, so it is paired with the invariants and reviewed by hand. Truncated input leaves the partial frame unconsumed and malformed input is reported without being applied.

Check that every ring is bounded and each stage tests its output room, every intent is accounted for, behaviour is independent of buffer size, input errors are reported rather than applied, golden values are reviewed rather than copied blindly, and mutating a risk or back-pressure rule makes the tests fail.
challenge: Write decode_orders(bytes) -> Result<Vec<Order>, PipelineError>, the inverse of the gateway encoding, with a TruncatedFrame error for a partial last frame. Test that the pipeline's outbound bytes decode to the approved orders with ids 1, 2 in sequence and quantity 10, and that a truncated or mistyped frame is rejected.
question: Why does a stage in the pump loop only run when the ring it writes to has room?
correct: It guarantees no push ever hits a full ring, so nothing is dropped and nothing blocks; back-pressure becomes an invariant
wrong: Because Rust forbids pushing to a VecDeque twice per iteration, so the stages must alternate
Because full rings automatically grow on the next call, so the check only avoids a reallocation
To make the pipeline run faster than its slowest stage, since idle stages can then skip work
reasoning: A bounded ring cannot accept items when full. Checking room first propagates pressure backwards through the stages. A ring that grew on demand would defeat the bounded-memory design.
