quiz.question: What does the ring-size independence test establish?
quiz.correct: Back-pressure does not change results: identical input gives identical counters, bytes and book at any ring size
wrong: That smaller rings are always faster, because they fit in cache, so the smallest ring should be used
That ring capacity can never be changed, because the counters depend on the size of each ring
That the strategy is profitable, because identical results show the quotes are correct
quiz.reasoning: It is a metamorphic test: change an irrelevant parameter and require the same output. It catches stages that drop or reorder data when queues fill.

quiz.question: Why is the golden-session test paired with invariant tests?
quiz.correct: Golden numbers pin current behaviour but are not independent proof; invariants hold for any input
wrong: Golden tests cannot fail on their own, so invariants are needed to give the suite any failures
Invariants make golden tests unnecessary, but golden tests are kept as a second copy of them
Golden values are generated by the compiler, so they need a human-written check beside them
quiz.reasoning: If the implementation had a bug when the golden value was recorded, the test would preserve it. Invariants check properties that must be true regardless.

quiz.question: Why is it useful that Ring::reserved() is checked before and after processing?
quiz.correct: It shows that the preallocated storage never grew, supporting the claim of no allocation in the steady-state queues
wrong: It measures how fast the pipeline ran, by comparing the ring capacity with the elapsed time
It counts how many orders were approved, since each approved order grows a ring by one slot
It proves the whole program never allocates, including the outbound byte buffer and the book
quiz.reasoning: The check covers the rings only: the outbound Vec was also pre-sized, but other allocations would need a counting allocator to rule out.

quiz.question: What happens to a trailing partial frame in process()?
quiz.correct: It is left unconsumed and the returned byte count tells the caller where to resume once more bytes arrive
wrong: It is dropped silently, because only whole frames are meaningful to the stages after the parser
It is zero-padded and parsed, so a message is produced even from an incomplete read
It causes a panic, because the parser treats every short read as a fatal protocol error
quiz.reasoning: Streams deliver arbitrary chunks, so the parser reports how much it consumed and the caller keeps the rest.

title: Drill: best single trade and maximum drawdown in one pass
body: Problem: given a price series, find the largest profit from one buy followed by one later sell (zero if prices only fall). The brute-force solution tries every pair (buy at i, sell at j > i) in O(n^2). The one-pass solution observes that the best sale on day j uses the lowest price seen before j, so keep a running minimum and a running best: for each price, best = max(best, price - minimum so far), then minimum = min(minimum, price). That is O(n) time and O(1) space, and it is the pattern for most "best pair with ordering constraint" questions.

Interview answers are judged on edge cases as much as on the loop. An empty or single-element series yields 0. A strictly falling series yields 0, not a negative number, because not trading is allowed. Subtraction of two i64 prices could overflow if prices are extreme, so the difference is computed in i128; with realistic non-negative prices that is overkill, but saying why you chose it is the point. Returning the indices (buy day, sell day) turns the answer into something a trader can act on, and requires remembering where the running minimum occurred.

The mirror problem is maximum drawdown: the largest fall from a peak to a later trough, the standard measure of how bad a strategy's worst stretch was. It is the same pass with the roles swapped: keep the running maximum and track the largest (peak - price). The program checks both fast versions against the quadratic brute force on 2,000 pseudo-random series of varying length, which is also how to answer "how would you test this?".

State complexity and the empty or all-falling cases first, keep one pass with O(1) state, use wide arithmetic for differences when inputs are unbounded, return positions if the business answer needs them, and test against a brute-force oracle on small random inputs.
expectedStdout:
[7, 1, 5, 3, 6, 4] -> best trade Some((5, 1, 4)), max drawdown 6
falling series: profit 0, trade None
empty: 0, single: 0
extreme values: 18446744073709551615
fast versions match the quadratic brute force on 2000 random series: true
challenge: At most two transactions: find the maximum total profit from at most two non-overlapping trades (sell before the second buy) in O(n) with four running states, and check it against an O(n^4) brute force on short random series. Series [3, 3, 5, 0, 0, 3, 1, 4] gives 6.
question: Why does the one-pass best-trade algorithm work?
correct: The best sale on day j uses the lowest price seen before j, so a running minimum and a running best suffice
wrong: It sorts the prices and subtracts the first from the last, which gives the widest possible gap
It tries every pair of days but stops early once the profit stops improving along the series
It buys on the highest price seen so far and sells on the lowest price that follows it
reasoning: For each possible sell day, the best buy is the earliest-minimum-so-far. Tracking that minimum while scanning makes the whole answer O(n) time and O(1) space.

quiz.question: What should the function return for a strictly falling series?
quiz.correct: 0 (or None for the trade), because not trading is allowed and a negative profit is never chosen
wrong: The smallest loss, because every trade on a falling series loses money and one must be made
An error, because a series with no profitable trade has no valid answer to return
The difference between the first and last price, because that is the whole span of the series
quiz.reasoning: The problem asks for the maximum profit with the option to skip trading, so the answer is never negative.

quiz.question: Why compute price differences in i128?
quiz.correct: Subtracting two extreme i64 prices can overflow i64; the wider type makes the result exact
wrong: i128 subtraction is faster than i64 on current CPUs, so wide arithmetic is chosen for speed
Because the prices are stored as i128, so every difference has to use the same wide type
Because i64 cannot hold negative numbers, so differences of falling prices need a wider type
quiz.reasoning: i64::MAX - i64::MIN overflows i64. Realistic prices never reach that, but a robust solution notes the assumption or avoids it.

quiz.question: How does maximum drawdown differ from the best-trade problem?
quiz.correct: It tracks a running maximum and the largest later fall below it, mirroring the running minimum and the largest later rise
wrong: It uses a running average instead of a minimum, since a drawdown is measured from the mean price
It requires sorting the series first, because the peak must be known before the troughs
It is only defined for rising series, because a falling series has no peak to fall from
quiz.reasoning: Both are one-pass scans with a running extreme, applied in opposite directions.

quiz.question: What is a good way to gain confidence in the fast solution?
quiz.correct: Compare it with a simple quadratic brute force on many small random inputs including empty and constant series
wrong: Run it once on the sample input and check that the printed answer looks plausible to a reader
Trust the complexity analysis, since an O(n) algorithm cannot have an edge case that fails
Test only with sorted inputs, because unsorted series never occur in real price data
quiz.reasoning: A brute-force oracle is easy to get right, and random small cases hit the edge conditions interviewers probe.

title: Drill: Kadane's algorithm for the best contiguous stretch
body: Problem: given daily profit and loss values, find the contiguous stretch with the largest total. Brute force sums every subarray in O(n^2) (or O(n^3) if each sum is recomputed). Kadane's algorithm is one pass: let best_ending_here be the best sum of a stretch that ends at the current element. Either that stretch extends the previous one (previous + x) or it starts fresh at x, whichever is larger, so best_ending_here = max(x, previous + x); the overall answer is the maximum over all positions. O(n) time, O(1) space.

The classic mistakes are edge cases. If every value is negative the answer is the largest single element, not 0, unless the problem explicitly allows an empty stretch, so initialise from the first element instead of 0 and say which convention you chose. Track start and end indices by remembering when a fresh start won. Sums of many i64 values can overflow; accumulate in i128 if inputs are unbounded. The empty slice has no answer, so return an Option rather than a made-up value.

The quant reading is "which window was the best run?" and its negative twin is the worst stretch, which is the same code on negated values. Kadane also hints at dynamic programming: the state is tiny (one number) because the optimal substructure only needs the best stretch ending at the previous element. Tests compare against the O(n^2) brute force for 2,000 random arrays that include all-negative and all-zero cases, and check that the reported indices really sum to the reported total.
Decide the empty-stretch convention up front, initialise from the first element, track indices on a fresh start, accumulate wide, return Option for empty input, and verify with a brute-force oracle.
expectedStdout:
best stretch of [-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1, -5, 4] is [3..=6] = [4, -1, 2, 1] with sum 6
all negative: Some((-2, 1, 1))
empty: None, single: Some((7, 0, 0))
worst stretch: [7..=7] with sum -5
matches brute force and the reported range sums correctly on 2000 random arrays: true
challenge: Circular variant: the series wraps around (a stretch may run off the end and continue at the start). Return the maximum circular subarray sum using max(kadane_max, total - kadane_min), taking care when every element is negative (then total - min would select the empty stretch). Check against brute force on short arrays; [5, -3, 5] gives 10.
question: What is Kadane's recurrence?
correct: best_ending_here = max(x, previous + x), and the answer is the maximum of best_ending_here over all positions
wrong: best_ending_here = the sum of all elements so far, and the answer is the largest prefix sum
best_ending_here = max(x, 0), and the answer is the sum of all the positive elements seen
best_ending_here = previous - x, and the answer is the largest such difference over all positions
reasoning: At each element the best stretch ending there either continues the previous best stretch or starts over. Resetting to zero instead would silently mishandle all-negative inputs.

quiz.question: What should be returned for an all-negative array such as [-5, -2, -9]?
quiz.correct: The largest single element (-2), unless the problem explicitly allows an empty stretch
wrong: 0, always, because an empty stretch is the best choice when every value is negative
The sum of all elements (-16), because the best stretch must cover the whole array
An error, because a stretch with no positive profit does not exist for this input
quiz.reasoning: A non-empty stretch must contain at least one element, so the best is the least negative one. State the convention if empty is allowed.

quiz.question: Why is the function return type Option<(i128, usize, usize)>?
quiz.correct: An empty slice has no stretch, so no sensible number exists; Option makes the caller handle that case
wrong: Because Option is faster than returning a bare tuple, since the compiler can keep it in registers
Because indices can be negative, so a missing start index has to be represented separately
Because Rust requires Option for every tuple returned from a function that loops over a slice
quiz.reasoning: Inventing 0 for the empty case would be indistinguishable from a real stretch summing to 0.

quiz.question: How do you find the worst stretch with the same code?
quiz.correct: Run it on the negated values and negate the result
wrong: Reverse the array and run the same code again
Sort the array in ascending order, then take the first run
It cannot be done with the same Kadane recurrence
quiz.reasoning: The maximum of -x over a stretch is the minimum of x, so negation turns the worst stretch into the best one.

quiz.question: Why accumulate in i128?
quiz.correct: The sum of many i64 values can overflow i64; i128 keeps the answer exact for any realistic length
wrong: i128 makes the loop O(1), because the wide type removes the need to visit every element
Because Kadane requires 128-bit arithmetic, so a narrower accumulator gives wrong answers
To avoid negative numbers, since an i128 total is always stored as an unsigned value
quiz.reasoning: Overflow in a running sum is a classic hidden bug. Wide accumulators or checked arithmetic make it explicit.

title: Drill: the running median with two heaps
body: Problem: values arrive one at a time and after each one you must report the median of everything seen so far. Re-sorting after every arrival costs O(n log n) each time. Two heaps give O(log n) per insert and O(1) per median query. Keep the smaller half in a max-heap (its top is the largest of the small values) and the larger half in a min-heap (its top is the smallest of the large values). The median is then read from the tops: the top of the larger heap when the heaps have different sizes, or the average of the two tops when they are equal.

The invariants carry the whole solution. Every element of the low heap is at most every element of the high heap, and the sizes differ by at most one (here the low heap may hold one extra). Insert by pushing into the low heap, then moving its top to the high heap to preserve ordering, then rebalancing if the high heap became larger. Rust's BinaryHeap is a max-heap, so the high half uses std::cmp::Reverse to turn it into a min-heap. Stating these invariants out loud and then checking them in a debug assertion is what interviewers look for.

Avoid floating point in the answer. An even count has a median that is the average of two integers, which may end in .5, so the function returns twice the median as an integer, and the caller divides by two for display. The program compares the streaming result against sorting the whole prefix for 1,500 random values and verifies the invariants after each insertion. Sliding-window medians are harder because elements must also leave, which needs lazy deletion or an ordered structure; mention it as the follow-up.
State the heap invariants, use Reverse for the min-heap, rebalance after each insert, return exact values (twice the median) instead of floats, and check against a sort-the-prefix oracle.
expectedStdout:
empty: None
after  5: median = 5
after 15: median = 10
after  1: median = 5
after  3: median = 4
after  8: median = 5
after  7: median = 6
after  9: median = 7
after 10: median = 7.5
after 20: median = 8
after  2: median = 7.5
matches sorting the whole prefix after every one of 1500 inserts: true
challenge: Track the k-th smallest value of a stream (k fixed, k >= 1) with a single max-heap of size at most k: push each value, and when the heap exceeds k elements pop the largest. After each value the heap top is the k-th smallest seen so far (None until k values have arrived). Check against sorting the prefix.
solutionStdout: 3rd smallest after each of [9, 4, 7, 1, 8]: [None, None, Some(9), Some(7), Some(7)]
question: Why are two heaps used instead of re-sorting for each new value?
correct: Inserting costs O(log n) and the median is read from the heap tops in O(1), versus O(n log n) to re-sort every time
wrong: Heaps keep every element in fully sorted order, so the median is always the middle element
A single heap cannot store integers, so the stream needs one heap for each of the signs
Sorting is not allowed on a stream, so the median must be tracked by a different structure
reasoning: Only the middle of the ordering matters. The two heaps maintain just enough order around the middle to answer the median cheaply.

quiz.question: What invariants must the two heaps maintain?
quiz.correct: Every element of the low heap is at most every element of the high heap, and their sizes differ by at most one
wrong: Both heaps contain the same elements, so every value is stored twice for fast lookups
The low heap stays empty until the stream has more than a thousand values, then fills up
The heaps are each sorted ascending, so their first elements are the two middle values
quiz.reasoning: Ordering across the halves and balanced sizes guarantee that the median is at one or both tops.

quiz.question: How does Rust get a min-heap from BinaryHeap?
quiz.correct: By wrapping values in Reverse, which flips the ordering
wrong: By calling .reverse() on the heap in place
By constructing it with BinaryHeap::new_min()
By re-sorting the heap descending after each push
quiz.reasoning: BinaryHeap is a max-heap. Reverse<T> implements Ord with the comparison flipped, so the smallest T is the greatest Reverse<T>.

quiz.question: Why does median_x2 return twice the median?
quiz.correct: The median of an even count is the average of two integers and may end in .5, so doubling keeps it an exact integer
wrong: To avoid reading the heap top twice, since doubling lets one peek serve both middle values
Because heaps store doubled values, so the result has to be returned in the same scale
Because medians must be even, so an odd count is rounded up by multiplying by two
quiz.reasoning: Exact integer arithmetic avoids floating-point rounding. The caller halves the result for display.

quiz.question: What makes a sliding-window median harder than a running median?
quiz.correct: Elements must also leave the window, which a plain heap cannot do without lazy deletion or an ordered structure
wrong: Sliding windows have no median when the window length is even, so the value is undefined
Heaps cannot hold more than one element per value, so repeated prices in a window break them
The window always has an even size, so two middle values must be averaged with floats
quiz.reasoning: BinaryHeap only supports removing the top. Arbitrary removals need extra bookkeeping or a different structure such as an order-statistic tree.

title: Drill: an O(1) LRU cache with a hash map and an index-linked list
body: Problem: build a cache of fixed capacity that evicts the least recently used entry when full, with get and put both O(1). A HashMap alone gives O(1) lookup but no recency order. A list alone gives order but O(n) lookup. The classic answer combines them: the map goes from key to a node, and the nodes form a doubly linked list ordered from most to least recently used. A get moves the node to the front, a put inserts at the front, and eviction removes the tail.

Rust makes the textbook pointer-based list awkward, because doubly linked lists need shared mutable pointers (Rc<RefCell<..>> or unsafe). The idiomatic escape is to store nodes in a Vec and link them with indices: prev and next are usize positions, with usize::MAX meaning none. There is no unsafe code, no reference counting, and the nodes stay contiguous in memory. When the cache is full, the evicted node's slot is reused for the new entry with mem::replace, so the Vec never grows past capacity. unlink and push_front are two tiny helpers that maintain head and tail, and getting them right at the boundaries (empty list, single node, removing the head or the tail) is the real test.

How do you know it works? Write the obviously correct but slow version, a Vec ordered by recency where every operation is O(n), and compare both caches after every step of a random sequence of gets and puts, including the evicted key and the full recency order. The program does 5,000 steps over 8 keys with capacity 4, which hits every boundary case many times. State the complexity (O(1) amortised, with HashMap hashing as the caveat), the memory (O(capacity)), and that it is not thread-safe.

Cover capacity 1, updating an existing key (no eviction, moves to the front), eviction order, and the head/tail updates in unlink; verify with a simple model; mention thread safety (a Mutex around the whole cache) as the follow-up.
expectedStdout:
get a -> Some(1)
put c evicts Some(("b", 2))
get b -> None
order (most recent first): ["c", "a"]
update a keeps size: None, len 2
capacity 1: put 2 evicts Some((1, "x"))
matches the O(n) model for capacities 1, 4 and 7 over 5000 random steps: true
challenge: Add peek(&self, key) -> Option<&V> that reads a value without changing recency, and show with a test that peeking at the least recently used key does not save it from eviction while get does.
solutionStdout:
peek leaves recency alone; get promotes; len = 2
order: ["c", "a"]
question: Why does the LRU cache keep both a HashMap and a linked list?
correct: The map gives O(1) lookup of a node and the list gives O(1) reordering and eviction; neither alone offers both
wrong: The list stores the values and the map stores the keys, which saves memory over one table
Rust requires two structures for any cache, because one structure cannot be borrowed twice
The map keeps its entries sorted by recency, so the list is only used for iterating them
reasoning: A hash map cannot tell which entry is oldest, and a list cannot find a key quickly. Combined, each operation touches both in O(1).

quiz.question: Why are list links stored as indices into a Vec instead of pointers?
quiz.correct: Safe Rust makes doubly linked pointers awkward; indices avoid Rc<RefCell>, unsafe code and extra allocations
wrong: Indices are always faster than pointers, because the CPU can add them to the base address
Rust cannot hold references inside structs at all, so every link has to be a plain integer
A Vec cannot be resized after creation, so nodes must be addressed by fixed positions
quiz.reasoning: The index representation keeps nodes contiguous and the code safe. The borrow checker is satisfied because links are plain integers.

quiz.question: What happens when put is called with a key that already exists?
quiz.correct: The value is updated in place and the entry moves to the front; nothing is evicted
wrong: The oldest entry is evicted first, then the new value is stored at the front
A duplicate entry is added, and the older one is removed when the cache fills up
The call returns an error, because keys in the cache are required to be unique
quiz.reasoning: Updating counts as a use, and the cache size does not change, so no eviction is needed.

quiz.question: Which edge cases should unlink and push_front handle?
quiz.correct: Removing the head, the tail and the only node; inserting into an empty list, so head and tail stay consistent
wrong: Only nodes in the middle of the list, because the head and tail pointers never need to change
Only a full cache, because an empty or partly full list needs no unlinking at all
Nothing special; they are symmetric operations, so one test of a middle node covers every case
quiz.reasoning: The head and tail pointers must be updated at the boundaries. Most LRU bugs live there.

quiz.question: How would you make this cache safe to share between threads?
quiz.correct: Wrap it in a Mutex (or shard it across several Mutex-protected caches), because get mutates the recency list
wrong: Make get take &self, because reads do not change anything and so need no lock at all
Use unsafe to skip the lock, since the cache is only mutated in one place at a time
Replace the HashMap with a Vec, which is Sync and removes the need for locking
quiz.reasoning: Even a read updates recency, so reads need exclusive access. Sharding reduces contention.

title: Drill: rolling highs and lows with a monotonic deque
body: Problem: for every window of k consecutive prices, report the maximum (a rolling high, the upper line of a Donchian channel). Brute force scans each window, O(n k). The monotonic deque solves it in O(n) total. Keep a deque of indices whose values are strictly decreasing from front to back. A new value first removes every index from the back whose value is less than or equal to it, because those older, smaller values can never be a window maximum again: the new value is both larger and will outlive them. Then the new index joins the back.

The front of the deque is always the index of the current window's maximum. Two bookkeeping rules finish the algorithm. When the front index has slid out of the window (front + k <= i), pop it from the front. And only start reporting once a full window exists (i + 1 >= k). Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so although there is a while loop inside the for loop, the total work is O(n), the amortised argument interviewers want to hear. Storing indices rather than values is what lets you detect expiry.

The same code gives rolling minima by flipping the comparison, and running both deques gives the window range (high minus low), a volatility proxy. The program checks the deque result against the O(n k) brute force on 3,000 random inputs of random window sizes, including k = 1 (the identity) and k = n (one window). The edge cases to name aloud: k = 0 is invalid, k larger than n yields no windows, and equal values must be popped (<=) so ties do not leave stale indices.
State the monotonic invariant, store indices, pop expired fronts, report only for full windows, argue amortised O(n), and test k = 1, k = n and ties against a brute-force oracle.

rolling max (k=3): [3, 3, 5, 5, 6, 7]
rolling min (k=3): [-1, -3, -3, -3, 3, 3]
window range: [4, 6, 8, 8, 3, 4]
k = 1 is the identity: true
k = n gives one window: [7]
k > n gives none: []
ties: [2, 2, 2]
matches the O(n*k) brute force on 3000 random inputs: true
challenge: Count how many deque operations (pushes plus pops) the algorithm performs on a strictly decreasing series and on a strictly increasing series of length 1,000 with k = 50, and show both are at most 3n, demonstrating the amortised O(n) bound even though the increasing case pops from the back repeatedly.
solutionStdout:
decreasing: 1950 operations, increasing: 1999 operations for n = 1000
random series stays within 3n as well: true
question: Why is the monotonic-deque solution O(n) even though it has a while loop inside a for loop?
correct: Each index is pushed once and popped at most once, so the whole run does at most 2n deque operations
wrong: The inner loop never runs more than twice per element, so the work is at most 2n steps in total
Deque operations take zero time, so only the outer loop over the series is counted
The input is sorted, so the inner loop stops after the first comparison for every item
reasoning: Amortised analysis counts total work, not work per iteration. A single step may pop many indices, but those pops are paid for by the earlier pushes.

quiz.question: Why does the deque store indices instead of values?
quiz.correct: Indices let the algorithm detect when the front has left the window, and the values can still be read from the slice
wrong: Because values cannot be compared inside a deque, so only their positions can be ordered
Because indices are smaller than i64 values, so the deque uses less memory per element
Because a deque only accepts usize elements, so the stored type is fixed by the container
quiz.reasoning: Expiry depends on position. A value alone does not say whether it is still inside the window.

quiz.question: Why are equal values popped from the back (<=) in the maximum version?
quiz.correct: An older equal value expires sooner and can never be the unique extreme again, so it only wastes space
wrong: Equal values must be kept for tie-breaking, so the oldest of them is reported as the window maximum
It is required for the minimum version only, since the maximum version keeps equal values
To make the output descending, because popping equal values sorts the reported maxima
quiz.reasoning: When a new value is at least as large as an older one, the older one is dominated: the new value stays in the window longer.

quiz.question: What does the algorithm report before the first full window of k values exists?
quiz.correct: Nothing: results start at index k - 1, so n values give n - k + 1 windows (none if k > n)
wrong: The maximum of the partial window, so the first k - 1 outputs cover fewer than k values
Zero for each early index, so the output always has exactly one entry per input value
An error, because a window shorter than k is not a valid input to the algorithm
quiz.reasoning: A window needs k elements. Partial windows are a different (often unwanted) statistic.

quiz.question: How can the rolling range (high minus low) be computed?
quiz.correct: Run a max deque and a min deque over the same series and subtract the two outputs window by window
wrong: Sort each window and subtract its first element from its last, which costs O(k log k)
Use a single deque holding both extremes, since one deque can keep maximum and minimum
It needs O(n k) work, because the two extremes cannot be tracked by deques at once
quiz.reasoning: Each deque is independent and O(n), so the range is O(n) overall.

title: Drill: top-k with a bounded heap, floats and deterministic ties
body: Problem: from a stream of scored items (say, signal strengths per symbol) keep the k best. Sorting everything costs O(n log n) and needs all items in memory. A bounded min-heap of size k does it in O(n log k) with O(k) memory: the heap holds the k best so far with the worst of them at the top. For each new item, if the heap has room push it; otherwise compare with the worst and replace it only if the new item is better. With BinaryHeap (a max-heap), wrapping entries in std::cmp::Reverse puts the worst on top.

Floats make the comparison the interesting part. f64 is not Ord because of NaN, so entries use a small struct with a hand-written Ord based on f64::total_cmp, with NaN scores filtered out and counted before they reach the heap (a NaN would otherwise rank as the best score under total_cmp). Ties need a deterministic rule or results change from run to run: here, higher score wins and among equal scores the earlier index wins. That is encoded in the Ord impl as score first, then the other index compared with this one, so a smaller index is "greater". With a total order, comparing "is the new item better than the current worst" is a plain > on the struct.

Edge cases to say out loud: k = 0 returns nothing, k larger than the item count returns everything in order, equal scores keep the earliest items, and NaN is excluded and reported rather than silently dropped. The program compares against the obviously correct sort-everything version on 3,000 random inputs with heavy ties and NaNs. The follow-up is "top-k per group", which keeps one bounded heap per group in a map; the practice answer builds that.
State the O(n log k) cost, use a total order with explicit tie-breaks, treat NaN deliberately, handle k = 0 and k > n, and verify against a sort-based oracle.

top 3: ([1, 2, 5], 1)
top 0: ([], 1)
top 10 (more than exist): ([1, 2, 5, 6, 0, 4], 1)
ties keep the earliest index: ([0, 1], 0)
infinity beats everything, NaN never ranks: ([1, 0], 1)
matches the sort-everything oracle on 3000 random inputs with ties and NaN: true
challenge: Top-k per group: given (symbol, score) pairs, return for each symbol the k best scores in descending order using one bounded heap per symbol in a BTreeMap (so the output order is deterministic). Check against sorting each group.
question: Why does the top-k heap wrap its entries in Reverse?
correct: BinaryHeap is a max-heap, and Reverse puts the worst of the k kept items on top so a better new item can replace it
wrong: Reverse sorts the output best-first automatically, so the heap can be drained in order
Reverse makes the heap faster than a Vec, because it avoids comparing the second field
BinaryHeap cannot hold structs unless they are wrapped in Reverse, which adds the Ord trait
reasoning: To replace the worst kept item cheaply you need cheap access to it. A min-heap of the kept items (via Reverse) provides that in O(1), with O(log k) replacement.

quiz.question: Why are NaN scores filtered out before they reach the heap?
quiz.correct: Under f64::total_cmp a positive NaN sorts above infinity, so a NaN would rank as the best score
wrong: NaN cannot be stored in a struct, because the compiler rejects float fields that may be NaN
NaN is always smaller than every number, so it would never survive in the heap anyway
The heap panics on NaN, because BinaryHeap checks each pushed value for being a number
quiz.reasoning: total_cmp gives a total order that places NaN beyond the infinities. Excluding it explicitly (and counting it) matches what a data pipeline normally wants.

quiz.question: How does the Ord implementation make ties deterministic?
quiz.correct: It compares the other index with this one after the scores, so among equal scores the earlier index wins
wrong: It picks a random item among equal scores, using the heap's internal state as the seed
It sorts by the order the hash map happens to use, which is stable within one run
It drops all tied items, so only items with a unique score can ever enter the heap result
quiz.reasoning: A tie-break rule must be part of the ordering, otherwise results depend on heap internals and can change between runs.

quiz.question: What is the time and memory cost of the bounded heap for n items?
quiz.correct: O(n log k) time and O(k) memory, compared with O(n log n) time and O(n) memory for sorting everything
wrong: O(n^2) time and O(1) memory, because each new item is compared with all of the items that were kept before it
O(k log n) time and O(n) memory, because the heap has to hold every item in the stream
O(n) time because heaps are already sorted, so each insert takes constant time
quiz.reasoning: Each of n items causes at most one O(log k) heap operation, and the heap never holds more than k entries.

quiz.question: What should top_k return for k = 0 and for k larger than the number of items?
quiz.correct: An empty list for k = 0, and all non-NaN items in rank order when k exceeds the count
wrong: An error for both, because k must be at least 1 and no larger than the number of items
The single best item for k = 0, and every item padded with NaN when k is too large
Padding with NaN up to k, and an empty list for k = 0 because nothing is requested
quiz.reasoning: These are valid inputs with natural answers. Handling them explicitly is a standard interview check.

title: Drill: merging trading sessions and finding gaps
body: Problem: given possibly overlapping time intervals (trading sessions, order lifetimes, outage windows), merge them into a minimal set of disjoint intervals, then answer how much time is covered and where the gaps are. The approach is sort then sweep. Sort by start. Walk the intervals keeping the current merged interval: if the next one starts at or before the current end it overlaps or touches, so extend the end to the larger of the two ends; otherwise push the current interval and start a new one. Sorting dominates, so O(n log n), with O(n) extra space for the output.

Be precise about boundaries before coding. These intervals are half-open, [start, end), which composes without double counting: [1, 4) and [4, 5) touch and merge into [1, 5), and the length of an interval is end - start. Empty intervals (start >= end) are dropped on input instead of corrupting the sweep. Taking the max of the ends matters: a long interval can swallow later short ones ([1, 10) then [2, 3)), and assigning the end instead of maximising it would shrink the result.

Gaps are the complement inside a window [lo, hi): walk the merged list and emit the space before the first interval, between consecutive ones, and after the last, clipped to the window. Verification uses a different representation: mark covered unit cells in a boolean array and read off the maximal runs. The program compares the sweep with that bitmap oracle on 3,000 random interval sets, including empty, nested, touching and duplicate intervals. Follow-ups worth naming: inserting into an already merged set in O(n), and finding the maximum overlap count with a sweep over sorted start and end events.
Fix the boundary convention first, discard empty intervals, sort, maximise ends, compute gaps by clipping the complement to the window, and test against an independent bitmap representation.

merged = [(1, 6), (8, 12), (15, 18)], covered = 12
gaps in [0, 20) = [(0, 1), (6, 8), (12, 15), (18, 20)]
touching merges: [(1, 5)]
nested keeps the longer end: [(1, 10)]
empty and reversed intervals are dropped: [(1, 2)]
no intervals: gaps = [(0, 5)]
matches the bitmap oracle and covered + gaps = window on 3000 random sets: true
challenge: Intersect two merged interval lists (for example the hours when both venue A and venue B are open) with a two-pointer sweep in O(a + b). Check against the bitmap AND of the two sets on random inputs.
question: What does the sweep do when the next interval starts at or before the current merged end?
correct: It extends the current interval's end to the larger of the two ends; copying the new end could shrink it
wrong: It starts a new interval at that point, because every overlap marks a separate session
It discards the next interval, since the current merged interval already covers its start
It sorts the intervals again, because an overlap means the input order was wrong
reasoning: An overlapping interval might end earlier than the current one (nested), so copying its end could shrink the merged interval. max keeps the larger extent.

quiz.question: With half-open intervals, what happens to [1, 4) and [4, 5)?
quiz.correct: They touch and merge into [1, 5), with no gap and no double counting
wrong: They stay separate because 4 appears twice, once at each interval boundary
They merge into [1, 4), since the second interval is absorbed by the first
They overlap by one unit, so the merged length is counted as six
quiz.reasoning: In [start, end) form the point 4 belongs only to the second interval, so the two cover [1, 5) exactly.

quiz.question: Why is the merge sort step required?
quiz.correct: After sorting by start, any interval overlapping the current one is adjacent, so one sweep suffices
wrong: It removes empty intervals, because intervals whose start equals their end sort to the front
It is only needed for nested intervals, since other overlaps are found in input order
It reduces the memory used, because the sorted output can overwrite the input in place
quiz.reasoning: Without sorting, an overlapping interval might appear anywhere later in the list, forcing quadratic comparisons.

quiz.question: How are the gaps in a window [lo, hi) computed?
quiz.correct: Emit the space before the first interval, between consecutive ones and after the last, clipped to the window
wrong: Subtract the covered time from the window length, which also gives the position of each gap
Sort the gaps by length and keep the largest ones that still fit inside the window
Invert the sort order of the intervals and merge them again to obtain the free space
quiz.reasoning: The gaps are the complement of the union within the window, which needs the positions, not just the total length.

quiz.question: Why verify against a bitmap instead of a second merge implementation?
quiz.correct: An independent representation can expose mistakes in boundary logic that a similar algorithm would repeat
wrong: Bitmaps are always faster than a sweep, so the oracle also serves as the real implementation
Merge implementations cannot be tested directly, so a different structure has to stand in
The bitmap avoids sorting for large coordinates, which is what makes the sweep slow
quiz.reasoning: The oracle should be obviously correct and structurally different. Marking cells and reading runs shares no logic with the sweep.

title: Drill: union-find to cluster correlated instruments
body: Problem: given pairs of instruments whose correlation exceeds a threshold, group them into clusters, and answer "are A and B in the same cluster?" quickly as pairs arrive. A union-find (disjoint-set) structure does this in near-constant time per operation. Each element has a parent index; a root is its own parent. find follows parents to the root; union links one root under the other. Two optimisations give the near-constant bound: path compression (after a find, point every visited node directly at the root) and union by size (attach the smaller tree under the larger). Together the amortised cost per operation is the inverse Ackermann function, below 5 for any practical n.

In Rust, write find iteratively. A recursive find on a degenerate chain of a million nodes would overflow the stack, and without union by size such chains are easy to build. The iterative version makes two passes: the first walks to the root; the second walks the path again and rewrites each parent pointer to the root. The structure also tracks the number of components (decrementing on each successful union) and the size of each tree, which gives cluster sizes for free. union returns whether it merged anything, so callers can detect redundant edges (an edge inside an existing cluster).

The correlation example turns a threshold matrix into edges and clusters them: AAPL-MSFT-GOOG form a technology cluster, XOM-CVX an energy cluster, and JPM-BAC a bank cluster. Components are reported in a canonical form (sorted members sorted by first member) so output is deterministic. Verification builds the same partition by breadth-first search on 1,500 random graphs and compares canonical forms. Know the alternatives: BFS or DFS answer the same question for a static graph, but union-find wins when edges arrive over time and you must answer connectivity online.
Use iterative find with path compression, union by size, track component count, return whether a union merged anything, canonicalise output for comparison, and verify against a graph-search oracle.

Compare with a simple Prim's algorithm on random complete graphs of up to 8 nodes. This is how you would build a minimum-spanning-tree view of a correlation-distance matrix.
question: Why does union-find implement find iteratively with path compression?
correct: Iteration avoids stack overflow on deep chains, and path compression flattens the tree for later finds
wrong: Recursion is not allowed in Rust, so any function that follows parents must use a loop
Path compression changes which element is the root, so the cluster's name is updated
It makes union return a different cluster, because finds rewrite the sets they visit
reasoning: A long chain would overflow a recursive find. Compression points every node on the path at the root, so the next find from any of them takes one step.

quiz.question: What does union by size accomplish?
quiz.correct: It attaches the smaller tree under the larger root, keeping trees shallow so finds stay fast
wrong: It sorts the elements by size so the largest cluster can be found in constant time
It makes union O(n), because the smaller tree is copied element by element
It removes the need for path compression, since the trees can never grow deeper
quiz.reasoning: Without a balancing rule, unions can build tall chains. Union by size (or rank) bounds the height at O(log n); combined with path compression the cost is nearly constant.

quiz.question: Why does union return a bool?
quiz.correct: It says whether two different clusters were merged, which detects redundant edges and counts components
wrong: It reports whether the two elements are equal, so equal elements are never merged
It signals an error in the input, such as an index that is outside the structure
It is required by the borrow checker, which refuses a method that returns nothing
quiz.reasoning: A false return means both elements already shared a root. Kruskal's algorithm uses exactly this signal to skip edges that would form a cycle.

quiz.question: When is union-find a better choice than a breadth-first search for connectivity?
quiz.correct: When edges arrive over time and connectivity queries must be answered online without re-traversing the graph
wrong: When the graph is static and only one query is needed, since building the structure is cheap
When the graph has no edges at all, because every element is then its own cluster
Never; BFS is always faster, because a traversal visits each node only once
quiz.reasoning: Union-find processes each new edge in near-constant time and answers queries immediately. For a single static query a traversal is just as good.

quiz.question: How are clusters reported deterministically?
quiz.correct: Members are sorted within each cluster and clusters by their first member, giving a canonical form
wrong: By the iteration order of the hash map, which is stable for a fixed set of keys
By the root index of each cluster, which is the same whatever the order of the unions
By the size of each cluster only, with ties broken by insertion time
quiz.reasoning: Root indices depend on the sequence of unions, so they are not stable identifiers. A canonical form makes tests and output reproducible.

title: Drill: an arena-indexed trie for symbol prefix search
body: Problem: given a universe of tickers, support insert, exact lookup, "how many symbols start with AM?" and "list the first ten symbols starting with AM" in time proportional to the length of the prefix, not the number of symbols. A trie stores one node per distinct prefix; each edge is one character. Walking a prefix is O(L) regardless of how many words exist, and the words with that prefix are exactly the terminal nodes below the node you reach. A sorted Vec with binary search can answer prefix queries too, but a trie also answers counts for free and updates incrementally.

In Rust, store all nodes in a Vec and refer to them by index (an arena) instead of boxing children: Box<Node> trees mean one allocation per node and awkward borrows. Each node holds a BTreeMap<u8, usize> from the next byte to a child index, a terminal flag, and a words counter, the number of stored words passing through the node, maintained at insert time. With that counter count_prefix is O(L) and does not traverse the subtree. Because BTreeMap iterates in key order, a depth-first walk yields words in lexicographic order, which is what autocomplete wants. Only ASCII words are accepted so that a byte per edge is a character per edge; insert rejects the rest with an error instead of splitting a UTF-8 sequence.

Be ready to discuss the trade-offs. A BTreeMap per node is easy and ordered but heavy in memory; a fixed [u32; 26] array per node is faster and larger; a compressed (radix) trie merges single-child chains. The tests compare every query with a naive sorted Vec<String> filtered by starts_with, over 2,000 random word sets on a tiny alphabet so prefixes collide constantly, including the empty prefix, absent prefixes and duplicate inserts. Duplicates must not inflate the counters, so insert first checks contains.
Name the O(L) bounds, use an index arena, keep per-node counters consistent under duplicate inserts, validate ASCII, return results in lexicographic order, and test against a sorted-list oracle.

question: Why does each trie node keep a words counter?
correct: It records how many stored words pass through the node, so count_prefix takes O(prefix length) without a subtree walk
wrong: It stores the total length of all words below the node, which is needed to build the output
It prevents duplicate children, since a node refuses a second edge with the same byte
It orders the children lexicographically, so the results come out in alphabetical order
reasoning: The counter is updated once per insert along the path, which trades a little write cost for constant-time-per-character counting queries.

quiz.question: Why are nodes stored in a Vec and referenced by index?
quiz.correct: An arena avoids one allocation per node and awkward boxed ownership, and indices are trivially copyable
wrong: Rust does not allow Box in a struct, so every recursive node has to live in a Vec
Indices make lookups O(1) for every character, whatever the number of stored words
It guarantees the trie is balanced, because index order keeps the depth of each branch equal
quiz.reasoning: Arena indexing keeps nodes contiguous and sidesteps borrow-checker friction in recursive structures.

quiz.question: Why does insert check contains before updating counters?
quiz.correct: A duplicate insert must not increment the words counters, or count_prefix would over-report
wrong: Because the children map forbids duplicate keys, so a second insert of a word would panic
To keep the arena small, since a duplicate would otherwise allocate a whole new chain of nodes
Because duplicate words are an error, and the caller must be told with a failed result
quiz.reasoning: Counters represent distinct words. Returning early for an existing word keeps them consistent.

quiz.question: What is the time cost of with_prefix for a prefix of length L returning r words of average length m?
quiz.correct: O(L + total size of the explored subtree), roughly O(L + r * m) when the result is not limited by a small cap
wrong: O(n) in the number of all words always, because every stored word has to be examined
O(1) regardless of the prefix, because the node for a prefix is found by a stored table
O(L^2), since each character of the prefix is compared with all of the others in turn
quiz.reasoning: Reaching the prefix node takes L steps. Enumerating the matching words then costs time proportional to the part of the trie below it.

quiz.question: Why reject non-ASCII input in this trie?
quiz.correct: Edges are single bytes, so a multi-byte UTF-8 character would be split across edges and break ordering
wrong: ASCII characters are faster to hash, so the BTreeMap lookups stay cheap for every edge
Rust strings cannot contain non-ASCII text, so such input would be invalid anyway
BTreeMap only accepts ASCII keys, so any other byte value would make an insert fail
quiz.reasoning: Using chars as edge labels is an alternative, but bytes keep nodes small. Validating the input makes the byte model correct.

title: Drill: bit flags, lowest-set-bit tricks and safe shifts
body: Order flags, permission masks and feed bitmaps all pack booleans into integer bits, and interviews love the handful of identities that manipulate them. Test a flag with x & FLAG != 0, set it with x | FLAG, clear it with x & !FLAG and toggle it with x ^ FLAG. Two identities do most of the remaining work: x & (x - 1) clears the lowest set bit, and x & x.wrapping_neg() isolates it. Repeating the first until x is zero counts bits (Kernighan's method) or visits each set bit in turn; the standard library gives the same answers as count_ones and trailing_zeros, which compile to single instructions on modern CPUs.

Three classic problems fall out. A power of two has exactly one set bit, so x != 0 && x & (x - 1) == 0 (the zero check also protects x - 1 from underflow). The number of bits to flip to turn a into b is (a ^ b).count_ones(). And in a list where every value appears twice except one, XOR-ing everything leaves the odd one out, because x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, in O(n) time and O(1) space. Field extraction is (x >> shift) & mask, and rotating by four swaps the nibbles of a byte.

Shifts need care in Rust. Shifting a u32 by 32 or more is an overflow: it panics in debug builds and is a compile error for constants, so computing a mask as (1 << width) - 1 breaks when width is 32; checked_shl returns None instead. Right shift on signed integers is arithmetic (it copies the sign bit), so -8 >> 1 is -4, while shifting the same bits as unsigned is logical and gives a huge positive number. Know which one you want. The program verifies each trick against a straightforward loop over all 16-bit values.

Guard x - 1 against zero, choose checked or wrapping shifts on purpose, remember arithmetic versus logical right shift, prefer the standard bit methods in production, and verify tricks against simple loops.

question: What does x & (x - 1) do, and why must x be non-zero?
correct: It clears the lowest set bit; for x = 0 the subtraction underflows (a panic in debug builds), so zero is handled first
wrong: It sets the lowest clear bit; zero is fine, because 0 - 1 simply wraps around to all ones
It isolates the highest set bit; zero returns 1, since the highest bit of zero is bit zero
It reverses the bits of x; zero is fine, because reversing no set bits changes nothing
reasoning: Subtracting 1 flips the lowest set bit and every zero below it, so AND-ing with x clears exactly that bit. For x = 0 there is no set bit and x - 1 underflows.

quiz.question: How does XOR find the one value that appears once in a list where every other value appears twice?
quiz.correct: x ^ x = 0 and x ^ 0 = x, so XOR-ing everything cancels the pairs and leaves the single value
wrong: It sorts the list internally, then compares neighbouring values until one has no equal
It sums the values and subtracts twice the sum of the distinct ones to get the odd value
It only works when the single value is the largest, because XOR keeps the highest bit
quiz.reasoning: XOR is commutative and associative, so the order does not matter and each pair cancels itself.

quiz.question: Why is 1u32 << 32 a problem and how do you avoid it?
quiz.correct: A shift by the type's width or more overflows (panic in debug); use checked_shl, which returns None
wrong: It evaluates to 0 silently in every build, so the result is safe but useless as a mask
It silently evaluates to u32::MAX, because the shift fills every bit position
It is always a compile error, even when the shift amount is only known at run time
quiz.reasoning: Rust does not define shifts by 32 or more for u32. checked_shl, wrapping_shl and overflowing_shl make the behaviour explicit.

quiz.question: What does -8i32 >> 1 evaluate to, and why?
quiz.correct: -4, because right shift on signed integers is arithmetic and copies the sign bit
wrong: 2147483644, because the shift is logical and fills the top bit with zero
-16, because a right shift of a negative number multiplies by two
0, because shifting any negative value right by one clears its sign
quiz.reasoning: To get a logical shift, cast to an unsigned type first: (-8i32 as u32) >> 1 gives 2147483644.

quiz.question: How many bits must be flipped to turn 29 into 15?
quiz.correct: 2, because 29 ^ 15 = 0b10010, which has two set bits
wrong: 3, because 29 and 15 differ in the three lowest bits
5, because 29 needs five bits and every one must change
4, because 15 has four set bits and 29 has none of them
quiz.reasoning: The number of differing bits is the population count of the XOR: 29 is 0b11101, 15 is 0b01111, and they differ in bits 1 and 4.

title: Drill: quickselect, percentiles and why duplicates hurt Lomuto
body: Problem: find the k-th smallest value (the median, the 99th percentile) of an unsorted array without sorting it. Sorting is O(n log n). Quickselect is O(n) on average: pick a pivot, partition the array so smaller values are on the left and larger on the right, then recurse into only the side that contains position k. Because it throws away one side each round, the expected work is n + n/2 + n/4 + ... = O(2n). The standard library already ships this as slice::select_nth_unstable, which reorders the slice so that element k is in its sorted position, everything before it is no larger and everything after no smaller; use it in production and know how to write it for interviews.

The classic Lomuto partition scans once, moving elements smaller than the pivot to the front. It is easy to write and has a trap: when many elements equal the pivot, none counts as smaller, the pivot lands at the left edge and only one element is eliminated per round, giving O(n^2). An array of all-equal prices is not exotic in tick data. Median-of-three pivot selection protects against already-sorted input but not against duplicates. The fix is a three-way (Dutch national flag) partition into less than, equal to and greater than the pivot: the whole equal block is finished at once, so an all-equal array costs one pass. The program counts comparisons to show this: on 2,000 equal values Lomuto needs about 1.5 million comparisons and the three-way version about 2,000.

For guaranteed O(n) worst case the technique is median of medians (group by five, take the median of the group medians as the pivot), which is rarely worth its constant factor; introselect, used by many standard libraries, falls back to it only when quickselect misbehaves. Percentile definitions again need a stated convention: with nearest rank the index is ceil(n x p) - 1 in 0-based terms, computed in integers. The tests compare both quickselects with a full sort on 3,000 random arrays full of duplicates.

Choose three-way partitioning when duplicates are plausible, state average and worst-case costs, use select_nth_unstable in real code, define the percentile convention, and compare with a sorted oracle.
expectedStdout:
median of [9, 1, 8, 2, 7, 3, 6, 4, 5]: lomuto 5, three-way 5
percentiles of 1..=100: p50 = Some(50), p95 = Some(95), p99 = Some(99)
percentile of an empty slice: None
2000 equal values: lomuto 1500499 comparisons, three-way 2000
2000 sorted values: lomuto 3975 comparisons, three-way 2000 (both linear thanks to median-of-three)
both quickselects and select_nth_unstable match a full sort on 3000 duplicate-heavy arrays: true
challenge: Write percentile_f64(values: &mut [f64], per_10000) -> Option<f64> using select_nth_unstable_by with f64::total_cmp and the nearest-rank convention, returning None for an empty slice or any NaN. Check it against sorting for several percentiles on random data.
question: Why is a Lomuto partition quadratic on an array of identical values?
correct: No element is strictly smaller than the pivot, so the pivot lands at the edge and each round removes only one element
wrong: Identical values cannot be compared, so the loop never decides which side each belongs to
The pivot is chosen at random and is always wrong, so the partition cannot make progress
Lomuto cannot partition integers, because its scan assumes the values are distinct floats
reasoning: With all values equal, the loop moves nothing to the left of the pivot. The remaining range shrinks by one per round, so the total work is about n^2/2 comparisons.

quiz.question: How does a three-way partition fix the duplicate problem?
quiz.correct: It groups values into less than, equal to and greater than the pivot, so the whole equal block is finished in one pass
wrong: It sorts the array first, so the partition then needs only a single binary search for the pivot
It removes duplicates before partitioning, so the equal values are simply discarded
It always picks the maximum as pivot, so the rest of the array falls to the left side
quiz.reasoning: If k falls inside the equal block the answer is the pivot immediately; otherwise the search continues in the smaller or larger side without the equal elements.

quiz.question: What does select_nth_unstable guarantee about the slice afterwards?
quiz.correct: Element k is in its sorted position, with nothing greater before it and nothing smaller after it
wrong: The whole slice is fully sorted, so afterwards any element can be found by a binary search
Only the first k elements are sorted, and the remaining elements keep their original order
The slice is unchanged and a copy holding the k-th element is returned to the caller
quiz.reasoning: It reorders in place and does not fully sort, which is why it is cheaper than sorting the whole slice.

quiz.question: What is the expected cost of quickselect with good pivots and why?
quiz.correct: About 2n comparisons: n + n/2 + n/4 + ... because each round discards a constant fraction of the remaining range
wrong: n log n comparisons, the same as sorting, because every round must sort the part it keeps
n^2 comparisons in the average case, since each round only removes a single element
log n comparisons, because each round halves the range and the answer needs no scan
quiz.reasoning: Only the side containing the target is kept, so the work forms a geometric series.

quiz.question: In nearest-rank terms, which element is the 95th percentile of 100 values?
quiz.correct: The 95th smallest, because rank = ceil(100 x 0.95) = 95
wrong: The 96th smallest, because rank = ceil(100 x 0.95) + 1 = 96
The average of the 95th and 96th, because the rank falls between them
The 5th smallest, because the percentile counts from the top of the list
quiz.reasoning: Nearest rank picks an actual observation at position ceil(n p). Other conventions interpolate and may give different numbers.

title: Drill: exact probabilities with u128 fractions, combinatorics and DP
body: Probability questions in interviews reward exactness and a second route to the same answer. This drill computes probabilities as exact fractions of integers: a Frac holds a numerator and denominator in u128 and reduces by the greatest common divisor, so 6/36 prints as 1/6 and equality comparisons are exact. Counting outcomes is a combinatorics problem. The binomial coefficient C(n, k) is built iteratively as result = result x (n - i) / (i + 1); after each step the value is itself a binomial coefficient, so the division is exact and no fractions appear. Every multiplication uses checked_mul, so overflow produces None instead of a silent wrong answer.

Three techniques cover most questions. Complement counting: P(at least one six in 4 rolls) is easier as 1 - (5/6)^4 = 671/1296 than by adding cases. Dynamic programming over counts: the number of ways n dice sum to s is built one die at a time by adding each face to every previous sum, giving exact integer counts that divide by 6^n; the sum of three dice is at least 15 in 20 of 216 ways (10 + 6 + 3 + 1 for sums 15 to 18), which is 5/54. Direct combinatorics: exactly two aces in a five-card hand is C(4, 2) C(48, 3) / C(52, 5). A conditional probability such as "two children, at least one is a boy" is solved by listing the four equally likely families and conditioning: 1/3, not 1/2.

The habit that matters is cross-checking. Each closed-form answer is compared with brute-force enumeration of the sample space (all 1,296 four-roll outcomes, all two-child families) and the dice DP is compared with enumeration for up to five dice. u128 holds up to about 3.4 x 10^38, so 6^n fits only up to n = 49 dice, and choose(200, 100) correctly reports overflow. Be aware that the intermediate product can overflow even when the final coefficient would fit, which is why the comment on the loop matters. Floats appear only for display.
Use exact integer fractions, reduce them, count by complement, DP or combinatorics, cross-check against enumeration, and make overflow explicit with checked arithmetic.

C(52, 5) = 2598960

challenge: Exact coin-flip probabilities: using choose and Frac, compute the probability of exactly 5 heads in 10 fair flips (63/256) and of at least 8 heads (7/128). Verify both by enumerating all 1,024 sequences.
solutionStdout: P(5 heads in 10) = 63/256, P(at least 8 heads) = 7/128
question: Why does choose build the coefficient as result * (n - i) / (i + 1)?
correct: After each step the value is itself a binomial coefficient, so the division is exact
wrong: Because dividing first is always faster, and the final answer is then rounded to an integer
Because multiplication cannot overflow in u128, so the order of the operations does not matter
Because it avoids the checked_mul call, which would otherwise make the loop too slow
reasoning: Multiplying first keeps every intermediate an integer: C(n, i) x (n - i) / (i + 1) = C(n, i + 1). Dividing first could truncate and give a wrong result.

quiz.question: Why compute P(at least one six in four rolls) as 1 - (5/6)^4?
quiz.correct: The complement (no six at all) is a single product, while summing the one-to-four-six cases is long
wrong: Because probabilities must be subtracted from 1 before they can be compared with a count
Because the complement is always smaller, so its fraction needs less precision to store
Because (5/6)^4 is an integer, so no fraction has to be reduced by the gcd afterwards
quiz.reasoning: "At least one" events are naturally the complement of "none". The enumeration check confirms 671 of 1,296 outcomes contain a six.

quiz.question: Why is P(both boys | at least one boy) equal to 1/3 and not 1/2?
quiz.correct: Conditioning removes the girl-girl family, leaving three equally likely families BB, BG and GB, of which one is BB
wrong: Because boys are more common than girls, so the condition shifts the odds towards two boys
Because the second child is independent of the first, so the answer stays at one half
Because the answer should always be 1/2 whenever two outcomes are equally likely
quiz.reasoning: The condition "at least one boy" is information about the pair, not about a particular child, so the sample space shrinks to three outcomes.

quiz.question: What does choose(200, 100) return and why?
quiz.correct: None, because the checked multiplication detects that the intermediate values exceed u128
wrong: A wrapped-around wrong number, because u128 multiplication silently overflows
It panics on overflow in release builds, because checked_mul aborts the program
0, because the coefficient is too large to be represented and is clamped to zero
quiz.reasoning: C(200, 100) is about 9 x 10^58, far above u128. checked_mul turns that into a visible None instead of silent wrap-around.

quiz.question: Why is the result of a closed-form probability compared with enumeration?
quiz.correct: Two independent routes agreeing is strong evidence against a counting mistake, the usual error in these problems
wrong: Enumeration is always faster than a formula, so it is used to produce the final answer
Closed forms are never exact, so they are only used to approximate the enumerated count
Rust requires every formula to be enumerated, otherwise the compiler rejects the probability
quiz.reasoning: Counting arguments are easy to get subtly wrong. A brute-force check over a small sample space catches it.
